ax-0ac0175595.story: A schematic of probabilistic error cancellation on one qubit: a state |ψ⟩ passes a gate U and a noise channel (red), then a correction drawn at random from the Pauli operations I, X, Y and Z (green), and is measured. Each outcome is weighted by the sign and size of quasi-probabilities q, and averaging N samples gives the mitigated estimate; the 'inverse' channel is a sum of Pauli operations with real, possibly negative, weights. It is Figure 1 of arXiv 2607.25704 by Yang, Kashefi and Ollivier on verifiable blind error cancellation. Notice that nothing is encoded: noise is cancelled statistically, at a sampling cost.

It is Fig. 5 of arXiv 2608.17023 (August 2026) by Jason Ludmir, Aditya Ranjan, Nicholas S. DiBrita, Jason Han and Tirthak Patel, on running bivariate bicycle error-correcting codes on neutral atoms. There, acousto-optic deflector (AOD) tweezers carry atoms between fixed spatial-light-modulator (SLM) traps; this return move is called resync.

ax-4b239c22bd.story: A cartoon overview (drawing, not hardware): a surface-code qubit lattice, a classical controller sending microwave pulses, a robot "learning agent" turning knobs, and a decoder matching detection events. It comes from Sivak, Morvan, Broughton and co-authors, paper "Reinforcement Learning Control of Quantum Error Correction". The idea: the error-detection events of the surface code, normally used only by the decoder, also serve as a learning signal, so a reinforcement-learning agent keeps adjusting the control parameters during computation.

ax-4bb017ebbe.story: A multi-panel figure of real micrographs: false-coloured scanning-electron images, a dark-field optical image and a tilted cross-section of a microfabricated surface-electrode ion trap with built-in optical waveguides and grating couplers. It comes from M. Ivory and co-authors at Sandia National Laboratories, paper "Integrated optical addressing of a trapped ytterbium ion". Instead of free-space laser beams, light runs through waveguides inside the chip and exits upward through gratings to reach the ion; notice the overhanging electrodes and the loading hole cut through the chip.

Each bar alternates laser (Raman) gate periods with state preparation and mid-circuit measurement; notice how every added syndrome-extraction cycle lengthens the circuit, reaching about half a second.

ax-4eff14eadc.story: A four-panel drawing of how a conveyor-belt magneto-optical trap (MOT) for molecules works. Panel (a) is the level scheme with two laser frequencies; (b) shows four frequency components, a quarter-wave plate and a mirror; (c) shows the components adding into two slowly moving standing waves, the 'conveyor belts'; (d) shows how the Zeeman shift in the field gradient makes each side of the trap favour one belt. From arXiv paper 2409.18090 by Grace K. Li, Christian Hallas and John M. Doyle. Notice that the belts here trap and compress molecules; they do not carry atoms between zones as in continuous reloading of atom arrays.

Exchange between donor electrons falls off steeply with distance; coupling through intermediate electrons (superexchange) lets two donor qubits sit farther apart. Notice the two strong central lobes where the mediator electrons sit, and the nodal line in |Ψ2|².

ax-56715701be.story: Four-panel figure of renders and sketches of the chip-scale Gaussian boson sampling system Zhiyuan 3.0: the equipment cabinet with TuringQ logos, labelled controller, source, detection and processor units; sketches of earlier delay-loop time-multiplexing schemes and boson-sampling applications; stacked waveguide layers with coiled delay lines; and the photonic chip with its interferometer and gold electrodes. From arXiv paper 2609.11922 by Yu-Xuan Fu, He-Yu Shen, Ke-Ming Hu and co-authors. It is Figure 13 of the arXiv paper "Breakeven demonstration of quantum low-density parity-check codes" by Edwin Tham and co-authors. Duration grows linearly with the number of cycles, and the dashed guides are cycles times cycle time; notice that the largest code, BB[[30,4,5]], needs about half a second for six cycles, the time cost of repeated error correction.

From 'Josephson diode effect in multichannel Rashba nanowires: Role of inter-subband coupling' by Ardamon Sten and Sudeep Kumar Ghosh (arXiv 2604.19385). The zero-energy crossing is the signature sought for Majorana-based qubits; a shifted, asymmetric spectrum underlies the diode effect.

ax-cc24161dd7.story: A drawn gate schematic, not a photograph: two views of a 'tetron' qubit made of two parallel topological nanowires joined by a superconducting backbone, with Majorana zero modes numbered 1–4 at the wire ends and surrounding gate electrodes. It is Figure 2 of "Roadmap to fault tolerant quantum computation using topological qubit arrays" by Aasen, Aghaee, Alam and co-authors. The black loops show how gates connect pairs of Majorana modes through quantum dots to measure their joint parity (XX or ZZ), the basic operation of a measurement-based topological qubit.

Each shows two triangular patches tiled with red, green and blue faces (the code's checks) on a square grid: yellow data qubits, coloured auxiliary qubits, grey inactive ones; circled plus signs mark controlled-NOT gates, black boxes resets and measurements. It is Figure 15 of arXiv 2412.14256, 'Scaling and logic in the color code on a superconducting quantum processor' (Lacroix, Bourassa and co-authors). ax-cfda36acdf.story: Simulation drawings and a plot, not photographs, from supplementary Figure S3 of "Cryogenic ion trap system for high-fidelity near-field microwave-driven quantum logic" by Weber, Löschnauer, Wolf and co-authors. Panels show COMSOL models of a surface-electrode ion-trap chip with its RF feed and a meandering on-chip microwave line, a variant with a planar spiral inductor, an RF-line circuit, and a plot of where the microwave field minimum sits. The on-chip line serves laser-free near-field microwave gates, which drive the ions with the microwave field gradient near the chip rather than with laser beams. An impedance mismatch up the RF line moves that minimum; the inductor (squares) keeps it steady.

(A) The advection equation, which carries a quantity along d coordinates, is mapped onto continuous-variable (CV) light: x becomes the x̂ quadrature, ∂/∂x becomes ip̂, and each coordinate becomes a separate light pulse in time. (B) The workflow: one-mode squeezed, two-mode squeezed or multi-mode cluster-state pulses each receive a displacement, homodyne detection samples their quadratures, then statistics follow. It is Figure 1 of arXiv 2606.00581, 'Analog photonic simulator for large-scale transport' (Zhao, Su and co-authors). Notice why it works: a Hamiltonian linear in p̂ just displaces each pulse, so advection needs only displacements, a Gaussian operation.

ax-ee12c46cd1.story: Schematic drawing of a quantum-key-distribution link built on a single trapped ion. From arXiv paper 2609.25795 by Jonas Meiers, Christian Haen, Max Bergerhoff and colleagues. On Alice's side a calcium ion in a Paul trap emits 854 nm photons, collected by a high-aperture objective; a quantum frequency converter shifts them to 1550 nm for 25 km of fibre, and Bob converts them back and analyses their polarisation with superconducting nanowire detectors. A second 25 km fibre carries timing and heralding signals. Notice the converters at both ends: they let an ion's visible-range photon travel telecom fibre.

Fedyanin (Wikimedia Commons, 2018-02-21). It shows where a colour centre emits fastest, along the p–n junction, and the g(2) dip that signals single photons.
en-02188043ee.title: File:Enhancing the brightness of electrically driven single-photon sources using color centers in silicon carbide (Figure 3).png

en-025a69c7f5.attribution: “DC Squid01” by Adwaele, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DC_Squid01.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-025a69c7f5.creator: Adwaele
en-025a69c7f5.story: A flat colour drawing, not real hardware, of a direct-current superconducting quantum interference device (DC SQUID): a blue superconducting ring whose halves meet at two weak links, a and b, acting as Josephson junctions, with magnetic field B threading the loop, a bias current i and a voltmeter V. Drawn by Adwaele and dated 18 April 2012 on Wikimedia Commons; the credit reads 'Made by SliteWrite'. The voltage across the ring changes with the magnetic flux through it, which makes the SQUID one of the most sensitive magnetometers and a building block of flux qubits, couplers and amplifiers.
en-025a69c7f5.title: File:DC Squid01.jpg

en-0288ef81ea.attribution: “Bob - DARPA Quantum Network, in the BBN laboratory - December 2001 - P1010005” — Daderot, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bob_-_DARPA_Quantum_Network%2C_in_the_BBN_laboratory_-_December_2001_-_P1010005.jpg
en-0288ef81ea.creator: Daderot
en-0288ef81ea.story: A flash photograph of a crowded vibration-isolated optical table covered in yellow paper: fibre-optic parts, a pink foam-insulated box, black heat-sunk modules, fibre coils and two Ortec delay boxes, with pulse generators, counters and power supplies on a shelf above. Photographed by Daderot (own work); its Commons title names it 'Bob' of the DARPA Quantum Network, in the BBN laboratory, December 2001. It shows the receiving end of an early fibre quantum key distribution link, where single photons from 'Alice' are detected and timed; a partly legible note at the top reads '(Connected to Alice)'.
en-0288ef81ea.title: File:Bob - DARPA Quantum Network, in the BBN laboratory - December 2001 - P1010005.jpg

en-028903babe.attribution: “2DMOTarm” by Eric Magnan, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:2DMOTarm.JPG, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-028903babe.creator: Eric Magnan
en-028903babe.story: A close-up photograph of one arm of a two-dimensional magneto-optical trap (2D MOT): a black cage-rod assembly of beam-shaping optics, including a rotation mount with a degree scale, bolted at an angle onto a stainless-steel vacuum system with ConFlat (CF) flanges. Photographed by Eric Magnan (own work, 18 July 2014); according to its Commons description it creates a beam of rubidium atoms. Such 2D-MOT sources feed cold alkali atoms into the science chamber of neutral-atom quantum computers and sensors; notice the optics and vacuum flanges, not the atoms, which are not visible.
en-028903babe.title: File:2DMOTarm.JPG

en-043ed3355b.attribution: “NIST Demonstrates Sustained Quantum Processing in Step Toward Building Quantum Computers (5941059262)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NIST_Demonstrates_Sustained_Quantum_Processing_in_Step_Toward_Building_Quantum_Computers_%285941059262%29.jpg
en-043ed3355b.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-043ed3355b.story: A close-up photograph of a real ion-trap assembly: a white ceramic (alumina) board whose gold electrodes narrow to a dark slit at left-centre, with gold traces fanning out to wire-bonded components. It is from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), 2011, whose caption says NIST physicists demonstrated sustained, reliable quantum information processing in this trap, with ions held inside the slit, 3.5 millimetres long and 200 micrometres wide. It shows one way ion traps are built: gold electrodes patterned on stacked ceramic wafers, clamped by screws. Notice the many electrode fingers along the slit: separate voltages on them hold and move the ions.
en-043ed3355b.title: File:NIST Demonstrates Sustained Quantum Processing in Step Toward Building Quantum Computers (5941059262).jpg

en-04d67b32e1.attribution: “InP Mult-Project Wafer” by JonathanMarks, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:InP_Mult-Project_Wafer.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-04d67b32e1.creator: JonathanMarks
en-04d67b32e1.story: A colour photograph of a round indium phosphide (InP) wafer, about 3 inches across, with many different gold-metallised chip designs tiled over its blue surface. It was uploaded by JonathanMarks (2017-03-16), whose description calls it a multi-project wafer: start-ups share one wafer to cut development costs about 20 times, an approach pioneered by JePPIX in Eindhoven, The Netherlands. It illustrates the shared-foundry model for photonic integrated circuits; the chips here are general photonic designs, not specifically quantum hardware.
en-04d67b32e1.title: File:InP Mult-Project Wafer.jpg

en-05e413d034.attribution: “Optical fiber connectors-optical patch cable-01ASD” by Asurnipal, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Optical_fiber_connectors-optical_patch_cable-01ASD.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-05e413d034.creator: Asurnipal
en-05e413d034.story: A photograph of an ordinary duplex single-mode fibre patch cable, yellow jackets and blue SC connectors with protective caps, still in its bag with a test card listing insertion and return loss. It was taken by Asurnipal (2019-12-03); the description links it to a fibre-optic splice at the Feldkircher Hut in Vorarlberg, Austria, for the drinking-water supply. This is standard telecom equipment, not quantum hardware, but the same fibres and connectors link photonic modules, where every decibel of loss costs fragile single photons.
en-05e413d034.title: File:Optical fiber connectors-optical patch cable-01ASD.jpg

en-0665061200.attribution: “DEF-TECH Bharat 2026, KTPO Exhibition and Convention Centre, Bangalore 75” by Gpkp, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DEF-TECH_Bharat_2026%2C_KTPO_Exhibition_and_Convention_Centre%2C_Bangalore_75.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-0665061200.creator: Gpkp
en-0665061200.story: Photograph of a benchtop Tektronix AWG70001 arbitrary waveform generator from the AWG70000 series, shown on an exhibitor's table with its screen dark and a coaxial test cable on the lid. Taken by Commons user Gpkp at DEF-TECH Bharat 2026, KTPO Exhibition and Convention Centre, Bangalore. High-sample-rate arbitrary waveform generators of this kind shape the voltage and microwave pulses that drive qubits from room temperature; notice the few high-bandwidth outputs and marker ports rather than the dozens of channels of a dedicated qubit-control rack. It is a general-purpose instrument, not a quantum setup.
en-0665061200.title: File:DEF-TECH Bharat 2026, KTPO Exhibition and Convention Centre, Bangalore 75.jpg

en-072da11476.attribution: “Atom scheme” by Kchinni, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Atom_scheme.gif, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-072da11476.creator: Kchinni
en-072da11476.story: A simple line drawing, not a photograph: a triangular ring optical cavity of three mirrors with a cloud of atoms in one arm, pump beams (Ω_r, Ω_s) arriving at one mirror and light entering (a_in) and leaving (a_out) at another. It was uploaded by Kchinni (2017-12-14) and is described as an experimental implementation of the Dicke model. It shows many atoms coupling collectively to light circulating in a cavity, the basic idea behind atom–cavity interfaces between matter and photons.
en-072da11476.title: File:Atom scheme.gif

en-07a27660e8.attribution: “FZU MBE Veeco PJachimova 24” by Akademie věd České republiky / Czech Academy of Sciences (Pavlína Jáchimová), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FZU_MBE_Veeco_PJachimova_24.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-07a27660e8.creator: Akademie věd České republiky / Czech Academy of Sciences (Pavlína Jáchimová)
en-07a27660e8.story: A wide photograph of a large stainless-steel ultra-high-vacuum system: transfer tubes, flanges, viewports, magnetic transfer rods, a central chamber, pumps and electronics racks. It was taken by Pavlína Jáchimová for the Czech Academy of Sciences (2017-09-27) and shows a Veeco Gen II molecular beam epitaxy system at FZU – Institute of Physics, built to grow monocrystalline semiconductors and heterostructures. This is fabrication equipment, not a quantum computer; machines like it grow the layered III-V materials used for some quantum-dot photon sources and hybrid nanowires.
en-07a27660e8.title: File:FZU MBE Veeco PJachimova 24.jpg

en-07b48bccd5.attribution: “Ion Trap (6099414213)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ion_Trap_%286099414213%29.jpg
en-07b48bccd5.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-07b48bccd5.story: An optical micrograph of a gold surface-electrode ion-trap chip: electrode areas separated by narrow dark gaps; the red sphere is a drawn marker, not an imaged ion. It comes from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), 2011; the caption says the red dot marks where a beryllium ion hovers above the chip, the electrodes hold the ion and generate microwave pulses to manipulate it, and the chip was used in experiments demonstrating record-low error. It shows how a flat microfabricated chip replaces bulky 3D trap electrodes.
en-07b48bccd5.title: File:Ion Trap (6099414213).jpg

en-08e0d65299.attribution: “Single-Photon Detector, created by IBM Almaden Research Center - DARPA Quantum Network, in the BBN laboratory - P1010031” — Daderot, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Single-Photon_Detector%2C_created_by_IBM_Almaden_Research_Center_-_DARPA_Quantum_Network%2C_in_the_BBN_laboratory_-_P1010031.jpg
en-08e0d65299.creator: Daderot
en-08e0d65299.story: A photograph of a beige rack-mounted instrument with two detector channels, each with a fibre "optical input" port, a display and an "APD bias" control, and a checkout sheet dated 4/23/04 lying on top. Photographed by Daderot in May 2004, it is a single-photon detector created by IBM Almaden Research Center for the DARPA Quantum Network, in the BBN laboratory. It shows how early quantum-key-distribution networks counted single photons with avalanche photodiodes: ordinary-looking electronics doing a quantum-communication job.
en-08e0d65299.title: File:Single-Photon Detector, created by IBM Almaden Research Center - DARPA Quantum Network, in the BBN laboratory - P1010031.jpg

en-0a78d05726.attribution: “Cold atoms experiment 03” by Tomasz Kawalec, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cold_atoms_experiment_03.JPG, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-0a78d05726.creator: Tomasz Kawalec
en-0a78d05726.story: A photograph of a crowded optical table: mirrors, waveplates in rotation mounts, polarising beam-splitter cubes and irises on posts, with more lab benches and racks behind. It was taken by Tomasz Kawalec (2015-11-30) and shows part of an experimental setup for cooling (slowing) and trapping rubidium atoms. It illustrates how much free-space optics is needed to prepare laser beams for cold-atom work, the same kind of beam delivery neutral-atom quantum computers rely on; no atoms or vacuum chamber are visible here.
en-0a78d05726.title: File:Cold atoms experiment 03.JPG

en-0b071554c5.attribution: “Cryogenic Photon Number Resolving Detector” by Giorgio Brida from Torino, Italy, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cryogenic_Photon_Number_Resolving_Detector.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-0b071554c5.creator: Giorgio Brida from Torino, Italy
en-0b071554c5.story: A real fisheye photograph of a low-temperature lab: a blue liquid-helium dewar with a cryostat insert, a hose to a gas-handling cabinet with gauges, and a rack of resistance bridges and temperature controllers. It was uploaded by Giorgio Brida from Torino, Italy, on 18 October 2010 under the title "Cryogenic Photon Number Resolving Detector". The detector itself is hidden inside the cryostat; what you see is the cooling and thermometry equipment such detectors need, since photon-number-resolving sensors only work at very low temperatures.
en-0b071554c5.title: File:Cryogenic Photon Number Resolving Detector.jpg

en-0b18b83e20.creator: PieterJanStas
en-0b18b83e20.story: A black-and-white ball-and-stick drawing, not a photograph, of one diamond crystal cell holding a silicon-vacancy centre. It was made by PieterJanStas and dated 17 January 2025. Notice the red silicon atom sitting midway between two dashed empty sites: in this defect one silicon replaces two neighbouring carbon atoms. Colour centres like this trap an electron spin that can be controlled with light, which is why they are studied as qubits and as spin–photon interfaces for quantum networks.
en-0b18b83e20.title: File:Silicon-Vacancy Center.png

en-0c089fc5e0.attribution: “Quantum buffer (5940501733)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Quantum_buffer_%285940501733%29.jpg
en-0c089fc5e0.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-0c089fc5e0.story: A flat diagram of a 'quantum buffer' experiment: a rubidium vapour cell pumped by a laser makes two entangled light beams carrying images, and a second rubidium cell slows one beam down. It was made by A. Marino at the Joint Quantum Institute and published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in 2009. It matters for photonic quantum networks, where entangled light must arrive at the right time; notice that one image travels a centimetre while the other can travel up to 8 metres.
en-0c089fc5e0.title: File:Quantum buffer (5940501733).jpg

en-0cea58a9cb.attribution: “Dewar Quantum Setup” by OJB Quantum, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Dewar_Quantum_Setup.png, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-0cea58a9cb.creator: OJB Quantum
en-0cea58a9cb.story: A computer render of a stainless-steel liquid-helium dewar on wheels with a long dipstick insert and a connector box on top. According to its Commons description it was made in Blender by OJB Quantum and shows a 4 kelvin floor-standing cryostat set-up. Dipping a sample on a stick into a helium dewar is the cheapest way to test superconducting chips at 4 K; note it is a drawing, not a real unit, and it does not show a link between refrigerators.
en-0cea58a9cb.title: File:Dewar Quantum Setup.png

en-0ec97d2b80.attribution: “Superconducting nanowire single-photon detector in the DARPA Quantum Network (BBN) - June 2005 - P1010035” — Daderot, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Superconducting_nanowire_single-photon_detector_in_the_DARPA_Quantum_Network_%28BBN%29_-_June_2005_-_P1010035.jpg
en-0ec97d2b80.creator: Daderot
en-0ec97d2b80.story: A real flash photograph of an open equipment rack: bench instruments, a temperature monitor reading about 3.9 K and 4.3 K, and mid-rack a cryocooler cold head, with an oscilloscope beside it. Daderot took it in June 2005; the caption says it is the superconducting nanowire single-photon detector of the DARPA Quantum Network at BBN, a collaboration of NIST Boulder, the University of Rochester and BBN Technologies. The nanowire chip is not visible; the picture shows the closed-cycle cooling and electronics that keep it superconducting near 4 kelvin.
en-0ec97d2b80.title: File:Superconducting nanowire single-photon detector in the DARPA Quantum Network (BBN) - June 2005 - P1010035.jpg

en-117e3d7f5d.attribution: “Cloud of ultracold atoms levitated in a magneto-optical trap” by Balping, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cloud_of_ultracold_atoms_levitated_in_a_magneto-optical_trap.webp, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-117e3d7f5d.creator: Balping
en-117e3d7f5d.story: A real photograph of a clear glass ultra-high-vacuum cell; the small red glowing spot in the centre is a cloud of cold rubidium-87 atoms held in a magneto-optical trap. It was uploaded by Balping on 6 August 2024; the description says the atoms are later moved into an array of optical tweezers and combined with an optical cavity. Notice the two small mirrors facing each other across the cloud: they form the cavity that makes atoms and photons interact strongly, the basis of an atom–photon interface for quantum networking.
en-117e3d7f5d.title: File:Cloud of ultracold atoms levitated in a magneto-optical trap.webp

en-11a7a6bfa4.attribution: “New Quantum Key System Combines Speed, Distance (5884514248)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:New_Quantum_Key_System_Combines_Speed%2C_Distance_%285884514248%29.jpg
en-11a7a6bfa4.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-11a7a6bfa4.story: A real top-down photograph into an open rack drawer holding the detection stage of the NIST prototype quantum key distribution system, published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (dated 3 February 2004). Per the caption, incoming photons are up-converted from 1310 to 710 nm by one of two NIST-designed converters (right) and then counted by commercial silicon avalanche detectors (the two tall modules, left). The point: frequency conversion lets efficient silicon detectors count telecom-wavelength single photons; notice the fibre coils routing light between modules.
en-11a7a6bfa4.title: File:New Quantum Key System Combines Speed, Distance (5884514248).jpg

en-124f5d6d65.attribution: “Technology photomultiplier tube 212 (52279887037)” — Jan Helebrant, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Technology_photomultiplier_tube_212_%2852279887037%29.jpg
en-124f5d6d65.creator: Jan Helebrant
en-124f5d6d65.story: A real close-up photograph of a glass photomultiplier tube, a classical light detector rather than quantum-computing hardware. Per the caption it is a Czechoslovak photomultiplier made by TESLA – VÚVET, photographed by Jan Helebrant on 11 August 2022. Notice the stack of round metal dynode plates behind the glass: an electron freed at the photocathode window is multiplied at each dynode into a measurable pulse, which is how these tubes count single photons and why they are the older relatives of today's single-photon detectors.
en-124f5d6d65.title: File:Technology photomultiplier tube 212 (52279887037).jpg

en-13eac6ad15.attribution: “1225 site cold cesium atom array” by PrestonHuft, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1225_site_cold_cesium_atom_array.png, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-13eac6ad15.creator: PrestonHuft
en-13eac6ad15.story: A real false-colour fluorescence image, averaged over several shots, of 1225 individual cesium-133 atoms held in a 35 × 35 grid of laser-light optical traps. It was uploaded by PrestonHuft on 10 December 2021; the caption gives a 3-micron spacing, so the whole frame is about 100 × 100 microns, roughly a human hair's cross-section. Each red dot is one atom glowing under weak 852 nm light. It shows the neutral-atom tweezer approach: large, regular arrays of identical atom qubits read out with a camera.
en-13eac6ad15.title: File:1225 site cold cesium atom array.png

en-1536589ce3.attribution: “4 Qubit Chip, 10.1103.PhysRevX.5.021027 (A. Wallraff, 2015)” by Y. Salathé, M. Mondal, M. Oppliger, J. Heinsoo, P. Kurpiers, A. Potočnik, A. Mezzacapo, U. Las Heras, L. Lamata, E. Solano, S. Filipp, and A. Wallraff, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:4_Qubit_Chip%2C_10.1103.PhysRevX.5.021027_%28A._Wallraff%2C_2015%29.png, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-1536589ce3.creator: Y. Salathé, M. Mondal, M. Oppliger, J. Heinsoo, P. Kurpiers, A. Potočnik, A. Mezzacapo, U. Las Heras, L. Lamata, E. Solano, S. Filipp, and A. Wallraff
en-1536589ce3.story: A false-coloured optical micrograph of a 7 mm superconducting chip with four transmon qubits (Q1–Q4), four meandering coplanar-waveguide resonators (R1–R4) and drive, flux and input/output lines; an inset enlarges Q2 with a 700 µm scale bar. It comes from Salathé et al., "Digital Quantum Simulation of Spin Models with Circuit Quantum Electrodynamics", Physical Review X 5, 021027 (2015), with A. Wallraff. It illustrates circuit QED: qubits coupled and read out through microwave resonators. Notice the two capacitor pads per qubit and the grid of holes in the ground plane.
en-1536589ce3.title: File:4 Qubit Chip, 10.1103.PhysRevX.5.021027 (A. Wallraff, 2015).png

en-165b23abf3.attribution: “JEOL Electron Beam Lithography (EBL) (48539839262)” by Simon Fraser University - Communications & Marketing, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:JEOL_Electron_Beam_Lithography_%28EBL%29_%2848539839262%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-165b23abf3.creator: Simon Fraser University - Communications & Marketing
en-165b23abf3.story: A real photograph inside a cleanroom bay of the operator console of a JEOL electron-beam lithography (EBL) system, with a gowned user at the monitors; the electron-beam column itself is out of frame. It was published by Simon Fraser University Communications & Marketing on 12 April 2018. EBL draws nanometre-scale patterns with a focused electron beam and is a standard tool for writing small features in quantum devices, such as Josephson junctions and gate electrodes; here only the control side of the tool is shown.
en-165b23abf3.title: File:JEOL Electron Beam Lithography (EBL) (48539839262).jpg

en-197d275f84.attribution: “Fourier Transform, Beryllium Ions (5883951063)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fourier_Transform%2C_Beryllium_Ions_%285883951063%29.jpg
en-197d275f84.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-197d275f84.story: A real false-colour camera image of the fluorescence from three trapped beryllium ions lit by an ultraviolet laser, released by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (dated 3 May 2005). Colours encode brightness: blue/black is low, red and white high. Each spot is a single ion held in a line by the trap's electric fields, spaced by their mutual repulsion. It shows the basis of trapped-ion readout: an ion that scatters laser light shows up bright on the camera, so its state can be read from the image.
en-197d275f84.title: File:Fourier Transform, Beryllium Ions (5883951063).jpg

en-19effd32a2.attribution: “D0841 092” by Pressestelle PTB, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:D0841_092.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-19effd32a2.creator: Pressestelle PTB
en-19effd32a2.story: A panoramic collage photograph of four large laboratory clocks labelled CS1, CS2, CSF1 and CSF2. Per its record these are the four primary caesium atomic clocks of the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt in Braunschweig, from the PTB press office. It contrasts two caesium beam clocks with two taller caesium fountain clocks, where laser-cooled atoms are tossed upward; notice the size of these room-scale standards. It is a collage of separate shots, and not a chip-scale atomic clock.
en-19effd32a2.title: File:D0841 092.jpg

en-1ada78e3e8.attribution: “FBH DBR Trapezlaser” by FBH/P.Immerz, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FBH_DBR_Trapezlaser.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-1ada78e3e8.creator: FBH/P.Immerz
en-1ada78e3e8.story: A real photograph of three small gold-plated laser submounts next to a 5-euro-cent coin for scale, each carrying a tiny chip with gold wire bonds and engraved FBH serial numbers. It is by FBH/P. Immerz, dated 22 November 2019; the caption identifies them as DBR tapered lasers on screening submounts. These are classical semiconductor lasers, not quantum hardware: the Bragg-grating (DBR) section fixes the wavelength and the tapered section raises output power, the kind of compact, stable source used to cool and control atoms and ions.
en-1ada78e3e8.title: File:FBH DBR Trapezlaser.jpg

en-1dca59b5a1.attribution: “K14FS50 detail1” by PaulT, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:K14FS50_detail1.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-1dca59b5a1.creator: PaulT
en-1dca59b5a1.story: A close-up photograph through the glass of a photomultiplier tube, showing the ladder of curved metal plates (dynodes) that multiply a single photoelectron into a measurable pulse, with their wire leads. The file description names it as a K14FS50 photomultiplier made by Zeiss Jena; it was uploaded to Wikimedia Commons in 2016. Photomultipliers of this kind are used to count the fluorescence photons that reveal a trapped ion's qubit state; notice the staggered dynode geometry, but no ion experiment is shown.
en-1dca59b5a1.title: File:K14FS50 detail1.jpg

en-242b27da3a.attribution: “Non-metallic helium cryostat” by ILK Dresden, Ralf Knörnschild, Moritz Kuhn, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Non-metallic_helium_cryostat.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-242b27da3a.creator: ILK Dresden, Ralf Knörnschild, Moritz Kuhn
en-242b27da3a.story: A photograph of a tall, non-metallic liquid-helium cryostat: a yellowish glass-fibre vessel with a steel head, valves and a pressure gauge, clamped to an aluminium stand. According to its Commons record it was made by ILK Dresden, has under 0.1 W heat load in standby, and gives a low-noise magnetic environment for cooling SQUID sensors. Notice the absence of metal in the vessel wall, which avoids magnetic noise near sensitive superconducting sensors.
en-242b27da3a.title: File:Non-metallic helium cryostat.jpg

en-24bb61213f.attribution: “Acoustooptic modulator-ru” by Ximeg, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Acoustooptic_modulator-ru.svg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-24bb61213f.creator: Ximeg

Drawn by Ximeg (2013) for Wikimedia Commons, with Russian headings. It explains how acousto-optic modulators switch and pulse the laser beams that control trapped ions and neutral atoms; note it is a principle drawing, not an acousto-optic deflector moving atoms.

en-25207579cb.creator: OJB Quantum
en-25207579cb.story: A simple computer render of a closed floor-standing dilution-refrigerator cryostat next to a control cabinet with a monitor; nothing inside is shown. It was made in Blender by OJB Quantum and shared on Wikimedia Commons. It shows the outside of a cryogen-free system of the kind that cools superconducting quantum processors to millikelvin temperatures; it is a stylised render, not a photograph of a real machine.
en-25207579cb.title: File:Floor Standing Cryostat with DR Insert.png

en-255e7aa1fe.attribution: “Paul-Trap” by Arian Kriesch Akriesch 15:58, 14 April 2006 (UTC) (also de:Benutzer:Akriesch ), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Paul-Trap.svg, CC BY 2.5 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5)
en-255e7aa1fe.creator: Arian Kriesch Akriesch 15:58, 14 April 2006 (UTC) (also de:Benutzer:Akriesch )
en-255e7aa1fe.story: Two flat-colour drawings, not photographs, of a cross-section through a three-dimensional quadrupole Paul trap: end-cap electrodes (a), ring electrode (b), an AC source, blue field lines and a red positively charged particle at the centre. They were drawn by Arian Kriesch (Akriesch) on 14 April 2006. Compare panels 1 and 2: the voltage flips, so the squeezing force alternates between directions, and on average the charge is held at the centre. This oscillating-field principle underlies the ion traps used for trapped-ion qubits.
en-255e7aa1fe.title: File:Paul-Trap.svg

en-25bd1adcfd.attribution: “Molecular beam epitaxy” by Yakovlev Viktor, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Molecular_beam_epitaxy.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-25bd1adcfd.creator: Yakovlev Viktor
en-25bd1adcfd.story: Photograph of a lab hall holding a row of several similar ultra-high-vacuum growth machines: tall stainless chambers bristling with flanged ports, on blue cabinets between the yellow posts of an overhead crane. It is filed on Wikimedia Commons as molecular beam epitaxy, photographed by Yakovlev Viktor in May 2014; the lab and maker are not recorded. Molecular-beam epitaxy grows the III-V semiconductor layers used for quantum-dot light sources and hybrid nanowires; notice how a facility runs many such chambers side by side.
en-25bd1adcfd.title: File:Molecular beam epitaxy.jpg

en-26f8d3360d.attribution: “Ytterbium Lattice Atomic Clock (10444764266)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ytterbium_Lattice_Atomic_Clock_%2810444764266%29.jpg
en-26f8d3360d.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-26f8d3360d.story: A photograph of a complete atomic-physics apparatus on an optical table: a large cylindrical vacuum section at left (the atom oven), a central vacuum chamber ringed by copper coils and viewports, and dense laser optics around it. It is NIST's ytterbium optical lattice atomic clock, credited Burrus/NIST and dated 2013. It is a clock, not a quantum computer, but it uses the same toolkit as neutral-atom machines: ultra-high vacuum, magnetic coils and fibre-delivered laser light (note the yellow fibre at lower centre).
en-26f8d3360d.title: File:Ytterbium Lattice Atomic Clock (10444764266).jpg

en-28e6c088ac.attribution: “DILUTION REFRIGERATOR GUST - INSERT - NARA - 17424260” — Martin Brown, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DILUTION_REFRIGERATOR_GUST_-_INSERT_-_NARA_-_17424260.jpg
en-28e6c088ac.creator: Martin Brown
en-28e6c088ac.story: A black-and-white archival photograph of a single dilution-refrigerator insert hanging vertically, with a 0–2.5 cm scale card near the top. It was taken by Martin Brown on 12 November 1974; the title names it a 'GUST' insert held by the US National Archives (NARA). Dilution refrigerators cool superconducting and spin qubits to millikelvin temperatures; notice the pumping tubes and flange plates at the top, the coiled heat-exchanger tubing, and the cylindrical can at the bottom, where the coldest stage normally sits.
en-28e6c088ac.title: File:DILUTION REFRIGERATOR GUST - INSERT - NARA - 17424260.jpg

en-2a48352e35.attribution: “Atomic Clock; Optical Tubes (5940426959)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Atomic_Clock%3B_Optical_Tubes_%285940426959%29.jpg
en-2a48352e35.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-2a48352e35.story: A computer render, not a photograph: two crossing red laser beams form an array of green 'optical tubes', each holding one to three atoms (blue spheres). Credited Baxley/JILA and published by NIST in 2011, it illustrates JILA's strontium atomic clock, where the tubes pack atoms close together to enhance their interaction. The item is a clock, not a quantum computer, but the same optical-lattice trapping by interfering laser beams is used to hold neutral-atom qubits.
en-2a48352e35.title: File:Atomic Clock; Optical Tubes (5940426959).jpg

en-2bf51a3d13.attribution: “Keynote - Entering the Era of Quantum Utility (IBM Research) 11” by IBM Research, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Keynote_-_Entering_the_Era_of_Quantum_Utility_%28IBM_Research%29_11.png, CC BY 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/)
en-2bf51a3d13.creator: IBM Research
en-2bf51a3d13.story: A frame from IBM Research's keynote video 'Entering the Era of Quantum Utility' (IBM Quantum Summit 2023, dated 5 December 2023): a timeline 2016–2023 beside a rendered card reading 'Condor / 1121 qubits / scale | yield'. It is a slide graphic, not a photograph; no chip or qubit layout is visible. It records how IBM presented its Condor superconducting processor, framing the 1,121-qubit count as a step in scale and fabrication yield.
en-2bf51a3d13.title: File:Keynote - Entering the Era of Quantum Utility (IBM Research) 11.png

en-2f48c8da6b.attribution: “Quantum Simulator Crystal (6967363274)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Quantum_Simulator_Crystal_%286967363274%29.jpg
en-2f48c8da6b.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-2f48c8da6b.story: A real fluorescence camera image of a flat crystal of a few hundred trapped ions, each glowing spot one ion, arranged in a triangular lattice about 300 µm across. It comes from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (credit Britton/NIST, 2012) and its quantum simulator. It shows how trapped ions repel each other into an ordered crystal; notice the near-perfect triangular pattern and the arrow marking the crystal's rotation.
en-2f48c8da6b.title: File:Quantum Simulator Crystal (6967363274).jpg

en-303b15065d.attribution: “Alice & Bob Helium Chip” by Nilhope, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Alice_%26_Bob_Helium_Chip.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-303b15065d.creator: Nilhope
en-303b15065d.story: A studio photograph of a gloved hand holding, with tweezers, a dark chip about 1 cm long, above a metal sample package engraved with the Alice & Bob logo. Uploaded by Nilhope in 2024; the title calls it the Alice & Bob Helium chip (which Helium generation cannot be told). It belongs to the cat-qubit approach, where superconducting circuits store information in microwave 'cat states' that resist bit flips and a repetition-type code corrects the rest; notice the central chain of about ten repeated circuit cells.
en-303b15065d.title: File:Alice & Bob Helium Chip.jpg

en-306c39a30d.creator: Philipp Schindler, Daniel Nigg, Thomas Monz, Julio T Barreiro, Esteban Martinez, Shannon X Wang, Stephan Quint, Matthias F Brandl, Volckmar Nebendahl, Christian F Roos, Michael Chwalla, Markus Hennrich and Rainer Blatt
en-306c39a30d.story: A three-panel figure: a photograph of a linear blade Paul trap, plus front and side line drawings of its electrodes. It comes from Schindler, Nigg, Monz and co-authors (NJP 15, 123012, 2013) and shows the trap used in the Blatt group's quantum information experiments in Innsbruck; the endcaps are 5 mm apart and the RF blades 1.6 mm. Radio-frequency voltage on the four blades holds ions radially while the tip electrodes confine them along the axis, lining them up as a string of ion qubits.

en-32e1a0c141.attribution: “Anna at BBN - DARPA Quantum Network - DSCF0006” — Daderot, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Anna_at_BBN_-_DARPA_Quantum_Network_-_DSCF0006.jpg
en-32e1a0c141.creator: Daderot
en-32e1a0c141.story: A photograph of an open equipment rack labelled 'Anna', filled with instruments, controllers, a foam-insulated box and coils of optical fibre. It was taken by Daderot at BBN in January 2004 and filed on Wikimedia Commons under the DARPA Quantum Network. 'Anna' was one of the nodes of that network, which carried quantum key distribution over telecom fibre; notice that the whole node fits in one rack. It shows no trapped ions.
en-32e1a0c141.title: File:Anna at BBN - DARPA Quantum Network - DSCF0006.jpg

en-3339ef2e9a.attribution: “Sr lattice breadboard for the SOC mission” by Stepschiller, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sr_lattice_breadboard_for_the_SOC_mission.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-3339ef2e9a.creator: Stepschiller
en-3339ef2e9a.story: A photograph of a whole laboratory set-up: a compact optics-and-vacuum assembly on a wheeled aluminium frame, laser and electronics units on its lower shelves, flanked by racks of power supplies and oscilloscopes and by a vibration-isolated platform carrying more optics; two people stand in front. Uploaded to Wikimedia Commons by Stepschiller, dated 23 August 2016, as the strontium lattice breadboard for the SOC mission, operated at PTB, Braunschweig. It shows the hardware of a strontium optical lattice clock, whose narrow optical clock transition is the same kind used as a qubit in neutral-atom and trapped-ion quantum computers; the atoms are not visible.
en-3339ef2e9a.title: File:Sr lattice breadboard for the SOC mission.jpg

en-34e9d1e4aa.attribution: “Fluxonium Qubit” by Cottet, N., Xiong, H., Nguyen, L.B. et al., https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fluxonium_Qubit.png, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-34e9d1e4aa.creator: Cottet, N., Xiong, H., Nguyen, L.B. et al.
en-34e9d1e4aa.story: A composite figure: the main panel is an electron micrograph (5 µm scale bar) of a fluxonium superconducting loop, with a circuit schematic and a false-colour optical micrograph of the antenna pads (50 µm scale bar) as insets. It is credited to Cottet, Xiong, Nguyen et al., dated 2021. Fluxonium shunts one small Josephson junction with a long chain of larger junctions acting as a large inductance; notice the ladder-like chains along both sides and the single small junction at top left.
en-34e9d1e4aa.title: File:Fluxonium Qubit.png

en-355ccac248.attribution: “Penning Trap” by Arian Kriesch Akriesch 23:40, 6 April 2006 (UTC), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Penning_Trap.svg, CC BY 2.5 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5)
en-355ccac248.creator: Arian Kriesch Akriesch 23:40, 6 April 2006 (UTC)
en-355ccac248.story: A vector drawing of a Penning trap: end caps (a) and a ring electrode (b) form a static quadrupole electric field (blue), and a surrounding cylindrical coil (c) adds a homogeneous magnetic field (red); a positive particle follows a dashed circular orbit at the centre. Drawn by Arian Kriesch (Akriesch) in April 2006. It illustrates storing charged particles with constant fields only, an alternative to the radio-frequency Paul traps used by most trapped-ion quantum computers.
en-355ccac248.title: File:Penning Trap.svg

en-377393081a.attribution: “FiberCoupling” by Eric Magnan, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FiberCoupling.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-377393081a.creator: Eric Magnan
en-377393081a.story: A studio photograph of a small metal fibre coupler clamped in a black bracket: a threaded fibre-connector socket sits in a plate ringed by adjustment screws marked X and Z. It was uploaded to Wikimedia Commons by Eric Magnan in 2014 and described as a free-space/optical-fibre coupler used in cold-atom experiments. Such couplers carry laser light between the optical table and the vacuum chamber; notice the fine screws that align the fibre to the laser beam. It shows no fibre link between photonic modules.
en-377393081a.title: File:FiberCoupling.jpg

en-37cfee6f48.creator: IBM Research
en-37cfee6f48.story: A frame from IBM Research's keynote video 'Entering the Era of Quantum Utility' (dated 5 December 2023): a rendered close-up of a dark plate engraved with a line drawing of a condor, beside a dot-perforated panel and a faint IBM mark. It is a decorative render, not a photograph, and shows no chip or qubits. It serves only as the emblem of IBM's Condor superconducting processor; for the hardware itself, look elsewhere in the register.
en-37cfee6f48.title: File:Keynote - Entering the Era of Quantum Utility (IBM Research) 13.png

en-39f733cdfb.story: A false-colour fluorescence (photoluminescence) map of a diamond, showing a bright disc about 5 µm across on a dark background, with a 1 µm scale bar and a brightness scale in thousands of counts per second. It comes from Hughes, Zhang, Jin and co-authors (Bleszynski Jayich group), dated 2023: a CVD-grown diamond was irradiated with electrons in one spot, then annealed so vacancies joined nitrogen to form nitrogen-vacancy centres. It shows how these colour-centre spin qubits can be created locally; the bright disc is the irradiated area.
en-39f733cdfb.title: File:Irradiated spot of diamond with high concentration of nitrogen-vacancy centers.jpg

en-3b29441e62.attribution: “Single photon probability question.” by Illusterati, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Single_photon_probability_question..png, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-3b29441e62.creator: Illusterati
en-3b29441e62.story: A flat vector drawing of a thought experiment: a single-photon source sends light to a beam splitter, with Detector A at distance L and Detector B at distance 3L, and a text box asking for the detection probabilities. Made by Illusterati in 2013; it is a question diagram, not a real experiment. It illustrates discrete-variable single photons: each photon is detected at one detector or the other, and in an ideal lossless setup the splitting ratio, not the path length, sets the odds.
en-3b29441e62.title: File:Single photon probability question..png

en-3bc9e3317c.attribution: “SPDC figure mk” by original upload by Neolexx derivative by B. Jankuloski, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:SPDC_figure_mk.png, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-3bc9e3317c.creator: original upload by Neolexx derivative by B. Jankuloski
en-3bc9e3317c.story: A 3-D-shaded drawing of spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC): a red laser beam passes a nonlinear crystal, and two cones of photons leave it, one vertically and one horizontally polarised; crosses mark the two points where the cones intersect, labelled as entangled photons. Labels are in Macedonian. It is a derivative by B. Jankuloski, dated 27 October 2022 on Wikimedia Commons, of the drawing 'SPDC figure.png' by Neolexx. It explains how many photonic experiments make entangled photon pairs: a photon found where the cones cross could belong to either cone, so the pair is polarisation-entangled.
en-3bc9e3317c.title: File:SPDC figure mk.png

en-3bca9ddcdd.attribution: “FZU MBE detail PJachimova 26” by Akademie věd České republiky / Czech Academy of Sciences (Pavlína Jáchimová), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FZU_MBE_detail_PJachimova_26.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-3bca9ddcdd.creator: Akademie věd České republiky / Czech Academy of Sciences (Pavlína Jáchimová)
en-3bca9ddcdd.story: A photograph looking down the stainless-steel transport tunnel of a Veeco Gen II molecular beam epitaxy system, with a small sample-holder carriage on a rail at the far end. Taken by Pavlína Jáchimová for the Czech Academy of Sciences (FZU) in 2017; the caption says the system grows monocrystalline semiconductors, heterostructures and spintronics materials. This is fabrication equipment, not a quantum computer; the ultra-high-vacuum tunnel moves wafers between chambers without exposing them to air, which keeps grown layers clean.
en-3bca9ddcdd.title: File:FZU MBE detail PJachimova 26.jpg

en-3bedbe6edc.attribution: “Photos; Quantum Dots (6283421382)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Photos%3B_Quantum_Dots_%286283421382%29.jpg
en-3bedbe6edc.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-3bedbe6edc.story: An illustration, not a photograph, titled 'Making indistinguishable photons', published by NIST in 2011. A quantum dot emits a single photon while a parametric down-conversion crystal produces a pair; one photon of the pair is detected to herald the other, which passes through a cavity and filter so it matches the quantum-dot photon. Photonic quantum computing needs photons identical in every property so they interfere; notice the two matching fast-rise, exponential-decay pulse shapes in step 3.
en-3bedbe6edc.title: File:Photos; Quantum Dots (6283421382).jpg

en-3ce1ecf48c.attribution: “Acousto-optic Modulator-ru” — Original: Cwbm (commons) Vector: Д.Ильин, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Acousto-optic_Modulator-ru.svg
en-3ce1ecf48c.creator: Original: Cwbm (commons) Vector: Д.Ильин
en-3ce1ecf48c.story: A vector diagram, with Russian labels, of an acousto-optic modulator: a piezoelectric transducer launches sound waves through a quartz block toward an acoustic absorber, and a light beam passing through leaves as five diffracted beams at equal angles θ. Vectorised by D. Ilyin in 2022 from an original by Cwbm. Acousto-optic modulators switch, frequency-shift and steer laser beams; in trapped-ion and neutral-atom machines they pulse and aim the control lasers, using the diffracted orders shown here.
en-3ce1ecf48c.title: File:Acousto-optic Modulator-ru.svg

en-3d0190ed73.attribution: “Sandia-Thunderbird-trap schematic+cross-section NJP15.093018” by Emily Mount, So-Young Baek, Matthew Blain, Daniel Stick, Daniel Gaultney, Stephen Crain, Rachel Noek, Taehyun Kim, Peter Maunz and Jungsang Kim, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sandia-Thunderbird-trap_schematic%2Bcross-section_NJP15.093018.svg, CC BY 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/)
en-3d0190ed73.creator: Emily Mount, So-Young Baek, Matthew Blain, Daniel Stick, Daniel Gaultney, Stephen Crain, Rachel Noek, Taehyun Kim, Peter Maunz and Jungsang Kim
en-3d0190ed73.story: A two-panel drawing, not a photograph, of the Sandia Thunderbird surface-electrode ion trap: a top view of the electrodes with a 1 mm scale bar, and a cross-section of the fabricated layer stack. Credited to Emily Mount, Jungsang Kim and co-authors (2013-09-13); the file name cites NJP15.093018. Notice the six-rail layout: inner DC rails (blue), 60 μm wide RF rails, segmented outer DC electrodes for holding and moving ions above the chip, and a slot cut through the silicon under the trap site.
en-3d0190ed73.title: File:Sandia-Thunderbird-trap schematic+cross-section NJP15.093018.svg

en-3d4b94f438.attribution: “Paul quadrupole trap” by Jan Pavelka, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_quadrupole_trap.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-3d4b94f438.creator: Jan Pavelka
en-3d4b94f438.story: A photograph, taken in the dark, of a hand-built linear four-rod quadrupole (Paul) trap: four parallel copper rods held between two black 3D-printed end mounts, with a green laser lighting a long cloud of dozens of charged flour grains stretched along the axis between the rods. Photographed by Jan Pavelka (own work), dated 19 November 2017, on Wikimedia Commons. It is a tabletop demonstration, not a quantum device, but it uses the same oscillating-electric-field trapping principle that holds trapped-ion qubits, which line up along the axis of such a trap.
en-3d4b94f438.title: File:Paul quadrupole trap.jpg

en-3e5ccb6aae.story: A labelled computer drawing, a simplified scale model, of a compact trapped-ion quantum computer built into two 19-inch racks. The 'optics rack' holds laser generation (including 729 nm light), stabilisation, fibre distribution and switching, and control electronics; the 'trap rack' holds the trap module with its rf and dc drive, amplifiers for the acousto-optic modulators, a 729 nm splitting module, a wavemeter and the computer and network hub. It comes from a 2021 study by I. Pogorelov, T. Feldker and colleagues, as recorded on Commons. It shows how an ion-trap machine's lasers and optics fit into racks instead of an optical table; it does not show an ion–photon network link.

Published by IBM Research on 2023-12-05 from the keynote 'Entering the Era of Quantum Utility'; the footer reads IBM Quantum Summit 2023. It marks the 2021 Eagle superconducting processor as a roadmap milestone, but it is a render of the closed package; no chip or qubits are visible.

en-42483b67f7.attribution: “Cold atoms experiment 04” by Tomasz Kawalec, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cold_atoms_experiment_04.JPG, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-42483b67f7.creator: Tomasz Kawalec
en-42483b67f7.story: A photograph looking through the bore of a large magnetic coil towards a rectangular glass vacuum cell; the faint yellow-orange specks near its centre are a cloud of cold atoms. Taken by Tomasz Kawalec (2015-11-30); the caption describes about 10 million atoms at 30 microkelvins, with coils producing a quadrupole magnetic field. This is a magneto-optical trap, the laser-and-magnetic-field stage that cools and gathers atoms before neutral-atom experiments load them into optical tweezers or lattices.
en-42483b67f7.title: File:Cold atoms experiment 04.JPG

en-434ad53455.attribution: “IonSpec FT-ICR (Fourier transform Ion cyclotron resonance) Mass spectrometer” by Michael Pereckas from Milwaukee, WI, USA, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IonSpec_FT-ICR_%28Fourier_transform_Ion_cyclotron_resonance%29_Mass_spectrometer.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-434ad53455.creator: Michael Pereckas from Milwaukee, WI, USA
en-434ad53455.story: A photograph of a laboratory room dominated by a cream-coloured superconducting magnet labelled IonSpec 7.0T, with a vacuum ion-optics line, an electronics console, a laser module and liquid-chromatography equipment. Taken by Michael Pereckas (2010-12-23); it shows an IonSpec Fourier-transform ion cyclotron resonance (FT-ICR) mass spectrometer. This is a chemistry instrument, not quantum-computing hardware; it is related only because it holds ions in a strong magnetic field, as a Penning trap does, using a cryogen-cooled magnet.
en-434ad53455.title: File:IonSpec FT-ICR (Fourier transform Ion cyclotron resonance) Mass spectrometer.jpg

en-44343da7fe.attribution: “Kane QC” by Diagram drawn by Tim Starling, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kane_QC.png, CC BY SA 3.0 (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)
en-44343da7fe.creator: Diagram drawn by Tim Starling
en-44343da7fe.story: A simple cross-section line drawing of the Kane quantum computer: two phosphorus-31 atoms buried 25 nm deep in silicon and 20 nm apart, under a 5 nm silicon-oxide layer with surface gates labelled A, J, A and a back gate below. Drawn by Tim Starling; no date is recorded. It shows the donor-spin idea in silicon: each phosphorus atom holds a qubit, the A gates tune individual donors, and the J gate between them controls their coupling.
en-44343da7fe.title: File:Kane QC.png

en-447b0caa68.attribution: “Quantum entanglement vs classical correlation video short” by JozumBjada, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Quantum_entanglement_vs_classical_correlation_video_short.gif, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-447b0caa68.creator: JozumBjada
en-447b0caa68.story: An animated 3D render, not a photograph, of two photon-polarization experiments side by side: a central source sends photon pairs through analysers to detectors in arms A and B, and a time line below records each pair's outcomes as coloured squares. Made by JozumBjada (2020-12-01) to contrast a maximally entangled singlet state (left) with a dephased, only classically correlated state (right). Notice that both show correlated outcomes, but only entangled pairs stay correlated when the analysers are rotated to other settings.
en-447b0caa68.title: File:Quantum entanglement vs classical correlation video short.gif

en-45d1f8fc5b.attribution: “Cold Atoms; Hot Gallium; Focused Ion Beams (5887833284)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cold_Atoms%3B_Hot_Gallium%3B_Focused_Ion_Beams_%285887833284%29.jpg
en-45d1f8fc5b.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-45d1f8fc5b.story: A photograph of a laboratory apparatus: a stainless-steel vacuum chamber inside a frame of red-wound magnetic coils, with feedthroughs, cables and optics around it. The file comes from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), 2008; the caption says it is a new magneto-optical trap ion source for focusing ion beams to nanometre spots. It shows how a laser-cooled atom trap can serve fabrication instead of computing. The trapped atoms themselves are not visible.
en-45d1f8fc5b.title: File:Cold Atoms; Hot Gallium; Focused Ion Beams (5887833284).jpg

en-4757835947.attribution: “Scanning tunneling microscope-MHS 2237-IMG 3817-gradient” by Rama, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Scanning_tunneling_microscope-MHS_2237-IMG_3817-gradient.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/fr/deed.en)
en-4757835947.creator: Rama
en-4757835947.story: A museum photograph of a compact early scanning tunnelling microscope head: a steel block holding the scanner and tip, on a plate with ceramic insulators and fine wires, mounted on a stage moved by four micrometer screws. Photographed by Rama on 7 April 2018; the file name carries the reference MHS 2237. It is a historical instrument, not quantum-computing hardware; its relevance is that such microscope tips now pattern hydrogen-covered silicon atom by atom to place single phosphorus donor qubits.
en-4757835947.title: File:Scanning tunneling microscope-MHS 2237-IMG 3817-gradient.jpg

en-48fdfb0db2.attribution: “Superconducting Magnetic Separator Cryostat” — Antonín Ryska, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Superconducting_Magnetic_Separator_Cryostat.jpg
en-48fdfb0db2.creator: Antonín Ryska
en-48fdfb0db2.story: Black-and-white photograph of a large horizontal superconducting-magnet cryostat: a welded stainless-steel vessel with lifting eyes and side nozzles between the two white end housings of the separator, while two workers standing on it connect a thick wire bundle at the service turret on top. Photo by Antonín Ryska (own work, Wikimedia Commons record dated 2024), showing part of a high-gradient magnetic separator with a 5 T field at ZKZ Kaznějov, former Czechoslovakia. It is an industrial magnet, not quantum hardware, but it shows how a superconducting coil lives inside a cryogen-cooled vessel, with all valves and wiring entering through one top neck.
en-48fdfb0db2.title: File:Superconducting Magnetic Separator Cryostat.jpg

en-49a199f847.attribution: “Kirmik buyuklugu ve verim tr” by Oğuz Ergin, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kirmik_buyuklugu_ve_verim_tr.svg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-49a199f847.creator: Oğuz Ergin
en-49a199f847.story: An illustrative drawing, not measured data: three 300 mm wafers tiled with square dies of 40, 20 and 10 mm edge, with the same 30 defects on each; dies hit by a defect are red, clean dies green. Made by Oğuz Ergin (2026-09-15), labels in Turkish, based on Hennessy and Patterson's Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. The yields of 52, 83 and 96 percent show why large chips are costly, which matters as qubit chips move to 300 mm foundry processes.
en-49a199f847.title: File:Kirmik buyuklugu ve verim tr.svg

en-4c9a04a9bd.attribution: “Coulomb crystal 2D TEM” by Tanja Mehlstäubler, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Coulomb_crystal_2D_TEM.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-4c9a04a9bd.creator: Tanja Mehlstäubler
en-4c9a04a9bd.story: A camera image of about 22 trapped ions, each a blue spot of fluorescence, lying in single file at both ends and in a two-row zigzag in the middle; no scale bar is shown. Credited to Tanja Mehlstäubler (2026-08-05) and captioned as a 2D ion Coulomb crystal in a linear RF trap. It shows how mutual repulsion spaces the ions evenly; when many ions are squeezed along the trap axis the line buckles into a zigzag, changing the shared vibrations used for trapped-ion gates.
en-4c9a04a9bd.title: File:Coulomb crystal 2D TEM.jpg

en-4ca402dd73.attribution: “CVD diamond” by Kugel, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:CVD_diamond.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-4ca402dd73.creator: Kugel
en-4ca402dd73.story: A scanning electron micrograph of a polycrystalline diamond film: interlocking faceted crystals roughly 0.3–2 µm across, with a 1 µm scale bar. Credited to Kugel (2010-10-22); the description says it was grown for 2 hours by hot-filament chemical vapour deposition on seeded Si(100) from 99% hydrogen and 1% methane. It shows what diamond growth produces; colour-centre qubits such as nitrogen-vacancy centres usually use high-purity single-crystal diamond, so the many grain boundaries seen here are what device makers try to avoid.
en-4ca402dd73.title: File:CVD diamond.jpg

en-4d99a46213.attribution: “The Beauty of Quantum Computers (25215168907)” by Steve Jurvetson from Menlo Park, USA, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Beauty_of_Quantum_Computers_%2825215168907%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-4d99a46213.creator: Steve Jurvetson from Menlo Park, USA
en-4d99a46213.story: A photograph of a person at an event holding up a patterned wafer, roughly 150–200 mm across, carrying a grid of rectangular chips that shimmer with rainbow diffraction colours. Credited to Steve Jurvetson (2018-02-01); the caption says it shows him holding a wafer of D-Wave processors. It shows that superconducting annealing processors are made like ordinary chips, many at once on one wafer by lithography, before each die is cut out, packaged and cooled.
en-4d99a46213.title: File:The Beauty of Quantum Computers (25215168907).jpg

en-4ded775e92.attribution: “Scanning tunneling microscope-MHS 2237-IMG 3820” by Rama, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Scanning_tunneling_microscope-MHS_2237-IMG_3820.JPG, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/fr/deed.en)
en-4ded775e92.creator: Rama
en-4ded775e92.story: Close-up photograph of the working heart of an early scanning tunnelling microscope: a fine metal tip in a white ceramic holder, hanging on springs just above a small round sample disc. Photographed by Rama on 7 April 2018; the title gives museum inventory MHS 2237. The tip-to-sample gap is where the tunnelling current flows; the same principle, in ultra-high vacuum, is used to write atom-precise phosphorus donor patterns in silicon. This is an early ambient instrument, not a lithography system.
en-4ded775e92.title: File:Scanning tunneling microscope-MHS 2237-IMG 3820.JPG

en-4e95c1cf1e.attribution: “Quantum Computer (3796519198)” by Steve Jurvetson from Los Altos, USA, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Quantum_Computer_%283796519198%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-4e95c1cf1e.creator: Steve Jurvetson from Los Altos, USA
en-4e95c1cf1e.story: A photograph of a tall closed cryostat on a lift cart inside a metal-lined room, with a large pumping line and cables at its top. Steve Jurvetson took it at D-Wave in Burnaby, British Columbia, in 2009; the caption says a 128-qubit quantum computer was inside for tests. It shows how a quantum annealer based on superconducting flux qubits lives: the chip is hidden in a very cold dilution refrigerator, shielded from magnetic noise. The qubits themselves are not visible.
en-4e95c1cf1e.title: File:Quantum Computer (3796519198).jpg

en-4fda7f5136.attribution: “Ion trap (5941060224)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ion_trap_%285941060224%29.jpg
en-4fda7f5136.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-4fda7f5136.story: Two photographs: above, a white alumina carrier board with about 50 gold traces fanning in to a diamond-shaped trap assembly; below, a close-up of gold-coated electrode wafers around a dark X-shaped slot. From the National Institute of Standards and Technology (2011-07-15), described as the NIST X-trap, a sandwich of two alumina wafers with a trench cut through both. Ions are created in the lower-left arm; the X-junction lets electrode voltages shuttle ions between arms, a key step for multi-zone trapped-ion processors.
en-4fda7f5136.title: File:Ion trap (5941060224).jpg

en-502af64c82.attribution: “Atom cooling and trapping” by Tomasz Kawalec, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Atom_cooling_and_trapping.JPG, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-502af64c82.creator: Tomasz Kawalec
en-502af64c82.story: Photograph looking through a crowded cold-atom experiment: copper magnetic-field coils, mirrors, lenses and cables on an optical table, with a person working in the background. Its Commons description (by Tomasz Kawalec, 2015) calls it a magneto-optical trap and optical dipole trap for cooling neutral atoms close to absolute zero. It shows the real complexity behind neutral-atom qubits and sensors; the atoms themselves are not visible.
en-502af64c82.title: File:Atom cooling and trapping.JPG

en-50f7755a46.attribution: “IBM Q system (Fraunhofer 2)” by IBM Research, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IBM_Q_system_%28Fraunhofer_2%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-50f7755a46.creator: IBM Research
en-50f7755a46.story: A photograph of IBM Quantum System One: a tall glass cube in a dark room, inside which a black cylindrical cryostat can hangs from a lit frame. From IBM Research (2021-06-04); the caption places the system in Ehningen, Germany. The black can is the outer shell of a dilution refrigerator that cools a superconducting processor to near absolute zero; the processor itself is hidden inside and cannot be identified from this picture.
en-50f7755a46.title: File:IBM Q system (Fraunhofer 2).jpg

en-5122401d9f.creator: Mwjohnson0
en-5122401d9f.story: A close-up photograph of a square processor chip named WASHINGTON, wire-bonded into a gold-plated holder on a green circuit board, with traces running out to fine-pitch connectors. Credited to Mwjohnson0 (2015-11-02); the caption identifies it as the D-Wave TwoX 1000-qubit quantum annealing processor, introduced in 2015 with 128,472 Josephson junctions. The pinkish grid in the centre is the repeated array of superconducting flux-qubit cells; the ring of hundreds of wire bonds shows how many control lines such a chip needs.
en-5122401d9f.title: File:D-Wave-Washington-1000Q.jpg

en-550894030d.attribution: “Nitrogen-Vacancy Center” by Stacylee14, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nitrogen-Vacancy_Center.PNG, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-550894030d.creator: Stacylee14
en-550894030d.story: A 3D ball-and-stick render, not an image of a real crystal, of a diamond unit cell: blue carbon atoms in a tetrahedral network, one red nitrogen atom replacing a carbon, and a yellow sphere marking the empty site (vacancy) beside it. Made by Stacylee14 (2015-03-18) as 'Figure 2: View A' of a nitrogen-vacancy centre. It shows the structure of this colour-centre qubit: the nitrogen–vacancy pair holds electrons whose spin can be set with microwaves and read out optically, even at room temperature.
en-550894030d.title: File:Nitrogen-Vacancy Center.PNG

en-5527dcc97c.attribution: “Setup to generate an extremely precise Wavelength of Infrared light” by Steve Jurvetson from Menlo Park, USA, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Setup_to_generate_an_extremely_precise_Wavelength_of_Infrared_light.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-5527dcc97c.creator: Steve Jurvetson from Menlo Park, USA
en-5527dcc97c.story: A photograph of a large optical table crowded with free-space optics (dozens of mirror mounts, lens and beam-splitter mounts, fibre parts, a coiled blue fibre) with several people around it, two in laser-safety glasses. Taken by Steve Jurvetson on 28 February 2010; his caption describes a setup to generate a very precise infrared wavelength, using PPLN nonlinear crystals for wavelength shifting. It is a laser lab, not quantum-computer hardware, but shows the bulk optics that photonic and atom-based systems rely on; the beams are invisible.
en-5527dcc97c.title: File:Setup to generate an extremely precise Wavelength of Infrared light.jpg

en-5662bded75.attribution: “Pockels cell modulaliing light polarization” by Ben Smith, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pockels_cell_modulaliing_light_polarization.png, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-5662bded75.creator: Ben Smith
en-5662bded75.story: A 3D-rendered diagram, not a photograph, of a Pockels cell: a beam passes a tilted Brewster window and a grey cylinder (the cell), with green arrows marking linear and circular polarisation. Made by Ben Smith (2017-01-24); the description says the cell acts here as a quarter-wave plate, and the Brewster window turns the polarisation change into an intensity change. Pockels cells are electro-optic modulators used to switch laser beams, for example in optical qubit control; notice the cell changes polarisation, not brightness, directly.
en-5662bded75.title: File:Pockels cell modulaliing light polarization.png

en-57fa6faab8.attribution: “Qinetiq free-space QKD system in the DARPA Quantum Network - March 2005” — Daderot, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Qinetiq_free-space_QKD_system_in_the_DARPA_Quantum_Network_-_March_2005.jpg
en-57fa6faab8.creator: Daderot
en-57fa6faab8.story: A photograph of a small black laser box on a tripod with fine-adjustment screws, aimed through a rain-spotted window at a building across a courtyard. Its Commons record calls it the QinetiQ (Malvern) free-space quantum key distribution system, one link of the DARPA Quantum Network on the BBN campus, March 2005. It shows that quantum keys can be sent through open air between buildings, not only through optical fibre.
en-57fa6faab8.title: File:Qinetiq free-space QKD system in the DARPA Quantum Network - March 2005.jpg

en-58ee14fa00.attribution: “FZU MBE detail PJachimova 25” by Akademie věd České republiky / Czech Academy of Sciences (Pavlína Jáchimová), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FZU_MBE_detail_PJachimova_25.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-58ee14fa00.creator: Akademie věd České republiky / Czech Academy of Sciences (Pavlína Jáchimová)
en-58ee14fa00.story: A close-up photograph of the source flange of a molecular beam epitaxy growth chamber: about nine source-cell ports ringed by black pneumatic shutter actuators, air lines and connectors, with a 'REMOVE BEFORE BAKEOUT' tag. Taken by Pavlína Jáchimová for the Czech Academy of Sciences on 27 September 2017; the description names a Veeco Gen II system for growing semiconductor heterostructures. This is fabrication equipment, not a qubit: it grows the III-V layers behind semiconductor-superconductor nanowires and quantum-dot photon sources, each shutter gating one element's beam.
en-58ee14fa00.title: File:FZU MBE detail PJachimova 25.jpg

en-5a913faa8b.creator: RuinDig/Yuki Uchida
en-5a913faa8b.story: A photograph through a glass showcase of the cryogenic 'chandelier' in a Fujitsu quantum-computer exhibit: about six stacked plates, silver above and gold below, wrapped in loops of silver coaxial cable. Taken by RuinDig/Yuki Uchida on 31 October 2025 at the Japan Mobility Show 2025, Tokyo Big Sight, in the 'Tokyo Future Tour 2035' booth. It shows the dilution-refrigerator stages that cool the processor, with coax lines carrying signals from room-temperature electronics to each qubit; the 'SKYDRIVE' sign across it is a reflection.
en-5a913faa8b.title: File:Japan-Mobility-Show-2025-RuinDig 0571.jpg

en-5aca0fd074.attribution: “Molecular-beam epitaxy 412 RIBER system at LAAS-CNRS” by QGravelier, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Molecular-beam_epitaxy_412_RIBER_system_at_LAAS-CNRS.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-5aca0fd074.creator: QGravelier
en-5aca0fd074.story: A photograph of a complete molecular beam epitaxy system in a clean room: a gold-coloured RIBER growth chamber with radial source-cell ports, a grey insulated preparation chamber and load-lock modules on blue frames. Taken by QGravelier on 22 June 2021 at the LAAS-CNRS technology facility in Toulouse, France; the file title names it a RIBER 412 system. It is fabrication equipment, not a quantum computer, but shows the scale of the ultra-high-vacuum tools that grow III-V heterostructures for nanowire and quantum-dot devices.
en-5aca0fd074.title: File:Molecular-beam epitaxy 412 RIBER system at LAAS-CNRS.jpg

en-5af1f27a5b.creator: Geek3
en-5af1f27a5b.story: A photograph of an acousto-optic modulator: a black box about 4 cm long with a small window onto a blue crystal and a gold SMA radio-frequency connector, on a kinematic tilt mount on an optical table. Photographed by Geek3 in December 2016; the description names model ATM-3501A2, working in the 100 MHz range. A sound wave driven into the crystal deflects and frequency-shifts a laser beam, which is how ion and neutral-atom experiments switch and tune control lasers; the tilt mount sets the beam angle.
en-5af1f27a5b.title: File:Acousto-optic-modulator-ATM-3501A2 2.jpg

en-5b06ca427d.attribution: “B92 protocol quantum key distribution” by Sat-Electric, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:B92_protocol_quantum_key_distribution.svg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-5b06ca427d.creator: Sat-Electric
en-5b06ca427d.story: A flat-colour drawing, with Russian labels, of the B92 quantum key distribution protocol: a light source emits photons in four polarisations, a filter plate marked 1 and 0 passes only diagonal or vertical ones, and a second analyser plate reads them. Drawn by Sat-Electric (2012-11-26), based on the review 'Quantum cryptography: principles, protocols, systems' by K. E. Rumyantsev and D. M. Golubchikov. B92 encodes bits in two non-orthogonal photon states, so eavesdropping causes errors; this is quantum communication, not computing hardware.
en-5b06ca427d.title: File:B92 protocol quantum key distribution.svg

en-5b6691bca6.creator: RuinDig/Yuki Uchida
en-5b6691bca6.story: A photograph looking steeply along the axis of the exhibited Fujitsu dilution-refrigerator chandelier, through showcase glass: gold-plated stage plates carry looped silver coax lines and rectangular component blocks around a central column. Taken by RuinDig/Yuki Uchida on 31 October 2025 at the Japan Mobility Show 2025, Tokyo Big Sight, in the 'Tokyo Future Tour 2035' booth. It shows how densely coaxial wiring from room-temperature electronics to the qubits is packed on each cooling stage; the glass walls mirror the object, so some copies are reflections.
en-5b6691bca6.title: File:Japan-Mobility-Show-2025-RuinDig 0573.jpg

en-5b77517277.attribution: “Single electron transistor” by Dschwen, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Single_electron_transistor.svg, CC BY SA 2.5 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.5/)
en-5b77517277.creator: Dschwen
en-5b77517277.story: A drawing of two energy-level diagrams for a single-electron transistor: source and drain on either side, two tunnel barriers, and a small island with discrete levels. Made by Dschwen (uploaded 3 March 2006); the top panel shows the blocking state (Coulomb blockade), and in the bottom a gate voltage lowers the island levels so an electron tunnels through in steps 1–4. Such charge sensors read out semiconductor spin qubits: spin is converted to charge, then sensed, often with rf reflectometry.
en-5b77517277.title: File:Single electron transistor.svg

en-5cada3eca4.attribution: “Plasma Processing (32925141021)” by Oak Ridge National Laboratory, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Plasma_Processing_%2832925141021%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-5cada3eca4.creator: Oak Ridge National Laboratory
en-5cada3eca4.story: Artistic 3D render of a multi-cell niobium superconducting cavity cut open to show plasma processing: glowing plasma cleans one cell at a time and the burnt-off hydrocarbons leave as gas. Made by Oak Ridge National Laboratory (image credit ORNL/Jill Hemman).
