It is a drawing of an accelerator cavity, not a qubit device, but it explains a surface treatment that raises the quality factor of superconducting cavities, the property that makes 3D cavities useful as long-lived quantum memories.
en-5cada3eca4.title: File:Plasma Processing (32925141021).jpg

en-5cb20c12be.attribution: “FZU cryostat PJachimova 10” by Akademie věd České republiky / Czech Academy of Sciences (Pavlína Jáchimová), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FZU_cryostat_PJachimova_10.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-5cb20c12be.creator: Akademie věd České republiky / Czech Academy of Sciences (Pavlína Jáchimová)
en-5cb20c12be.story: Laboratory photograph of a blue box-shaped magnetic cryostat on an optical table; through its round aluminium window flange one sees a copper-coloured inner shield and a sample holder with gold contact pads. In front stand a lens on a post and a steel square, with a coaxial connector at the cryostat base and, blurred at left, a white light-source housing. Photo by Pavlína Jáchimová for the Czech Academy of Sciences, FZU – Institute of Physics, Department of Dielectrics, Prague (2017). It shows an optical-access cryostat, where light from the source passes through windows to a cooled sample; the magnet itself is hidden inside.
en-5cb20c12be.title: File:FZU cryostat PJachimova 10.jpg

en-5d9480e7fd.creator: ISCIX-Ex
en-5d9480e7fd.story: A magnified photograph of part of a 300 mm silicon test wafer: rows of identical chips, each about 2.5 mm across according to the description, separated by thin scribe lines and glowing in rainbow colours from light diffraction; the bright swirl at upper right is the reflection of the spiral lamp used to light it. It was taken by ISCIX-Ex and is dated 28 November 2012 on Commons. It shows the kind of 300 mm wafer that CMOS foundries also use for silicon spin qubits and cryogenic control chips, but this one carries ordinary test circuits, not quantum devices.
en-5d9480e7fd.title: File:Wafer300mm-LargeIC-testset.jpg

en-5dc4edf808.attribution: “ALMA cryostat (dsc-6991-cc)” by S. Otarola/ESO, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ALMA_cryostat_%28dsc-6991-cc%29.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-5dc4edf808.creator: S. Otarola/ESO
en-5dc4edf808.story: A photograph of the top plate of a large blue cryostat, with gold flat and pyramid-shaped mirrors over windows marked 'BAND 9' and 'BAND 10' and a red 'PRESSURE VESSEL' label. Taken by S. Otarola/ESO on 26 October 2016; the caption identifies it as a cryostat of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, fitted in its antennas, where the mirrors redirect the incoming radio signal. This is radio-astronomy equipment, not a quantum computer, but shows the vacuum vessel and windows used to keep sensitive detectors cold.
en-5dc4edf808.title: File:ALMA cryostat (dsc-6991-cc).jpg

en-60251e0ca6.attribution: “Scanning Tunneling Microscope schematic” by Michael Schmid and Grzegorz Pietrzak, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Scanning_Tunneling_Microscope_schematic.svg, CC BY SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/)
en-60251e0ca6.creator: Michael Schmid and Grzegorz Pietrzak
en-60251e0ca6.story: A coloured schematic drawing of a scanning tunnelling microscope: a sharp tip on a piezoelectric tube over a sample, a tunnelling-current amplifier feeding a distance-control and scanning unit, and an inset of the tip's apex atoms above the sample atoms. Drawn by Michael Schmid and Grzegorz Pietrzak (2020-04-16). The same instrument is used in hydrogen lithography to place single phosphorus donors in silicon for donor-spin qubits; the feedback loop holding the tunnelling current constant is what lets the tip resolve single atoms.
en-60251e0ca6.title: File:Scanning Tunneling Microscope schematic.svg

en-606e83c390.attribution: “Surface-ion-trap allcock NJP12.053026” by D T C Allcock, J A Sherman, D N Stacey, A H Burrell, M J Curtis, G Imreh, N M Linke, D J Szwer, S C Webster, A M Steane and D M Lucas, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Surface-ion-trap_allcock_NJP12.053026.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-606e83c390.creator: D T C Allcock, J A Sherman, D N Stacey, A H Burrell, M J Curtis, G Imreh, N M Linke, D J Szwer, S C Webster, A M Steane and D M Lucas
en-606e83c390.story: A close-up photograph of a surface-electrode ion trap: a square chip with long, finely segmented electrode stripes, wire-bonded to a gold chip carrier ringed by small gold capacitors. By D. T. C. Allcock and co-authors (2010-05-17), from the group of D. M. Lucas in Oxford; the file title cites NJP 12 053026, and the caption says the gold squares are single-layer capacitors. Ions float just above the flat electrodes, and the segmented stripes let voltages move them along the chip; note how many electrodes need their own bond.
en-606e83c390.title: File:Surface-ion-trap allcock NJP12.053026.jpg

en-6225e3c576.attribution: “FIB schematic (14168806752)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FIB_schematic_%2814168806752%29.jpg
en-6225e3c576.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-6225e3c576.story: A labelled 3D drawing of a focused ion beam instrument whose ions come from a magneto-optical trap. It comes from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), 2014: lithium atoms are laser-cooled in the trap, ionized by another laser, then accelerated and focused onto a target. Notice the crossing red trap beams, the two ring magnets, and the ion-optics stack (acceleration tube, deflectors, Einzel lens). It is a drawing, and it shows the trap used as an ion source, not as a qubit array.
en-6225e3c576.title: File:FIB schematic (14168806752).jpg

en-624a44086a.attribution: “N-V center based thermal probe” by Abdelghani Laraoui, Halley Aycock-Rizzo, Yang Gao, Xi Lu, Elisa Riedo & Carlos A. Meriles, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:N-V_center_based_thermal_probe.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-624a44086a.creator: Abdelghani Laraoui, Halley Aycock-Rizzo, Yang Gao, Xi Lu, Elisa Riedo & Carlos A. Meriles
en-624a44086a.story: A five-panel paper figure: a rendered setup with a diamond nanocrystal, hosting a nitrogen-vacancy centre, on the tip of a heated AFM cantilever, plus plotted spectra and fluorescence and temperature maps. By Abdelghani Laraoui, Halley Aycock-Rizzo, Yang Gao, Xi Lu, Elisa Riedo and Carlos A. Meriles (2015). Panel (b) shows the NV resonance dips shifting between 298, 367 and 478 K; this colour-centre spin, a qubit candidate, here serves as a nanoscale thermometer.
en-624a44086a.title: File:N-V center based thermal probe.jpg

en-6280d36340.attribution: “Ultrafast Single-Photon Detector (5941070174)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ultrafast_Single-Photon_Detector_%285941070174%29.jpg
en-6280d36340.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-6280d36340.story: A false-coloured scanning electron micrograph of a superconducting nanowire single-photon detector: about 20 parallel nanowires, roughly 0.9 µm apart, folded into a meander about 20 µm across between wide contact pads. From the National Institute of Standards and Technology (2011-06-30); the caption says the wires were patterned by electron-beam lithography on a tungsten-silicon film. A photon absorbed in the meander locally breaks superconductivity and produces a click; such detectors read out photonic qubits. The colours are added.
en-6280d36340.title: File:Ultrafast Single-Photon Detector (5941070174).jpg

en-62a4b4fa37.creator: Geek3
en-62a4b4fa37.story: A photograph of a compact electro-optic phase modulator: a gold-plated body with a grey lid engraved with a beam-direction arrow, a gold SMA input connector and a small aperture, mounted on a post. Photographed by Geek3 in December 2016; the description says the case holds a crystal whose birefringence changes with an applied high voltage, acting as a variable waveplate. It changes the phase or polarisation of a laser beam quickly, as used to tune and shape control lasers in atom and ion experiments.
en-62a4b4fa37.title: File:Electro-optic-phase-modulator.jpg

en-62aefdaea8.attribution: “A Field of Dreams (40054482212)” by Steve Jurvetson from Menlo Park, USA, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_Field_of_Dreams_%2840054482212%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-62aefdaea8.creator: Steve Jurvetson from Menlo Park, USA
en-62aefdaea8.story: A close, angled photograph of a silicon wafer covered in rows of square chips, with colourful test structures between them. It was taken by Steve Jurvetson in 2018; the caption says the wafer holds 500-, 1000- and 2000-qubit D-Wave quantum computers. Each chip is a quantum annealing processor made of superconducting flux-qubit loops; notice how they are made many at a time on one wafer, like ordinary chips. The individual qubits are too small to see.
en-62aefdaea8.title: File:A Field of Dreams (40054482212).jpg

en-633214c18e.attribution: “Initial-CSACs” — NIST, Robert Lutwak, William Jennings, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Initial-CSACs.jpg
en-633214c18e.creator: NIST, Robert Lutwak, William Jennings
en-633214c18e.story: A composite of two photographs: a brushed-metal chip-scale atomic clock module beside a US quarter coin for scale, and an inset of a wire-bonded layer stack on a gold-traced substrate. Per the caption, the main photo is Symmetricom's first autonomous Chip Scale Atomic Clock and the inset a NIST physics package, both circa 2005; composite credited to NIST, Robert Lutwak and William Jennings (2012). This is a clock, not quantum-computing hardware, but it shows atomic vapour-cell physics shrunk to coin size.
en-633214c18e.title: File:Initial-CSACs.jpg

en-63ae1341bc.attribution: “High-Speed Quantum Key System Wins Research Award (5884514398)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:High-Speed_Quantum_Key_System_Wins_Research_Award_%285884514398%29.jpg
en-63ae1341bc.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-63ae1341bc.story: Two side-by-side photographs of equipment racks labelled 'NIST QKD System / Alice' and 'Bob': fibre patch panels, piezo driver units and rack-mount computers, with fibre cords looping between ports. NIST (2007) describes it as its high-speed fibre quantum key distribution system, cited among the '100 most technologically significant' developments of the previous year. It is quantum communication, not a quantum computer: Alice sends photon signals over fibre and Bob measures them to build a shared secret key. Notice how much is ordinary rack electronics.
en-63ae1341bc.title: File:High-Speed Quantum Key System Wins Research Award (5884514398).jpg

en-651c88f436.attribution: “Cryostat, Museum Boerhaave Leiden” by Photograph by Mike Peel ( www.mikepeel.net )., https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cryostat%2C_Museum_Boerhaave_Leiden.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-651c88f436.creator: Photograph by Mike Peel ( www.mikepeel.net ).
en-651c88f436.story: Museum photograph of a tarnished metal cryostat on a wooden tripod: a tall, ribbed vessel with a bolted top flange and pipe tee, a wooden collar marked 'C3', flanged side ports (one with a round window) and a wide port near the base, set before a large backlit archive photo of an old cryogenic laboratory. As recorded, the cryostat was made by J. J. Curvers, Leiden, about 1890, and is in Museum Boerhaave, Leiden; photo by Mike Peel (2013). It is an early bath cryostat for liquefied gases, an ancestor of the liquid-helium cryostats used in low-temperature and quantum experiments.
en-651c88f436.title: File:Cryostat, Museum Boerhaave Leiden.jpg

en-65c2fb2349.attribution: “Keynote - Entering the Era of Quantum Utility (IBM Research) 06” by IBM Research, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Keynote_-_Entering_the_Era_of_Quantum_Utility_%28IBM_Research%29_06.png, CC BY 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/)
en-65c2fb2349.creator: IBM Research
en-65c2fb2349.story: A frame from a keynote video: a slide titled 'Tunable Coupler architecture – Performance' with a small render of an IBM Quantum processor, a line drawing of a heavy-hex qubit layout, and text comparing Eagle R3 with Heron R1. It comes from IBM Research's keynote 'Entering the Era of Quantum Utility' (IBM Quantum Summit 2023). It contrasts fixed-frequency cross-resonance (ECR) gates with tunable-coupler CZ gates on superconducting processors: notice Heron's 96 ns CZ versus Eagle's 537 ns ECR, allowing more gates despite a shorter mean T1.
en-65c2fb2349.title: File:Keynote - Entering the Era of Quantum Utility (IBM Research) 06.png

en-65e3f7a0b9.attribution: “Apparatus for creating Bose-Einstein condensate” by Tiia Monto, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Apparatus_for_creating_Bose-Einstein_condensate.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-65e3f7a0b9.creator: Tiia Monto
en-65e3f7a0b9.story: A photograph of a museum exhibit: a stainless-steel ultra-high-vacuum chamber with bolted flanges and viewports on a steel stand, and below it a small vertical glass cell held between two copper-wound magnetic coils. Per the caption it is an apparatus for creating Bose-Einstein condensates, originally from the Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics (G. Rempe and colleagues, 1997), now in the Deutsches Museum, Munich; photographed by Tiia Monto. Notice the same core parts as today's neutral-atom quantum computers: vacuum chamber, glass cell and trap coils.
en-65e3f7a0b9.title: File:Apparatus for creating Bose-Einstein condensate.jpg

en-67038093c8.attribution: “Molecular-beam epitaxy system at LAAS 0513” by Guillaume Paumier (user:guillom), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Molecular-beam_epitaxy_system_at_LAAS_0513.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-67038093c8.creator: Guillaume Paumier (user:guillom)
en-67038093c8.story: A photograph of the growth chamber of a molecular beam epitaxy machine: a gold-coloured, RIBER-labelled vessel with bolted flanges and windows, its source ports wrapped in aluminium foil, next to a load-lock box marked 'LOAD'. The caption places it at the LAAS-CNRS facility in Toulouse, photographed by Guillaume Paumier in October 2007. Inside such a chamber, heated cells send atomic beams onto a wafer to build III-V semiconductor layers; the foil is typical of bakeout to reach ultra-high vacuum.
en-67038093c8.title: File:Molecular-beam epitaxy system at LAAS 0513.jpg

en-6743a3afb2.attribution: “CSES2 CDSM flight model” by A. Pollinger, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:CSES2_CDSM_flight_model.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-6743a3afb2.creator: A. Pollinger
en-6743a3afb2.story: Studio photograph of the flight model of the CDSM magnetometer for the CSES-2 satellite, laid out in parts: an open black electronics box with a green circuit board and ports labelled X01–X03, two coiled orange optical fibres, a white harness cable with a gold connector, and a foil-wrapped cylindrical sensor head in a beige bracket. Photographed by A. Pollinger (own work, Wikimedia Commons, 2022). It is a room-temperature, light-based atomic magnetometer, not a superconducting quantum interference device: the atoms' response to laser light reveals the magnetic field. Notice how the light reaches the sensor head through the fibres.
en-6743a3afb2.title: File:CSES2 CDSM flight model.jpg

en-685f18341c.attribution: “QuEra Aquila Magneto-Optical Trap 2” by QuEra Computing, Inc., https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:QuEra_Aquila_Magneto-Optical_Trap_2.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-685f18341c.creator: QuEra Computing, Inc.
en-685f18341c.story: A studio photograph of a vacuum and optics assembly on an optical breadboard: a stainless-steel vacuum chamber topped by a SAES Getters pump housing, a rectangular glass cell wrapped in copper-wire coils, and black lens mounts that deliver laser light. QuEra Computing (2023) captions it as the magneto-optical trap of its first-generation neutral-atom quantum computer (Aquila). Laser beams plus a magnetic field gradient cool and gather atoms inside the glass cell before they are loaded into optical tweezers as qubits.
en-685f18341c.title: File:QuEra Aquila Magneto-Optical Trap 2.jpg

en-68a0ada0cb.attribution: “Scanning tunneling microscope-MHS 2237-IMG 3818” by Rama, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Scanning_tunneling_microscope-MHS_2237-IMG_3818.JPG, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/fr/deed.en)
en-68a0ada0cb.creator: Rama
en-68a0ada0cb.story: Photograph of a small early scanning tunnelling microscope, a hand-sized steel scanner block on a micrometer-driven stage, displayed on a wooden base. Photographed by Rama on 7 April 2018; the title gives museum inventory MHS 2237, and the engraved plaque reads GAP Biomédical, Uni Genève, 1990. It shows the basic tool behind STM hydrogen lithography, where a sharp tip scanned over a surface places phosphorus donors atom by atom; note this is an ambient instrument, not the ultra-high-vacuum machines used for that work.
en-68a0ada0cb.title: File:Scanning tunneling microscope-MHS 2237-IMG 3818.JPG

en-694daf40d0.attribution: “Experimental Atomic Clock; ytterbium atoms (5941021758)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Experimental_Atomic_Clock%3B_ytterbium_atoms_%285941021758%29.jpg
en-694daf40d0.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-694daf40d0.story: A computer illustration, not a photograph: a glowing horizontal band divided into 13 pancake-shaped wells, each holding a small stack of spheres coloured blue or yellow. Per NIST's caption (2011), it depicts an experimental atomic clock in which a lattice of laser beams traps small numbers of ytterbium atoms, and a yellow laser switches them between a lower (blue) and higher (yellow) energy level. It is a clock, not a quantum computer, but the same optical-lattice trapping and laser-driven transitions underlie neutral-atom qubits.
en-694daf40d0.title: File:Experimental Atomic Clock; ytterbium atoms (5941021758).jpg

en-69b0663b5d.attribution: “ALMA cryostat (dsc-6991-cc)” by S. Otarola/ESO, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ALMA_cryostat_%28dsc-6991-cc%29.tiff, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-69b0663b5d.creator: S. Otarola/ESO
en-69b0663b5d.story: A close photograph of the top plate of a large blue cylindrical cryostat, with gold-coloured flat and pyramid-shaped mirrors over circular windows marked 'Band 9' and 'Band 10', and 'Pressure Vessel' warning labels. Photographed by S. Otarola/ESO in October 2016, it is the upper surface of a cryostat for the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), installed in some of its 66 antennas, where the mirrors redirect radio signals from space. It is astronomy hardware, but shows the vacuum-vessel and window engineering shared with quantum-processor cryostats.
en-69b0663b5d.title: File:ALMA cryostat (dsc-6991-cc).tiff

en-6b055862f4.creator: aegon
en-6b055862f4.story: Flat colour drawing, labelled in German, of Kerr-lens mode-locking in a titanium-sapphire laser: a grey block ('TiSa-Kristall', the Ti:sapphire crystal) sits on the beam path; the continuous-wave beam ('cw Strahl', dark pink) keeps its width, while the pulsed beam ('gepulster Strahl', light pink) narrows as it crosses the crystal. At right an aperture ('Blende') blocks the wide continuous light and lets the narrower pulses through. Drawn by the Commons user aegon (own work, 2006). Intense pulses focus themselves in the crystal, so the aperture favours pulsing, which gives Ti:sapphire lasers their femtosecond pulses; this is a principle sketch, not real hardware.
en-6b055862f4.title: File:TiSa-scheme.png

en-6cc0831d1d.creator: Geek3
en-6cc0831d1d.story: A close-up photograph of an acousto-optic modulator: a small black anodised housing with an IntraAction label, an oval window revealing the crystal, and a gold SMA radio-frequency connector, clamped on a mounting plate. Photographed by Geek3 (December 2016); the caption identifies it as model ATM-3501A2, working in the 100 MHz range. A radio-frequency signal launches a sound wave in the crystal that deflects and frequency-shifts a laser beam; such devices switch the laser pulses that control trapped-ion and neutral-atom qubits.
en-6cc0831d1d.title: File:Acousto-optic-modulator-ATM-3501A2 1.jpg

en-6ccde0e6f3.attribution: “Google Sycamore Chip 002” by Google (https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCK8sQmJBp8GCxrOtXWBpyEA), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Google_Sycamore_Chip_002.png, CC BY 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/)
en-6ccde0e6f3.creator: Google (https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCK8sQmJBp8GCxrOtXWBpyEA)
en-6ccde0e6f3.story: A computer-animation frame, not a photograph: a rectangular carrier board with hundreds of fine wiring traces radiating from its centre and a smaller dark square die stacked on top, under the title 'Sycamore Chip'. It is a screenshot from a Google video (2019) about its Sycamore quantum processor. The render illustrates the flip-chip stacking used in superconducting processors, where a smaller die is bonded face-down onto a larger wiring chip that fans control lines out; real surface detail is idealised away.
en-6ccde0e6f3.title: File:Google Sycamore Chip 002.png

en-6d6293053e.attribution: “OneAtomRydbergFlopping ManimCE v0.19.0” by LXDX, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:OneAtomRydbergFlopping_ManimCE_v0.19.0.png, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-6d6293053e.creator: LXDX
en-6d6293053e.story: Drawing of three identical two-level energy diagrams: a ground state |g⟩ and a Rydberg state |r⟩ linked by a laser drive of strength Ω_L, whose frequency sits below |r⟩ by a detuning Δ_L that shrinks from left to right toward resonance. A still from a Manim animation of one-atom Rydberg Rabi flopping, made by LXDX and shared on Wikimedia Commons in December 2025. It shows the ground–Rydberg qubit of neutral-atom analog machines in its simplest form: the upper state is the Rydberg level itself, and the drive strength and detuning are the two knobs such machines turn.
en-6d6293053e.title: File:OneAtomRydbergFlopping ManimCE v0.19.0.png

en-6de0829288.creator: Torsten Henning
en-6de0829288.story: Measured data from a single-electron transistor: (a) top left, current–voltage curves at maximum (black) and minimum (green) Coulomb blockade, with red and blue segments showing the swing under two bias methods; (b) top right, current oscillating with gate voltage under voltage bias; (c) bottom left, voltage oscillating with gate voltage under resistor bias; (d) bottom right, sketches of the two bias circuits. From Torsten Henning's PhD thesis 'Charging effects in niobium nanostructures' (Chalmers and Göteborg University, 1999; arXiv cond-mat/9901308). Notice the period ΔQ_g = 1e: the output repeats each time the gate adds one electron's worth of charge, which is why such transistors serve as charge sensors for spin-qubit readout.
en-6de0829288.title: File:TySETcharacteristics.png

en-6f91efff9b.attribution: “Sycamore Quantum Chip” by Coldupnorth, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sycamore_Quantum_Chip.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-6f91efff9b.creator: Coldupnorth
en-6f91efff9b.story: A photograph of Google's Sycamore quantum chip on display at the Deutsches Museum, Munich: a thick brushed-aluminium mount engraved 'Google' and 'Sycamore', holding a light-grey carrier die with radial wiring lines and a smaller dark die mounted face-down on it. Photographed by Coldupnorth (November 2025). Sycamore is a superconducting processor built from transmon qubits; the thing to notice is the two-die flip-chip stack, since individual qubits are too small to see at this resolution.
en-6f91efff9b.title: File:Sycamore Quantum Chip.jpg

en-6fe7b94787.attribution: “Wafer scale integrated circuit on 300 mm wafer” — Wikideas1, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wafer_scale_integrated_circuit_on_300_mm_wafer.webp
en-6fe7b94787.creator: Wikideas1
en-6fe7b94787.story: A computer render, not a photograph: a 300 mm wafer seen at an angle, almost entirely covered by one large gold-coloured square die with clipped corners and a faint grid of reticle tiles. Made by Wikideas1 (2026) to illustrate a wafer-scale integrated circuit. It shows classical chip-making, not quantum hardware; it is included for the 300 mm wafer format that some quantum-chip efforts, such as silicon spin qubits, borrow from standard semiconductor fabs. Surfaces are idealised.
en-6fe7b94787.title: File:Wafer scale integrated circuit on 300 mm wafer.webp

en-701bd3e9ed.attribution: “Single Photon Detectors (5941086280)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Single_Photon_Detectors_%285941086280%29.jpg
en-701bd3e9ed.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-701bd3e9ed.story: Optical micrograph of four square single-photon detectors on a chip: the two upper squares are 25 by 25 micrometres and the two lower ones 50 by 50 micrometres, with gold leads running upward. Published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, which states they reached a record 88 percent efficiency as of June 2005. Their plain square form (rather than a folded nanowire) is typical of transition-edge sensors, superconducting detectors that can also count how many photons arrive.
en-701bd3e9ed.title: File:Single Photon Detectors (5941086280).jpg

en-7021f4885b.attribution: “Single Photons; Quantum Dots (5941075542)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Single_Photons%3B_Quantum_Dots_%285941075542%29.jpg
en-7021f4885b.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-7021f4885b.story: A flat schematic drawing: photons from a quantum-dot single-photon source (QD SPS) are combined with a pump laser in an up-conversion crystal that changes their colour, then split by a 50:50 beam splitter onto two detectors feeding a correlator. Per NIST's caption (2010), it illustrates experiments converting quantum-dot photons to a more convenient wavelength while testing that they stay single. Notice the correlator trace: the suppressed central peak shows photons still arrive one at a time, the key property for photonic quantum computing and communication.
en-7021f4885b.title: File:Single Photons; Quantum Dots (5941075542).jpg

en-70e4998448.attribution: “Alice and Bob - DARPA Quantum Network, in the BBN laboratory - IMG 2687” — Daderot, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Alice_and_Bob_-_DARPA_Quantum_Network%2C_in_the_BBN_laboratory_-_IMG_2687.jpg
en-70e4998448.creator: Daderot
en-70e4998448.story: A flash photograph of a laboratory: black vibration-isolated optical tables with pink foam boxes covering the optics, shelves of rack instruments and cables above, and a banner reading 'Alice Transmitter'. Per the caption it shows the Alice and Bob stations of the DARPA Quantum Network in the BBN laboratory, November 2003; photographed by Daderot. It is an early quantum key distribution testbed, not a quantum computer; notice the room-sized table optics, typically boxed against air currents and temperature drift, compared with later rack-mounted systems.
en-70e4998448.title: File:Alice and Bob - DARPA Quantum Network, in the BBN laboratory - IMG 2687.jpg

en-711d1d643b.attribution: “Cat-state-wigner-function” by R. P. Rundle, P. W. Mills, Todd Tilma, J. H. Samson, and M. J. Everitt, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cat-state-wigner-function.png, CC BY 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/)
en-711d1d643b.creator: R. P. Rundle, P. W. Mills, Todd Tilma, J. H. Samson, and M. J. Everitt
en-711d1d643b.story: A computer-rendered 3D plot of a calculated state, not a measurement: the Wigner function of a Schrödinger cat state, with two bell-shaped peaks labelled 'dead' and 'alive' and, between them, positive and negative (red) lobes marked 'Quantum Interference'. Made by R. P. Rundle, P. W. Mills, Todd Tilma, J. H. Samson and M. J. Everitt (2017) as a textbook example. Cat qubits store information in two such well-separated states, which suppresses bit flips (biased noise); the negative fringes mark a true quantum superposition.
en-711d1d643b.title: File:Cat-state-wigner-function.png

en-716b8add57.attribution: “Alice in BBN laboratory - DARPA Quantum Network, January 2003” — Daderot, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Alice_in_BBN_laboratory_-_DARPA_Quantum_Network%2C_January_2003.jpg
en-716b8add57.creator: Daderot
en-716b8add57.story: A photograph of a laboratory optical table with a long pink foam box covering the optics, a shelf of electronic instruments above it and oscilloscopes around it. Daderot took it in the BBN laboratory in January 2003; its Commons title calls it 'Alice' of the DARPA Quantum Network. Alice was the sending end of a quantum key distribution link, which sends single photons through fibre; the foam keeps the optics at a steady temperature. It shows no trapped ions.
en-716b8add57.title: File:Alice in BBN laboratory - DARPA Quantum Network, January 2003.jpg

en-71a607de45.attribution: “Kerr's Kerr cell (Hunterian museum)” by Andy Dingley, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kerr%27s_Kerr_cell_%28Hunterian_museum%29.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-71a607de45.creator: Andy Dingley
en-71a607de45.story: Photograph of a small museum object: a glass plate framed in corroded metal, with two electrodes facing each other across a narrow gap at its centre. According to its Commons record it is John Kerr's 1878 Kerr cell, shown at the Hunterian Museum, University of Glasgow (photo by Andy Dingley). A voltage across the electrodes makes the glass birefringent (the Kerr effect), the earliest form of electro-optic light modulation behind today's electro-optic modulators. It is a historical instrument, not a modern modulator.
en-71a607de45.title: File:Kerr's Kerr cell (Hunterian museum).jpg

en-747446502d.attribution: “Researchers reach quantum networking milestone in real-world environment (53804795475)” by Oak Ridge National Laboratory, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Researchers_reach_quantum_networking_milestone_in_real-world_environment_%2853804795475%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-747446502d.creator: Oak Ridge National Laboratory
en-747446502d.story: A photograph of a laboratory optical table crowded with fibre-optic parts: coiled yellow single-mode patch cords, taped-down fibre devices and small fibre stages, below a shelf of bench instruments. Oak Ridge National Laboratory published it in June 2024 (credit Carlos Jones/ORNL) as the 'Alice' laboratory, where the photon source and the first node of the team's quantum network are kept. Notice that a fibre quantum-network node is largely telecom-style fibre hardware on an optical table.
en-747446502d.title: File:Researchers reach quantum networking milestone in real-world environment (53804795475).jpg

en-754e234b90.attribution: “QuEra Aquila Magneto-Optical Trap” by QuEra Computing, Inc., https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:QuEra_Aquila_Magneto-Optical_Trap.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-754e234b90.creator: QuEra Computing, Inc.
en-754e234b90.story: A photograph of the magneto-optical trap of QuEra Computing's first-generation neutral-atom quantum computer, credited to QuEra Computing, Inc. (2023). Two square copper coils wrapped in orange Kapton tape surround a small rectangular glass vacuum cell, with a flanged vacuum section, a getter pump, mirrors and fibre-coupled optics around it. A magneto-optical trap uses laser beams and a magnetic field gradient to cool and gather a cloud of atoms, the first step before single atoms are held as qubits.
en-754e234b90.title: File:QuEra Aquila Magneto-Optical Trap.jpg

en-75ac790ea0.attribution: “Photomultiplier-1 hg” by Hannes Grobe, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Photomultiplier-1_hg.png, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-75ac790ea0.creator: Hannes Grobe
en-75ac790ea0.story: Two photographs side by side of glass photomultiplier tubes, Hamamatsu types R1463 (left, in a mounting block) and R106UH (right, on a pin base), by Hannes Grobe (2020). A photomultiplier turns a single photon into a measurable electrical pulse through a chain of dynodes, visible as stacked electrode cages inside the glass. These are classical light detectors, not quantum-computing hardware, though tubes like these can collect fluorescence to read out trapped-ion or neutral-atom qubits.
en-75ac790ea0.title: File:Photomultiplier-1 hg.png

en-75eb75b70c.creator: Pjstas
en-75eb75b70c.story: A tilted-view scanning electron micrograph of a diamond photonic-crystal optical cavity: a narrow suspended nanobeam with a single row of about 26 holes whose size tapers toward both ends. Posted to Wikimedia Commons by Pjstas (2025); no scale bar. Such cavities concentrate light around colour centres in diamond, such as silicon-vacancy or nitrogen-vacancy centres, strengthening the spin–photon link used for quantum networking; notice the undercut below the beam and the hole taper that confines light at the centre.
en-75eb75b70c.title: File:Diamond nanophotonic cavity.jpg

en-7746cc6d2c.attribution: “Linear Paul ion trap” by Coldsmokerider, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Linear_Paul_ion_trap.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-7746cc6d2c.creator: Coldsmokerider
en-7746cc6d2c.story: A photograph through a viewport of a stainless-steel ultra-high-vacuum chamber, showing a small linear Paul ion trap on a white ceramic mount with wires at the centre. Posted by Coldsmokerider (2023), whose caption notes that the view ports around the chamber let laser light pass through. A linear Paul trap holds charged atoms in a line with oscillating radio-frequency electric fields; such ions are the qubits of trapped-ion quantum computers, and the windows are how cooling, gate and readout lasers reach them.
en-7746cc6d2c.title: File:Linear Paul ion trap.jpg

en-7795f7867c.attribution: “Impedence-Matched Lambda-type Three-Level System, 10.1038.ncomms12303 (Inomata et al., 2016)” by Kunihiro Inomata, Zhirong Lin, Kazuki Koshino, William D. Oliver, Jaw-Shen Tsai, Tsuyoshi Yamamoto & Yasunobu Nakamura, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Impedence-Matched_Lambda-type_Three-Level_System%2C_10.1038.ncomms12303_%28Inomata_et_al.%2C_2016%29.png, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-7795f7867c.creator: Kunihiro Inomata, Zhirong Lin, Kazuki Koshino, William D. Oliver, Jaw-Shen Tsai, Tsuyoshi Yamamoto & Yasunobu Nakamura
en-7795f7867c.story: A two-panel paper figure drawn as 3D renders, not photographs, from Inomata, Lin, Koshino, Oliver, Tsai, Yamamoto and Nakamura (2016, DOI 10.1038/ncomms12303). Panel (a) shows a chip with a flux qubit coupled to a superconducting microwave resonator, which under a suitable drive acts as an impedance-matched Λ-type three-level system; panel (b) shows the resulting itinerant microwave-photon detector, linked through three circulators to a parametric phase-locked oscillator. It illustrates detecting single travelling microwave photons with superconducting circuits.
en-7795f7867c.title: File:Impedence-Matched Lambda-type Three-Level System, 10.1038.ncomms12303 (Inomata et al., 2016).png

en-7a64ee5929.creator: Bilovitskiy
en-7a64ee5929.story: A close-up photograph of five small synthetic diamond crystals, the smallest yellow one about 0.3 mm across. Photographer Bilovitskiy bought them for this picture (Wikimedia Commons, 2022). The yellow crystals contain more nitrogen in the carbon lattice, the colourless one is nearly pure carbon. For diamond-based quantum technology this contrast matters: nitrogen is what forms nitrogen-vacancy centres, while quantum devices usually start from very pure diamond into which colour centres are placed deliberately.
en-7a64ee5929.title: File:Diamonds7.jpg

en-7c3e6b2282.attribution: “Operational (25455593154)” by Billie Grace Ward from New York, USA, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Operational_%2825455593154%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-7c3e6b2282.creator: Billie Grace Ward from New York, USA
en-7c3e6b2282.story: Low-light close-up photograph of a powered-up green Xilinx Kintex FPGA development board: a long high-pin-count mezzanine connector runs along the top edge, lit green status lights with power-rail labels such as VCCINT, MGTAVCC and 'POWER GOOD' crowd one corner, and a cable is plugged in at lower right. Photo by Billie Grace Ward from New York, USA, taken on 5 March 2016 and titled 'Operational'. Field-programmable gate array boards like this are used for fast control and real-time error-correction decoding in quantum computers; this one is a generic board, not shown running a decoder.
en-7c3e6b2282.title: File:Operational (25455593154).jpg

en-7cbdb5c211.attribution: “Full wafer of Intel quantum computers” by Steve Jurvetson from Menlo Park, USA, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Full_wafer_of_Intel_quantum_computers.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-7cbdb5c211.creator: Steve Jurvetson from Menlo Park, USA
en-7cbdb5c211.story: A close-up photograph of the lower half of a patterned silicon wafer on a display stand, lit from behind so that its fine patterning splits the light into rainbow bands; columns of small rectangular chips with rows of square pads cover it. Taken by Steve Jurvetson on 11 April 2018 and titled 'Full wafer of Intel quantum computers', noted as its first public showing. It shows quantum chips made in bulk on an industrial silicon wafer, the route of 300 mm CMOS-foundry fabrication; the wafer diameter and qubit type cannot be read from the picture.
en-7cbdb5c211.title: File:Full wafer of Intel quantum computers.jpg

en-7cf2acc6fa.attribution: “Optical atomic clock (5881387757)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Optical_atomic_clock_%285881387757%29.jpg
en-7cf2acc6fa.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-7cf2acc6fa.story: A computer illustration, not a photograph, published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (2006) of its optical atomic clock: two copper-coloured magnetic coils, crossing violet laser beams that cool ytterbium atoms, and a red beam forming the optical lattice; the atoms themselves are not drawn. It depicts a precision clock, not a quantum computer, but the same tools, laser cooling, magnetic fields and a lattice of light that holds atoms in place, underlie neutral-atom quantum computers.
en-7cf2acc6fa.title: File:Optical atomic clock (5881387757).jpg

en-7ed5bc3144.attribution: “Ring resonator in fiber laser” — Alex-engraver, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ring_resonator_in_fiber_laser.svg
en-7ed5bc3144.creator: Alex-engraver
en-7ed5bc3144.story: A black-and-white schematic drawing of a typical ring resonator for a fibre laser: a closed fibre loop with an active fibre coil (1), a polariser (2), an optical isolator (3) and a wavelength-division-multiplexing coupler (4) where pump light enters and laser output leaves. Drawn by Alex-engraver (2011). This is classical laser optics, not quantum-computing hardware; it shows how fibre ring cavities and fibre amplifiers, used in lasers and optical links around quantum systems, are put together.
en-7ed5bc3144.title: File:Ring resonator in fiber laser.svg

en-803c69464c.attribution: “Atomic Clockbeling002” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Atomic_Clockbeling002.jpg
en-803c69464c.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-803c69464c.story: A black-and-white photograph of a precision mechanical part captioned 'Adjustable center collimating slit': a machined flange with a rod carrying a small coil and slit piece, on a translation stage with a micrometer adjuster. Credited to the National Institute of Standards and Technology, from its atomic clock series; no date is recorded. In an atomic-beam clock, slits like this narrow the beam of atoms. It is historical clock hardware, not quantum-computing hardware, showing early precision control of atoms.
en-803c69464c.title: File:Atomic Clockbeling002.jpg

en-8070387b8d.attribution: “Dual comb chip” by Quantumavik, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Dual_comb_chip.png, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-8070387b8d.creator: Quantumavik
en-8070387b8d.story: An artist's impression, not a photograph, of a silicon nanophotonic chip for high-speed dual-comb spectroscopy: a pump laser enters at the right, travels along silicon nitride waveguides (blue) and is enhanced in two ring resonators with heaters on top, producing two frequency combs whose beat notes reach a detector. Made by Quantumavik (2016). It illustrates microring frequency combs on silicon nitride photonic chips, a building block also used in integrated photonics for quantum technologies; the floating spectrum cards are illustrative.
en-8070387b8d.title: File:Dual comb chip.png

en-812814991d.attribution: “Yoctonewton (5941075782)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Yoctonewton_%285941075782%29.jpg
en-812814991d.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-812814991d.story: A photograph of a NIST ion-trap force sensor: a stack of copper cylindrical electrodes held in a cage of white insulating rings and rods, with wires running along it. Per the National Institute of Standards and Technology caption (2010), a crystal of ions is trapped in the upper copper cylinder, cooled by an upward laser beam, and an applied oscillating electric force is measured from light reflected off the ions. It is a sensor, not a quantum computer, but shows cylindrical trap electrodes that hold ion crystals.
en-812814991d.title: File:Yoctonewton (5941075782).jpg

en-8143141f9b.attribution: “FMN Lab team (2)” by FMNLab, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FMN_Lab_team_%282%29.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-8143141f9b.creator: FMNLab
en-8143141f9b.story: A cleanroom photograph of an FMN Laboratory researcher assembling a neuromorphic processor based on a photonic integrated circuit, at a probe station where a microscope objective and multi-axis stages with fibre and probe holders converge on the sample. Posted by FMNLab (2021), whose caption describes low-loss processes from wafer surface preparation and thin-film deposition to nanoscale circuit patterning. The processor is for classical optical computing, not quantum computing, but similar photonic-chip fabrication and fibre alignment underpin photonic quantum hardware.
en-8143141f9b.title: File:FMN Lab team (2).jpg

en-81b2c4b6e2.attribution: “Fig-QResonator E RS” by RSchnabel, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fig-QResonator_E_RS.jpeg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-81b2c4b6e2.creator: RSchnabel
en-81b2c4b6e2.story: A drawing of a squeezing resonator: a pumped nonlinear crystal between two mirrors, with pump light at twice the frequency (2ν) entering from one side and the squeezed light at ν leaving through the partly transmitting mirror. It was drawn by RSchnabel and uploaded to Wikimedia Commons in 2018. This cavity is the standard way to make squeezed light, the continuous-variable resource used in quantum optics and sensing; note the fully reflecting back mirror so all squeezed light leaves one port.
en-81b2c4b6e2.title: File:Fig-QResonator E RS.jpeg

en-82838d16e2.creator: Mrqm
en-82838d16e2.story: Hand-drawn energy-level diagram, in the top third of an otherwise blank page, of two neutral atoms, each with qubit levels |0⟩ and |1⟩ and a highly excited Rydberg level |r⟩. A red laser arrow (Rabi frequency Ω) drives |1⟩ towards a dashed level a detuning Δ below |r⟩; a magenta double arrow V_rr marks the strong interaction when both atoms are in |r⟩. Drawn by the Commons user Mrqm (2023) as the level diagram of the interaction Hamiltonian of two atoms with Rydberg interaction. This is the principle of the Rydberg-blockade gate: |0⟩ is not driven, and |r⟩ is only an auxiliary level, not part of the qubit.
en-82838d16e2.title: File:TwoAtomRydbergSystem.jpg

en-82dd451405.attribution: “LevitatedDiamond GWMorley” by Gavin Morley, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:LevitatedDiamond_GWMorley.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-82dd451405.creator: Gavin Morley
en-82dd451405.story: A photograph through a vacuum viewport into a chamber lit purple and green, with cage plates, lens mounts and a focusing lens inside. By Gavin Morley (2017): the small green dot near the centre is a nanodiamond of about 40 nm levitated in vacuum by a focused infrared laser beam (optical tweezers), work described by Frangeskou and colleagues on nanodiamonds for levitated optomechanics. It shows an object held by light alone, the same trapping method used to hold single neutral atoms.
en-82dd451405.title: File:LevitatedDiamond GWMorley.jpg

en-8392350131.attribution: “Single-Photon Detector (14914818924)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Single-Photon_Detector_%2814914818924%29.jpg
en-8392350131.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-8392350131.story: A close-up photograph of a small keyhole-shaped chip made by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, holding a single-photon detector made of superconducting nanowires; the gold pad at the round end carries the active area, and the nanowire is too fine to see. According to NIST (2014), four chips like this were used in an experiment that entangled three photons. Such detectors, cooled to cryogenic temperatures, register single photons efficiently, which makes them central to photonic quantum experiments.
en-8392350131.title: File:Single-Photon Detector (14914818924).jpg

en-83a64870cf.attribution: “HYH532BZ1.5 - Junction circulator structure” by Mister rf, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HYH532BZ1.5_-_Junction_circulator_structure.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-83a64870cf.creator: Mister rf
en-83a64870cf.story: A studio photograph of a disassembled RF junction circulator (part HYH532BZ1.5, rated 925–960 MHz): a metal disc on a stack of white discs, with two tab terminals sticking out. It was posted on Wikimedia Commons by Mister rf in 2023. This is a classical telecom component, not quantum hardware, but circulators and isolators do the same job in qubit readout lines: they pass microwaves one way only, shielding qubits from amplifier noise. Notice the layered construction; in such devices the white discs are typically ferrite.
en-83a64870cf.title: File:HYH532BZ1.5 - Junction circulator structure.jpg

en-85055f5d6b.attribution: “D-Wave Two 512 qubit Vesuvius chip” by Steve Jurvetson, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:D-Wave_Two_512_qubit_Vesuvius_chip.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-85055f5d6b.creator: Steve Jurvetson
en-85055f5d6b.story: A photograph of the D-Wave Two 512-qubit Vesuvius chip mounted in its gold-plated package, ready for cooling to near absolute zero. Steve Jurvetson took it at D-Wave's Canadian headquarters during a board meeting (uploaded 2018). The processor is a quantum annealer built from superconducting rf-SQUID flux qubits. Notice how small the square silicon die at the centre is compared with the circuit board, connector strips and coaxial cables that carry its control and readout signals.
en-85055f5d6b.title: File:D-Wave Two 512 qubit Vesuvius chip.jpg

en-851045c8f3.creator: Mbeljaars
en-851045c8f3.story: A line drawing, not a photograph, of how small gas elements move and change temperature inside a pulse-tube cooler: near X2 a gas element enters at the low temperature TL and leaves colder, near X3 it enters at TH and leaves warmer. It was drawn by Mbeljaars in 2007, with a Dutch caption, though the file is named after the Carnot cycle. Pulse-tube cryocoolers provide the first cooling stages of most dry dilution refrigerators; notice there are no numbers, only the idea of heat being pumped along the tube.
en-851045c8f3.title: File:Carnotcycle.jpg

en-86e83707d9.attribution: “The inner optical setup of a femtosecond Titanium-Sapphire Pulsed laser” by Aksy88, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_inner_optical_setup_of_a_femtosecond_Titanium-Sapphire_Pulsed_laser.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-86e83707d9.creator: Aksy88
en-86e83707d9.story: Top-down photograph into the opened housing of a femtosecond titanium-sapphire pulsed laser, lit by green pump light: small mirror mounts, a slanted crystal assembly and prisms sit on a black perforated breadboard, crossed by a grey ribbon cable. Uploaded to Wikimedia Commons by Aksy88 (own work, 2016). The mirrors make the light bounce back and forth through the crystal, which amplifies it and builds up short pulses, while prisms, as usual in such lasers, compensate dispersion to keep the pulses short; notice how compact the cavity is. Ti:sapphire lasers are widely used in atomic physics, though nothing here is specific to quantum hardware.
en-86e83707d9.title: File:The inner optical setup of a femtosecond Titanium-Sapphire Pulsed laser.jpg

en-883b038553.attribution: “Laboratorium FAMO UMK A 234” by Ciacho5, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Laboratorium_FAMO_UMK_A_234.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-883b038553.creator: Ciacho5
en-883b038553.story: A photograph of the vacuum part of an ultracold-atom apparatus: steel vacuum chambers with a large window, joined by a tube wound with copper coils, inside an aluminium frame above optical tables. It was taken on 13 December 2016 at the National Laboratory of Atomic, Molecular and Optical Physics of Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, Poland. The coil-wound tube is likely a Zeeman slower, which slows a beam of atoms so they can be captured and cooled, the first step before atoms can serve as qubits.
en-883b038553.title: File:Laboratorium FAMO UMK A 234.jpg

en-8843b2ca88.attribution: “17jila003 3d strontium atomic clock” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:17jila003_3d_strontium_atomic_clock.jpg
en-8843b2ca88.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-8843b2ca88.story: A laboratory photograph of the upper optical table of JILA's three-dimensional quantum-gas atomic clock, released by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in 2017. A blue laser beam excites a cube-shaped cloud of strontium atoms behind the round window at the centre; the atoms fluoresce strongly in blue light. This is an optical lattice clock, not a quantum computer, but neutral-atom quantum computers use the same ingredients: strontium-type atoms, laser grids of light, lenses and an ultra-high-vacuum chamber.
en-8843b2ca88.title: File:17jila003 3d strontium atomic clock.jpg

en-88f5ad526b.creator: Stexparma
en-88f5ad526b.story: A photograph of the front of a rack-mount arbitrary waveform generator from the Active Technologies AWG-5000 series, posted by Stexparma in 2021. It is a classical test instrument, not quantum hardware; in quantum labs such generators synthesise the shaped microwave and baseband pulses that drive qubit gates and readout. Notice the eight differential channel outputs, the marker and trigger connectors used to synchronise equipment, and the pulse sequence editor on the touchscreen.
en-88f5ad526b.title: File:AWG5068.jpg

en-89293b8da4.creator: Christian Schirm
en-89293b8da4.story: An isometric drawing, not a photograph, of a resist-coated layer stack after development: a narrow line with two wider end openings is cut through a two-layer resist, and the lower resist layer is cut back so the top layer overhangs. It is step 6 of a 2011 Wikimedia Commons series on electron-beam lithography by Christian Schirm. Notice the undercut: this overhanging resist mask is what allows metal lift-off and angled (shadow) evaporation of Josephson junctions, though the drawing itself is generic and unlabelled.
en-89293b8da4.title: File:E-beam-litho 6.svg

en-892b2f5977.attribution: “STM at the London Centre for Nanotechnology” by O. Usher (UCL MAPS), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:STM_at_the_London_Centre_for_Nanotechnology.jpg, CC BY 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/)
en-892b2f5977.creator: O. Usher (UCL MAPS)
en-892b2f5977.story: A photograph of a large scanning tunnelling microscope system: a blue Oxford Instruments liquid-helium cryostat mounted above a stainless-steel ultra-high-vacuum chamber, with an access stair beside it. Its metadata says it stands in the labs of the London Centre for Nanotechnology (photo O. Usher, UCL MAPS, 2014). Such cold, vacuum-isolated STMs are the kind of tool used for atom-precise hydrogen lithography of donors in silicon, though the picture shows only the instrument, not the patterning.
en-892b2f5977.title: File:STM at the London Centre for Nanotechnology.jpg

en-8c478482a0.attribution: “Синтез фотонных материалов для Индустрии 4.0” by FMNLab, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%D0%A1%D0%B8%D0%BD%D1%82%D0%B5%D0%B7_%D1%84%D0%BE%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%BD%D0%BD%D1%8B%D1%85_%D0%BC%D0%B0%D1%82%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%B8%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%BE%D0%B2_%D0%B4%D0%BB%D1%8F_%D0%98%D0%BD%D0%B4%D1%83%D1%81%D1%82%D1%80%D0%B8%D0%B8_4.0.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-8c478482a0.creator: FMNLab
en-8c478482a0.story: A cleanroom photograph of a suited engineer at a vacuum process tool, with stacks of silicon wafers showing iridescent pink and green thin films. FMNLab posted it in 2022; the caption says an FMN Laboratory engineer is forming specialised materials for ultra-low-loss photonic integrated circuits, made at high temperature in vacuum chambers fed with very pure gases. Low optical loss matters for photonic quantum computing, where every lost photon is lost information. The colours come from light interfering in the thin films.
en-8c478482a0.title: File:Синтез фотонных материалов для Индустрии 4.0.jpg

en-8cdc0503bb.attribution: “FMN Lab single photon detector” by FMNLab, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FMN_Lab_single_photon_detector.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-8cdc0503bb.creator: FMNLab
en-8cdc0503bb.story: Scanning-electron micrograph (3 µm scale bar) of the sensitive element of a superconducting nanowire single-photon detector: a very thin wire folded back and forth to cover a diamond-shaped area. It comes from the FMN Laboratory (fmn.bmstu.ru); the micrograph is dated 21 Nov 2022 and the description says the film is 5 nm thick. Notice the tiny hairpin turns along the edges, where current crowding matters, and how densely the wire fills the area to absorb single photons.
en-8cdc0503bb.title: File:FMN Lab single photon detector.jpg

en-8cf42d1dc9.attribution: “Wignerfunction marginal projection” by Geek3, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wignerfunction_marginal_projection.png, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-8cf42d1dc9.creator: Geek3
en-8cf42d1dc9.story: Computer-drawn 3D surface plot of a Wigner function W(Q,P), the phase-space picture of a single light mode, here for a squeezed coherent state: one smooth peak set off from the origin. Its shadow, the marginal distribution pr(Q_θ, θ), appears as a bell curve on a yellow plane along the axis Q_θ, rotated by the angle θ from Q. Drawn by Geek3 with Mathematica (own work, Wikimedia Commons, 2019). The projected curve is what a homodyne detector measures at that phase; recording many angles lets one rebuild the state. Note that it shows a single peak, not a cat state, despite its Commons category.
en-8cf42d1dc9.title: File:Wignerfunction marginal projection.png

en-8e07ceffbf.attribution: “Flux qubit potential” by Srjmas, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Flux_qubit_potential.svg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-8e07ceffbf.creator: Srjmas
en-8e07ceffbf.story: A drawn energy diagram, not a measurement: a red potential curve against phase φ with a central double well, and the two lowest quantum states |0⟩ and |1⟩ drawn in blue; dashed curves are higher states. It was made by Srjmas in 2017 and captioned 'Flux qubit potential'. In a flux qubit the two wells correspond to current circulating one way or the other in a superconducting loop; notice that |0⟩ and |1⟩ spread over both wells, because tunnelling mixes the two current states. Quantum annealers use rf-SQUID flux qubits.
en-8e07ceffbf.title: File:Flux qubit potential.svg

en-8fd56f6b7f.attribution: “Molecular-beam epitaxy system at LAAS 0514” by Guillaume Paumier (user:guillom), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Molecular-beam_epitaxy_system_at_LAAS_0514.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-8fd56f6b7f.creator: Guillaume Paumier (user:guillom)
en-8fd56f6b7f.story: Photograph of a complete molecular-beam-epitaxy system in a clean room: a gold-coloured growth chamber with a ring of effusion cells and shutters, liquid-nitrogen hoses and a stainless transfer chamber on a blue frame. It was taken by Guillaume Paumier in October 2007 at the LAAS-CNRS technological facility in Toulouse, France. Molecular-beam epitaxy grows the III-V semiconductor layers used for quantum-dot photon sources and superconductor–semiconductor nanowires; notice the radial source cells aimed at the substrate.
en-8fd56f6b7f.title: File:Molecular-beam epitaxy system at LAAS 0514.jpg

en-8ff40bc499.attribution: “Alice and Bob Setup in a Polarization Quantum Entanglement Experiment” by Farbodk, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Alice_and_Bob_Setup_in_a_Polarization_Quantum_Entanglement_Experiment.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-8ff40bc499.creator: Farbodk
en-8ff40bc499.story: A labelled photograph of a tabletop polarization-entanglement experiment, posted by Farbodk in 2024. Two receiver stations, 'Alice' and 'Bob' (the usual names for two parties, not the company Alice & Bob), each have a fibre coupler, narrowband filter, polarizing beam splitter and rotatable half-wave plate; behind them are a single-photon counting module, an FPGA board counting coincidences and a laptop. It shows how photonic qubits encoded in polarization are measured: coincidence counts at different wave-plate angles reveal the entanglement.
en-8ff40bc499.title: File:Alice and Bob Setup in a Polarization Quantum Entanglement Experiment.jpg

en-901156cfdf.attribution: “Noiseless Amplifier (5941060720)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Noiseless_Amplifier_%285941060720%29.jpg
en-901156cfdf.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-901156cfdf.story: A colourised optical micrograph of the JILA/NIST 'noiseless' amplifier, released by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in 2008. A microwave line enters from the left and feeds a long chain of superconducting magnetic sensors, starting at the right, made of niobium–aluminium oxide–niobium sandwiches; together they form a metamaterial that selectively amplifies microwaves. Josephson parametric amplifiers like this read out superconducting qubits while adding almost no noise. Notice the identical repeated cells of the chain.
en-901156cfdf.title: File:Noiseless Amplifier (5941060720).jpg

en-919b653645.attribution: “Alice and Bob Cryostat” by Nilhope, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Alice_and_Bob_Cryostat.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-919b653645.creator: Nilhope
en-919b653645.story: A photograph of an open dilution-refrigerator insert with its shields removed, captioned as a quantum computer cryostat in the lab at Alice & Bob headquarters; posted by Nilhope in 2024. The fridge maker is not identifiable. Superconducting qubits must be cooled to millikelvin temperatures; notice the silver semi-rigid coaxial lines looping between the gold-coloured stage plates, the rows of inline attenuators and filters that cool and clean the signals, and the copper tower below the lowest plate where sample assemblies hang.
en-919b653645.title: File:Alice and Bob Cryostat.jpg

en-92119d29b3.attribution: “Original photo of oscilloscope traces (double exposure) (5940496029)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Original_photo_of_oscilloscope_traces_%28double_exposure%29_%285940496029%29.jpg
en-92119d29b3.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-92119d29b3.story: A scanned photograph of an analogue oscilloscope screen, a double exposure of two current-voltage traces, from the National Institute of Standards and Technology. Per the caption (credit Benz/NIST), in 1995 NIST showed the first quantized voltage steps in an array of 400 Josephson junctions, 1.7 by 1.7 micrometres, with niobium electrodes and gold-palladium barriers. This is voltage metrology, not quantum computing, but it rests on the same Josephson junction physics as superconducting qubits; notice the flat steps at equally spaced voltages.
en-92119d29b3.title: File:Original photo of oscilloscope traces (double exposure) (5940496029).jpg

en-926cafdefc.attribution: “Sandia-surface-junction-ion-trap NJP13.075018” by D L Moehring, C Highstrete, D Stick, K M Fortier, R Haltli, C Tigges and M G Blain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sandia-surface-junction-ion-trap_NJP13.075018.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-926cafdefc.creator: D L Moehring, C Highstrete, D Stick, K M Fortier, R Haltli, C Tigges and M G Blain
en-926cafdefc.story: A scanning electron micrograph of a Sandia surface-electrode ion trap with a Y-shaped junction, with an inset fluorescence image of a chain of 7 trapped ions. It comes from D L Moehring, C Highstrete, D Stick and colleagues (2011), cited as NJP 13 075018. Each trap has 47 independent DC electrodes; the RF electrodes are about 42.5 μm wide with 7 μm gaps. Junctions let ions be shuttled between arms, the key step of the quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architecture; notice the 100 µm scale bar.
en-926cafdefc.title: File:Sandia-surface-junction-ion-trap NJP13.075018.jpg

en-93ed191bff.attribution: “Molecular Beam Epitaxy System” by SJMW1987, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Molecular_Beam_Epitaxy_System.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-93ed191bff.creator: SJMW1987
en-93ed191bff.story: A close photograph of the source side of a molecular beam epitaxy system, a stainless-steel ultra-high-vacuum growth chamber, lit in magenta and blue. The caption says Sampson Wilcox took it in building 38 of MIT on 26 September 2016 (posted by SJMW1987 in 2019). Molecular beam epitaxy grows crystals layer by layer from heated source cells, and is used for III-V semiconductor heterostructures such as quantum-dot photon sources and hybrid nanowires. Notice the conical source ports, labelled PORT 9 and PORT 10, all aimed at the substrate.
en-93ed191bff.title: File:Molecular Beam Epitaxy System.jpg

en-940d509f11.attribution: “NV center in solid immersion lens” by David A. Hopper, Henry J. Shulevitz, Lee C. Bassett, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NV_center_in_solid_immersion_lens.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-940d509f11.creator: David A. Hopper, Henry J. Shulevitz, Lee C. Bassett
en-940d509f11.story: A two-part paper figure panel: a scanning electron micrograph of a dome-shaped solid immersion lens etched into diamond (1 µm scale bar), and a photoluminescence map showing a single NV centre at its middle, in photons per millisecond. It is by David A. Hopper, Henry J. Shulevitz and Lee C. Bassett (2018). The nitrogen-vacancy centre is a defect whose spin serves as a qubit; the lens, with the NV at its focus, directs its photons out of the diamond towards a detector, a setup often used for entanglement experiments.
en-940d509f11.title: File:NV center in solid immersion lens.jpg

en-94efd0010a.attribution: “The Beauty of Quantum Computers” by Steve Jurvetson, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Beauty_of_Quantum_Computers.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-94efd0010a.creator: Steve Jurvetson
en-94efd0010a.story: A photograph of a person holding a whole wafer of D-Wave quantum processors at the Age of AI conference, taken by Steve Jurvetson (uploaded 2018). Per the caption, three chip sizes are tiled across it, the same Washington architecture scaled to 500, 1000 and 2000 qubits; each chip is diced and wire-bonded. It shows that superconducting annealing processors are made with wafer-scale fabrication like ordinary chips. The rainbow colours are diffraction from the repeated pattern; individual circuits are too small to see.
en-94efd0010a.title: File:The Beauty of Quantum Computers.jpg

en-952e738133.attribution: “Bose-Einstein Condensate (5941063056)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bose-Einstein_Condensate_%285941063056%29.jpg
en-952e738133.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-952e738133.story: A photograph of a clear glass vacuum cell holding four small glass squares on a frosted holder, released by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in 2011 (credit: E. Cornell group/JILA). Per the caption, a Bose-Einstein condensate was held a few micrometres below one square, and its wiggling measured how temperature changes the Casimir-Polder force; warmer glass pulled the atoms harder. This is a precision-physics experiment, not a quantum computer, but neutral-atom machines also trap atoms inside glass cells, where surface forces matter.
en-952e738133.title: File:Bose-Einstein Condensate (5941063056).jpg

en-95d358522b.attribution: “HYH532BZ1.5” by Mister rf, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HYH532BZ1.5.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-95d358522b.creator: Mister rf
en-95d358522b.story: A studio photograph of a palm-sized, nickel-plated RF isolator/circulator, part HYH532BZ1.5, whose label shows the 925–960 MHz band and an arrow from port 1 to port 2. It is credited on Wikimedia Commons to 'Mister rf', dated 2023-02-15. This is a classical room-temperature telecom part, not quantum-computing hardware, but it shows the principle: magnetised ferrite lets microwave energy flow in one direction only. Superconducting quantum computers use cryogenic versions of this idea to shield qubits from noise travelling back from amplifiers.
en-95d358522b.title: File:HYH532BZ1.5.jpg

en-97a34798b4.creator: Torsten Henning
en-97a34798b4.story: Two panels: (a) left, a scanning electron micrograph (100 nm scale bar) of a single-electron transistor, two bright tapered leads meeting a thin horizontal island strip, with parallel bright bars below; (b) right, a drawing of the same area marking the niobium source and drain (red) and aluminium/aluminium-oxide shapes (blue), the central one the island. From Torsten Henning's PhD thesis 'Charging effects in niobium nanostructures' (Chalmers and Göteborg University, 1999; arXiv cond-mat/9901308); the micrograph is labelled '#743 971030'. Such transistors are sensitive charge sensors, as used for spin-to-charge readout of spin qubits; the parallel bars are stray shadow copies left by angle evaporation.
en-97a34798b4.title: File:TySETimage.png

en-98167870cf.attribution: “Micrograph of a SQUID amplifier (13586380573)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Micrograph_of_a_SQUID_amplifier_%2813586380573%29.jpg
en-98167870cf.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-98167870cf.story: An optical micrograph of a superconducting SQUID amplifier: four octagonal spiral coils surround two tiny squares in the centre, which are the SQUIDs; the scale bar is 40 micrometres. According to its record it was made at NIST in 2012 as part of a circuit that reads signals from arrays of superconducting sensors. Notice how small currents in the coils make magnetic fields that the SQUID detects, the same Josephson technology used in superconducting quantum circuits.
en-98167870cf.title: File:Micrograph of a SQUID amplifier (13586380573).jpg

en-992cf46095.attribution: “J nanoph-2019-0196 fig 001” by Jason M. Smith, Simon A. Meynell, Ania C. Bleszynski Jayich and Jan Meijer, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:J_nanoph-2019-0196_fig_001.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-992cf46095.creator: Jason M. Smith, Simon A. Meynell, Ania C. Bleszynski Jayich and Jan Meijer
en-992cf46095.story: A drawn paper figure (figure 1 of article nanoph-2019-0196) by Jason M. Smith, Simon A. Meynell, Ania C. Bleszynski Jayich and Jan Meijer, 2019, showing how nitrogen-vacancy centres are made in diamond. Step 1 adds nitrogen by plasma-assisted growth or implantation; step 2 creates vacancies by laser, ion implantation or electron irradiation; step 3 heats the crystal above 850 °C. The central inset shows the result: a nitrogen atom next to a missing carbon atom, the defect whose electron spin serves as a qubit.
en-992cf46095.title: File:J nanoph-2019-0196 fig 001.jpg

en-9ab15298fd.attribution: “ALMA assembled cryostat (max 016319s)” by ESO/Max Alexander, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ALMA_assembled_cryostat_%28max_016319s%29.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-9ab15298fd.creator: ESO/Max Alexander
en-9ab15298fd.story: A photograph of a large open cryostat being assembled: inside the blue vessel, a gold-coloured cold plate carries receiver assemblies and coiled wiring, while a technician works on it. The photo is by ESO/Max Alexander and shows the ALMA assembled cryostat, as its title states. It is not a link between two refrigerators but a radio-astronomy receiver cryostat; notice the shield, the cold plate and the wiring loops, the same building blocks used to cool quantum chips.
en-9ab15298fd.title: File:ALMA assembled cryostat (max 016319s).jpg

en-9c34223a2e.attribution: “Mojo v3 FPGA Development Board (9303578174)” by SparkFun Electronics from Boulder, USA, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mojo_v3_FPGA_Development_Board_%289303578174%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-9c34223a2e.creator: SparkFun Electronics from Boulder, USA
en-9c34223a2e.story: A product photograph of the Mojo v3, a small hobbyist FPGA development board built around a Xilinx Spartan-6 chip, with a microcontroller, USB port, eight LEDs and header strips. It is a SparkFun Electronics photo dated 2013-07-16. This is a classical device, not quantum-computing hardware; it stands in for the programmable logic that, in much larger form, sequences control pulses and processes fast measurement feedback in quantum-computer control stacks.
en-9c34223a2e.title: File:Mojo v3 FPGA Development Board (9303578174).jpg

en-9d93d53ba0.attribution: “N-V charge control PL maps” by C. Schreyvogel, V. Polyakov, R. Wunderlich, J. Meijer & C. E. Nebel, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:N-V_charge_control_PL_maps.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-9d93d53ba0.creator: C. Schreyvogel, V. Polyakov, R. Wunderlich, J. Meijer & C. E. Nebel
en-9d93d53ba0.story: A composite paper figure by C. Schreyvogel, V. Polyakov, R. Wunderlich, J. Meijer and C. E. Nebel (2015). The top draws an aluminium Schottky diode on hydrogen-terminated diamond, a laser focused at the contact edge; below are two false-colour confocal photoluminescence maps, 10 × 20 µm. Without bias (a) the contact edge is a plain boundary; with bias (b) bright spots appear in the depletion region. It shows the charge state of nitrogen-vacancy centres being switched electrically, which decides whether they fluoresce and work as spin qubits.
en-9d93d53ba0.title: File:N-V charge control PL maps.jpg

en-9de438fc17.attribution: “Entangled link - Barb - DARPA Quantum Network - P1010012” — Daderot, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Entangled_link_-_Barb_-_DARPA_Quantum_Network_-_P1010012.jpg
en-9de438fc17.creator: Daderot
en-9de438fc17.story: A photograph of an open equipment rack holding single-photon detectors, a delay box, an FPGA board, fibre-optic drawers and power supplies. Its Commons record calls it 'Barb', one end of the entangled link in the DARPA Quantum Network, BBN laboratory, December 2004, made by Boston University and BBN. It shows everything a quantum key distribution receiver needs besides the optics: photon counters, timing and fibre handling.
en-9de438fc17.title: File:Entangled link - Barb - DARPA Quantum Network - P1010012.jpg

en-9ee227a7b6.attribution: “MSS1 CDSM flight model” by A. Pollinger, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:MSS1_CDSM_flight_model.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-9ee227a7b6.creator: A. Pollinger
en-9ee227a7b6.story: Photograph of the flight model of the scalar magnetometer (CDSM) for the Macau Science 1 satellite: a cylindrical sensor head on mounts, a white cable harness, two orange optical fibres and an opened electronics box. Photo by A. Pollinger, dated 2021-12-20, on Wikimedia Commons; the description calls it an optical magnetometer used as the baseline to calibrate the satellite's fluxgate sensors. It is an optically pumped atomic magnetometer, not a SQUID despite its Commons category; notice the fibre-fed sensor head kept apart from its electronics.
en-9ee227a7b6.title: File:MSS1 CDSM flight model.jpg

en-a0dfc41a71.creator: RuinDig/Yuki Uchida
en-a0dfc41a71.story: A photograph of Fujitsu's quantum-computer exhibit at the Japan Mobility Show 2025 at Tokyo Big Sight, in the 'Tokyo Future Tour 2035' booth, taken by RuinDig/Yuki Uchida on 2025-10-31. A lit showcase holds the open dilution-refrigerator 'chandelier': stacked plates, gold-coloured cold stages and dense coaxial wiring, flanked by video screens. Notice how much wiring runs down through the stages: each line carries control or readout signals from room-temperature electronics to the superconducting chip at the bottom.
en-a0dfc41a71.title: File:Japan-Mobility-Show-2025-RuinDig 0570.jpg

en-a1b8f03f56.attribution: “D-Wave Two quantum computer inside the NASA Advanced Supercomputing Facility” by Oleg Alexandrov, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:D-Wave_Two_quantum_computer_inside_the_NASA_Advanced_Supercomputing_Facility.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-a1b8f03f56.creator: Oleg Alexandrov
en-a1b8f03f56.story: A photograph by Oleg Alexandrov (2017-02-15) of the D-Wave Two quantum computer inside the NASA Advanced Supercomputing Division building. The tall black enclosure with the lit D-Wave logo houses the refrigerator and magnetic shielding; the three glass-door racks in front hold classical control electronics. D-Wave Two is a quantum annealer built from superconducting flux qubits. Notice that the processor itself is not visible: almost all of the machine's size goes into cooling, shielding and room-temperature electronics.
en-a1b8f03f56.title: File:D-Wave Two quantum computer inside the NASA Advanced Supercomputing Facility.jpg

en-a26c59e95e.attribution: “Josephson Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifier (J-TWPA)” by OJB Quantum, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Josephson_Traveling_Wave_Parametric_Amplifier_%28J-TWPA%29.png, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-a26c59e95e.creator: OJB Quantum
en-a26c59e95e.story: A computer render, not a photograph, of a Josephson Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifier chip wire-bonded to a carrier, made by OJB Quantum and dated 2025-09-11. Its caption says the layout is to scale, drawn in KLayout and rendered in Blender. The meandering coplanar waveguide is lined with many Josephson junctions and crossed by air bridges. Such amplifiers are the first stage in dispersive readout of superconducting qubits, adding little noise over a wide bandwidth so many qubit signals can be read at once.
en-a26c59e95e.title: File:Josephson Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifier (J-TWPA).png

en-a3b43d0e17.attribution: “Wave packet squeezed states” by Gerd Breitenbach, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wave_packet_squeezed_states.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)
en-a3b43d0e17.creator: Gerd Breitenbach
en-a3b43d0e17.story: A scanned figure of five 3D data plots of measured wave packets of squeezed states of light, by Gerd Breitenbach, dated 1998-07-16. Each plot shows the probability distribution of a light-field quadrature as the measurement phase runs from 0 to 2π. In the top panel the ridge keeps a constant width; in the lower panels width and position oscillate with phase, narrow in one direction and broad in the other. That reduced noise in one quadrature is squeezing, the resource behind continuous-variable photonic quantum computing.
en-a3b43d0e17.title: File:Wave packet squeezed states.jpg

en-a3f4d1067e.creator: Mrqm
en-a3f4d1067e.story: Hand-drawn sketch of how a two-atom controlled-Z gate works: two level pairs (|01⟩ to |0r⟩, and |11⟩ to the shared blockaded state |b⟩) each driven by a detuned laser, the second one √2 times faster, with a Bloch sphere beside each showing the state's path out and back during two pulses. Made by Mrqm and shared on Wikimedia Commons in December 2023 as the Levine–Pichler gate for neutral-atom quantum computing using Rydberg blockade. Notice the √2 speed-up: blockade forbids both atoms being in the Rydberg state, which gives the two-qubit phase; the Rydberg level is visited only during the gate.
en-a3f4d1067e.title: File:PitchlerGate.jpg

en-a488842ed4.attribution: “Quantum refrigerator at UCL (17626619658)” by UCL Mathematical and Physical Sciences from London, UK, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Quantum_refrigerator_at_UCL_%2817626619658%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-a488842ed4.creator: UCL Mathematical and Physical Sciences from London, UK
en-a488842ed4.story: Photograph of the inside of a dilution refrigerator with its outer cans removed, showing gold-plated stage plates, copper braid heat links, a pumping bellows and wiring at centimetre scale.
