According to its Commons record it was published by UCL Mathematical and Physical Sciences in 2015 and shows a UCL fridge whose stages run from about 50 K down to 0.03 K. It illustrates how millikelvin cryostats used for superconducting and other solid-state quantum devices are built; it is not neutral-atom hardware.
en-a488842ed4.title: File:Quantum refrigerator at UCL (17626619658).jpg

en-a5efe544ed.attribution: “Flux qubit circuit” by Srjmas, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Flux_qubit_circuit.svg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-a5efe544ed.creator: Srjmas
en-a5efe544ed.story: A circuit diagram, drawn by Srjmas in 2017, of the flux qubit: a superconducting loop containing an inductor L and a Josephson junction EJ, with magnetic flux Φ applied through a coil driven by a current I0. Textbook physics: the flux through the loop tilts its energy landscape, and near half a flux quantum two states with current circulating in opposite directions form the qubit. This rf-SQUID-type loop is the building block of the qubits in quantum annealers.
en-a5efe544ed.title: File:Flux qubit circuit.svg

en-a62f85e807.attribution: “Lampes électroniques (51256664052)” by Frédéric BISSON from Rouen, France, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lampes_%C3%A9lectroniques_%2851256664052%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-a62f85e807.creator: Frédéric BISSON from Rouen, France
en-a62f85e807.story: A photograph of two glass electron tubes: an old red ECH3 radio valve and a Hamamatsu R3788 side-on photomultiplier tube, whose curved electron-multiplying electrodes show through the glass. According to the file description, the valve dates from the 1930s and the photomultiplier model was still marketed in 2022; the photographer is from Rouen. Photomultiplier tubes count single photons and are one of the usual detectors for reading out trapped-ion qubits by their fluorescence; this is the detector alone, not an ion experiment.
en-a62f85e807.title: File:Lampes électroniques (51256664052).jpg

en-a678eefc32.attribution: “Planar Ion Trap (5941086002)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Planar_Ion_Trap_%285941086002%29.jpg
en-a678eefc32.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-a678eefc32.story: An optical micrograph of a planar (surface-electrode) ion trap chip from the National Institute of Standards and Technology, dated 2006-06-30. Per its caption, gold electrodes confine magnesium ions 40 micrometres above the chip surface, lasers create the ions from metal vapour, and the design was meant to be easy to mass-produce. Notice that all electrodes lie in one plane, converging on the thin central slit where ions are held, with leads running out to wire-bonded pads; this is what makes the trap buildable with standard microfabrication.
en-a678eefc32.title: File:Planar Ion Trap (5941086002).jpg

en-a680689d46.creator: Qupybara
en-a680689d46.story: A drawing, not a photograph, of a linear ion trap by Qupybara, dated 2024-05-16: four blade electrodes surround a single ion, two end-cap electrodes sit on the trap axis, and a laser beam illuminates the ion. Textbook operation: radio-frequency voltage on the blades holds the ion radially, static voltage on the end caps holds it along the axis. Lasers cool the ion, drive gates on its internal states and read it out, which is the basis of trapped-ion quantum computing.
en-a680689d46.title: File:Ion trap.svg

en-a6a0e3ec1a.creator: Christian Schirm
en-a6a0e3ec1a.story: A simple coloured drawing, not a photograph, of a layered sample after metal (blue) has been evaporated over a patterned two-layer resist; the lower resist is undercut, so the metal in the opened track is cut off from the metal on top. It is step 7 ('Bedampfen', evaporation) of Christian Schirm's lithography drawing series on Wikimedia Commons (2011). It explains the lift-off stage that follows electron-beam exposure, the route used to make fine metal wiring and junctions in superconducting circuits.
en-a6a0e3ec1a.title: File:E-beam-litho 7.svg

en-a7d204ad40.attribution: “Embedded World 2014 Oszilloskop und Funktionsgenerator” — Ordercrazy, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Embedded_World_2014_Oszilloskop_und_Funktionsgenerator.jpg
en-a7d204ad40.creator: Ordercrazy
en-a7d204ad40.story: A photograph by Ordercrazy at Embedded World 2014 (dated 2014-02-27) of two HAMEG/Rohde & Schwarz bench instruments: an HMO 3004 oscilloscope on top of an HMF 2550 arbitrary waveform generator. A cable links the generator output to the scope, which displays the generated signal. These are general-purpose classical instruments, not quantum-computing hardware; they stand in for the much faster arbitrary waveform generators that synthesise the precisely timed control pulses driving qubits.
en-a7d204ad40.title: File:Embedded World 2014 Oszilloskop und Funktionsgenerator.jpg

en-a80cef7322.attribution: “Strontium Clock (12196092854)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Strontium_Clock_%2812196092854%29.jpg
en-a80cef7322.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-a80cef7322.story: A photograph from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (2012-11-09) of JILA's experimental strontium atomic clock, which the caption calls the world's most precise and stable atomic clock. Per the caption, it is a composite of long exposures that makes the laser beams visible around the central vacuum chamber and dense optics. This is a clock, not a quantum computer, but it uses the same toolkit as neutral-atom quantum computing: laser-cooled atoms held in a lattice of laser light inside an ultra-high-vacuum chamber.
en-a80cef7322.title: File:Strontium Clock (12196092854).jpg

en-a849974ac2.creator: Rolancito
en-a849974ac2.story: Computed drawing in four panels of a single ion's path in a radio-frequency Paul trap, over coloured arrows of the trap's electric field: the orange curve is the slow secular motion, the blue loops the actual path with the fast micromotion wiggle. (a) Top left, a circular orbit around the trap centre; (b) top right, straight-line motion through the centre, where the wiggle vanishes; (c, d) bottom, the same motions pushed off-centre by a stray field, with much larger wiggles. Drawn by the Commons user Rolancito (own work, 2021), citing Berkeland et al. Trapped-ion quantum computers must cancel this excess micromotion, which disturbs the ion's laser-driven transitions.
en-a849974ac2.title: File:Micromotion.png

en-a95addee08.attribution: “Quantum Computer with Dark Background 001” by OJB Quantum, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Quantum_Computer_with_Dark_Background_001.png, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-a95addee08.creator: OJB Quantum
en-a95addee08.story: A computer render of a dilution refrigerator's inner 'chandelier' on a plain black background: six stacked plates, wavy copper and gold ribbon cables with connectors at every stage, and fine wires reaching a small sample mount at the bottom. It was made by OJB Quantum and shared on Wikimedia Commons. It shows how high-density cryogenic flex cables, rather than individual coaxial lines, can carry control signals down to a quantum processor; it is an idealised render.
en-a95addee08.title: File:Quantum Computer with Dark Background 001.png

en-a9c2c10593.attribution: “Dual comb schematic” by Quantumavik, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Dual_comb_schematic.png, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-a9c2c10593.creator: Quantumavik
en-a9c2c10593.story: A schematic by Quantumavik (2016-10-07) of dual-comb spectroscopy using chip-scale silicon nanophotonics: light from a dual comb source passes a sample cuvette of CH2Cl2 molecules to a photodetector and RF spectral analysis. The right panel is a real optical micrograph of the chip, with two microring resonators (R1, R2) and metal heater leads (20 µm scale bar). It is a spectroscopy set-up, not quantum hardware, but microring resonators on a photonic chip are also a common way to generate light for integrated photonic quantum sources.
en-a9c2c10593.title: File:Dual comb schematic.png

en-aa25554ed9.attribution: “A Wafer of the Latest D-Wave Quantum Computers (39188583425)” by Steve Jurvetson from Menlo Park, USA, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_Wafer_of_the_Latest_D-Wave_Quantum_Computers_%2839188583425%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-aa25554ed9.creator: Steve Jurvetson from Menlo Park, USA
en-aa25554ed9.story: An oblique photograph by Steve Jurvetson (2018-02-01) of an undiced wafer that its caption describes as holding D-Wave quantum computers: a regular grid of roughly 120 square dies separated by dicing lanes. Each die is presumably one annealing processor; the individual qubit loops are too small to see at this scale. It shows that these superconducting processors are made like ordinary chips, many at a time on a wafer by lithography; the rainbow tints are thin-film interference, not colour of the circuits.
en-aa25554ed9.title: File:A Wafer of the Latest D-Wave Quantum Computers (39188583425).jpg

en-aa863e66bd.attribution: “Schematic pulstuberefridgerator” by Mbeljaars, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Schematic_pulstuberefridgerator.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)
en-aa863e66bd.creator: Mbeljaars
en-aa863e66bd.story: Line drawing (not a photograph) of a Stirling-type single-orifice pulse-tube refrigerator, labelled in Dutch: compressor piston, heat exchanger X1, regenerator, cold heat exchanger X2, the empty pulse tube ('pulsbuis'), heat exchanger X3, an orifice and a buffer volume. Uploaded to Wikimedia Commons by Mbeljaars in June 2007. Pulse-tube coolers provide the upper cooling stages of dry dilution refrigerators; notice that the cold end (X2) has no moving parts, since the oscillating gas in the tube does the cooling.
en-aa863e66bd.title: File:Schematic pulstuberefridgerator.jpg

en-ad5f3922b8.attribution: “Quantum Computing; Ion Trapping (5941055642)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Quantum_Computing%3B_Ion_Trapping_%285941055642%29.jpg
en-ad5f3922b8.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-ad5f3922b8.story: Photograph of an ion-trap apparatus: a small square gold trap chip under a fine wire mesh, clamped at the centre of a gold-plated circuit board with filter components, orange wiring and an RF connector, inside a copper housing. From the National Institute of Standards and Technology (2011); per the caption, NIST physicists used it to make two beryllium ions, trapped about 40 micrometres apart above the chip, swap the smallest units of energy. It shows how a tiny surface-electrode trap chip is packaged, wired and filtered.
en-ad5f3922b8.title: File:Quantum Computing; Ion Trapping (5941055642).jpg

en-ad91127a07.attribution: “Entangled link - Alex optical system - DARPA Quantum Network - P1010004” — Daderot, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Entangled_link_-_Alex_optical_system_-_DARPA_Quantum_Network_-_P1010004.jpg
en-ad91127a07.creator: Daderot
en-ad91127a07.story: A photograph of a laboratory optical table with a Ti:sapphire laser, a green pump laser and small fibre-coupled optics, with control electronics on a shelf above. According to its Commons record it is the 'Alex' optical system of the entangled link in the DARPA Quantum Network, in the BBN laboratory, December 2004, built by Boston University and BBN. It shows how an entangled photon source for quantum key distribution looked on a real bench; note it is photonic, not an ion-photon link.
en-ad91127a07.title: File:Entangled link - Alex optical system - DARPA Quantum Network - P1010004.jpg

en-ae578cc717.creator: Farbodk
en-ae578cc717.story: Schematic drawing, in paper-figure style, of three mobile robots: a leader robot makes entangled photon pairs in a nonlinear crystal and steers them with motorised mirrors to receiver robots Alice and Bob, which track the beams and send the photons by fibre to single-photon counters, an FPGA and a PC. Uploaded by Farbodk (2024-10-01) as 'Alice and Bob Quantum Robots Schematic Representation'. It illustrates single-photon entanglement distribution; 'Alice' and 'Bob' are the conventional names for two parties, not the company Alice & Bob.
en-ae578cc717.title: File:Fig1AliceBobQuantumRobotSchematic.jpg

en-b00879b63f.attribution: “Molecular-beam epitaxy system at LAAS 0506” by Guillaume Paumier (user:guillom), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Molecular-beam_epitaxy_system_at_LAAS_0506.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-b00879b63f.creator: Guillaume Paumier (user:guillom)
en-b00879b63f.story: A photograph of a complete molecular beam epitaxy installation in a clean room: a gold-coloured growth chamber joined to a row of steel vacuum chambers by a long transfer line, with pumps under the table and control racks beside it. The caption places it at the LAAS-CNRS technological facility in Toulouse, photographed by Guillaume Paumier in October 2007. Machines like this grow the layered III-V semiconductor crystals used for quantum-dot photon sources and semiconductor–superconductor nanowires; notice the RIBER labels and how wafers move between chambers without leaving vacuum.
en-b00879b63f.title: File:Molecular-beam epitaxy system at LAAS 0506.jpg

en-b0bd2cfda2.attribution: “Planar Ion Trap; Magnesium Ions (5884514798)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Planar_Ion_Trap%3B_Magnesium_Ions_%285884514798%29.jpg
en-b0bd2cfda2.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-b0bd2cfda2.story: Five false-colour camera images (not an ordinary photograph) of 1, 2, 3, 6 and 12 magnesium ions held in a line in NIST's then-new planar ion trap; each bright spot is one ion's fluorescence, red marking the brightest light. From the National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2006. Notice the ions squeezing closer as more are loaded until the 12-ion string buckles into a zig-zag, the balance between their mutual repulsion and the trap's confinement. Reading ions out by their fluorescence is standard in trapped-ion computing.
en-b0bd2cfda2.title: File:Planar Ion Trap; Magnesium Ions (5884514798).jpg

en-b0fc3ec5e1.creator: Geek3
en-b0fc3ec5e1.story: A computer-drawn 3D plot of the magnetic field strength around two circular coils carrying opposite currents (anti-Helmholtz arrangement). It was made by Geek3 and published on Wikimedia Commons in 2018. The field is zero at the centre and grows steadily outward; this gradient is what lets a magneto-optical trap push laser-cooled atoms back to the middle. Notice the four peaks at the coil wires and the sharp dip at the centre. It is a principle drawing, not a real apparatus.
en-b0fc3ec5e1.title: File:Anti-Helmholtz-coil-field-3D.png

en-b346a07fe4.attribution: “Model of nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond” by Materialscientist, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Model_of_nitrogen-vacancy_center_in_diamond.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-b346a07fe4.creator: Materialscientist
en-b346a07fe4.story: Ball-and-stick drawing (not a photograph) of a small cube of diamond lattice: white carbon atoms joined by bonds, one blue nitrogen atom 'N' beside an empty lattice site, and a small circle 'e' marking the extra electron of the negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy (NV-) centre. Credited to Materialscientist on Wikimedia Commons, undated. It shows the atomic structure of the defect whose electron spin serves as a qubit or sensor: a nitrogen replacing one carbon, paired with a missing neighbouring atom.
en-b346a07fe4.title: File:Model of nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond.jpg

en-b387bdd90d.attribution: “Josephson Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifier (J-TWPA) 002” by OJB Quantum, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Josephson_Traveling_Wave_Parametric_Amplifier_%28J-TWPA%29_002.png, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-b387bdd90d.creator: OJB Quantum
en-b387bdd90d.story: Computer render (not a photograph) of a Josephson travelling-wave parametric amplifier chip: a meandering coplanar-waveguide line lined with Josephson junctions and air bridges, with tapered launchers wire-bonded to gold pads on a carrier. Made by OJB Quantum (2025) in Blender from a to-scale KLayout layout; this version has glossy, reflective surfaces. Such amplifiers boost the faint microwave readout signals of superconducting qubits while adding very little noise; notice the long, periodic junction-loaded line along which the signal is amplified.
en-b387bdd90d.title: File:Josephson Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifier (J-TWPA) 002.png

en-b39945cc8d.attribution: “QuEra Aquila Optical Layout” by QuEra Computing, Inc., https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:QuEra_Aquila_Optical_Layout.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-b39945cc8d.creator: QuEra Computing, Inc.
en-b39945cc8d.story: Photograph of an optical table under blue-violet light, packed with mirrors in kinematic mounts, lenses, beam-splitter cubes, a fibre launch and enclosed laser housings. Credited to QuEra Computing, Inc. (2023) as the optical table and layout of QuEra's first-generation neutral-atom quantum computer, Aquila. It shows how much free-space optics is needed to deliver and shape the laser beams that trap, move and excite the atoms; the vacuum cell holding the atoms is not visible here.
en-b39945cc8d.title: File:QuEra Aquila Optical Layout.jpg

en-b47b792c42.attribution: “Cat Qubit Boson Chip” by SachaAB, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_Qubit_Boson_Chip.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-b47b792c42.creator: SachaAB
en-b47b792c42.story: Photograph of a small square superconducting chip held in tweezers by a gloved hand, beside a machined metal sample holder engraved with a cat-head logo; the chip is labelled 'GCT-0004-09' and carries two mirrored circuits with feedlines and launch pads. Uploaded by SachaAB (2022) as 'Cat Qubit Boson Chip'; the caption says such chips use superconducting circuits to generate, stabilise and control cat qubits. Cat qubits store information in two coherent states of a microwave resonator, which makes bit-flip errors very rare.
en-b47b792c42.title: File:Cat Qubit Boson Chip.jpg

en-b6ba82018a.attribution: “BEC-cavity-experiment-drawing NJP17.043012” by Alicia J Kollár, Alexander T Papageorge, Kristian Baumann, Michael A Armen and Benjamin L Lev, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BEC-cavity-experiment-drawing_NJP17.043012.jpg, CC BY 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/)
en-b6ba82018a.creator: Alicia J Kollár, Alexander T Papageorge, Kristian Baumann, Michael A Armen and Benjamin L Lev
en-b6ba82018a.story: Computer rendering (not a photograph) of a cold-atom apparatus: rubidium oven, Zeeman slower, ultracold-gas chamber with vacuum pumps, and a cavity science chamber on vibration isolation, with a red line tracing the optical-tweezer path; an inset photograph shows the multimode cavity inside the chamber. From Kollár, Papageorge, Baumann, Armen and Lev (2015): an adjustable-length cavity and Bose-Einstein condensate apparatus for multimode cavity QED. Notice how large the vacuum and transport hardware is compared with the cavity where atoms and light interact.
en-b6ba82018a.title: File:BEC-cavity-experiment-drawing NJP17.043012.jpg

en-b80767d180.creator: Geek3
en-b80767d180.story: Data plot of the optical squeezing achieved in published laboratory experiments versus year, in decibels, rising from about 0.3 dB in 1986 to a peak near 15 dB around 2016. Made by Geek3 (2018); values are raw measurements without correction for detection losses. Squeezed light, whose noise in one quadrature is below the vacuum level, is the basic resource of continuous-variable photonic quantum computing; notice the gap around 1999-2006 and the steep rise above 10 dB afterwards.
en-b80767d180.title: File:Squeezed-light-timeline.svg

en-b8ddce29f2.attribution: “Modulateur d'intensité optique 1” by Christophe.Finot, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Modulateur_d%27intensit%C3%A9_optique_1.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-b8ddce29f2.creator: Christophe.Finot
en-b8ddce29f2.story: Photograph of a fibre-pigtailed integrated-optic intensity modulator in its foam-lined box: a slim metal package labelled 'OTI 10 Gb/s Integrated Optic Intensity Modulator' with RF/bias connectors and fibre pigtails ending in FC connectors. Taken by Christophe.Finot (2011); the caption says it is older equipment from the Laboratoire de Physique, Université de Bourgogne, now used for teaching. It is a classical telecom component, not quantum hardware, but similar electro-optic modulators shape and switch laser light in photonic, ion and atom experiments.
en-b8ddce29f2.title: File:Modulateur d'intensité optique 1.jpg

en-b9587cbb75.attribution: “IQM Quantum Computers Design” by Ragsxl, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IQM_Quantum_Computers_Design.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-b9587cbb75.creator: Ragsxl
en-b9587cbb75.story: A computer render of three white, rounded cabinets with teal light strips and an IQM logo; the front unit is open and shows a hanging cryostat vessel. It is recorded on Wikimedia Commons as 'IQM Quantum Computers Design' by Ragsxl (2020). It shows how a superconducting quantum computer's cryostat might be housed as a finished product; it is a design render, and the metadata does not say it is an actual IQM machine.
en-b9587cbb75.title: File:IQM Quantum Computers Design.jpg

en-bb68f05b5c.attribution: “Superconducting Quantum-Limited Amplifier Chip in Navaho” by OJB Quantum, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Superconducting_Quantum-Limited_Amplifier_Chip_in_Navaho.png, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-bb68f05b5c.creator: OJB Quantum
en-bb68f05b5c.story: Two-panel rendered figure (not a photograph): left, a Josephson travelling-wave parametric amplifier chip with its meandering junction-loaded line, wire bonds and gold pads; right, a zoomed close-up of one Josephson junction (top electrode, thin barrier, bottom electrode) labelled in the Navajo language. Made by OJB Quantum (2025). The junction, two superconductors separated by a very thin insulating barrier, is the nonlinear element that lets the amplifier boost faint qubit readout signals; the zoom shows the small element repeated along the whole line.
en-bb68f05b5c.title: File:Superconducting Quantum-Limited Amplifier Chip in Navaho.png

en-bbf37bde06.creator: Christian Schirm
en-bbf37bde06.story: A simple coloured drawing, not a photograph, of a layered sample being written by an electron beam: the beam exposes a narrow, constricted track in the resist layers on top of a thin film and substrate. It is step 4 of a lithography drawing series by Christian Schirm on Wikimedia Commons (2011). It shows the core step of electron-beam lithography, the method used to pattern fine features such as the junctions of superconducting qubits; the layers are generic and not tied to any material.
en-bbf37bde06.title: File:E-beam-litho 5.svg

en-bc80a3cdcd.attribution: “Gold Ion Trap (6029437325)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gold_Ion_Trap_%286029437325%29.jpg
en-bc80a3cdcd.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-bc80a3cdcd.story: Photograph of a square gold surface-electrode ion-trap chip, 7.4 millimetres on a side, on an aluminium nitride backing with ribbon bonds, surface-mount parts and three wide gold transmission lines. From the National Institute of Standards and Technology (2011); per the caption, in NIST microwave quantum-computing experiments two ions hover above the middle of the trap and are manipulated and entangled with microwaves fed through wires on the chip. Notice the thick microwave lines and the scratches and solder of a well-used lab device.
en-bc80a3cdcd.title: File:Gold Ion Trap (6029437325).jpg

en-bc9017a2e4.creator: Torsten Henning
en-bc9017a2e4.story: A to-scale line drawing (100 nm scale bar) of the Niemeyer-Dolan technique: a suspended mask bridge shadows two metal evaporations from different angles, so aluminium leads and a niobium island overlap across thin oxide tunnel barriers. Drawn by Torsten Henning, Göteborg, 1998–1999, per the Commons record. The same double-angle shadow evaporation makes the Josephson junctions of superconducting qubits; notice the unwanted 'excess' copies every evaporation leaves beside the device.
en-bc9017a2e4.title: File:TyNiemeyerDolanTechnique.png

en-bcb5f75671.attribution: “HYH532BZ1.5 circulator teardown” by Mister rf, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HYH532BZ1.5_circulator_teardown.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-bcb5f75671.creator: Mister rf
en-bcb5f75671.story: Photograph of a small RF isolator/circulator taken apart: metal discs, two black ferrite discs, a stamped three-arm Y-junction centre conductor and the square housing, laid out in rows. Uploaded by Mister rf (2023); the part is an HYH532BZ1.5 for 925-960 MHz, a commercial radio component rather than quantum hardware. It shows how a junction circulator works: magnetised ferrite at a symmetric Y junction lets microwaves flow one way only, the principle behind the cryogenic circulators that shield superconducting qubits from amplifier noise.
en-bcb5f75671.title: File:HYH532BZ1.5 circulator teardown.jpg

en-bd88b11c45.attribution: “IQM Quantum Computer Espoo Finland” by Ragsxl, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IQM_Quantum_Computer_Espoo_Finland.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-bd88b11c45.creator: Ragsxl
en-bd88b11c45.story: Photograph of an open dilution-refrigerator insert (the 'chandelier') with its shields and vacuum cans removed: gold-plated stage plates hanging from a large top flange, each carrying rows of semi-rigid coaxial lines with coiled strain-relief loops, and flexible coax cables dangling below. Taken by Ragsxl (2020) and captioned 'IQM Quantum Computer in Espoo Finland'. It shows how many separate coaxial lines run from room temperature down through ever colder stages to the quantum chip, a wiring load that grows with every added qubit.
en-bd88b11c45.title: File:IQM Quantum Computer Espoo Finland.jpg

en-be67ed123c.attribution: “Front opening shipping box (bottom side)” by Cepheiden, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Front_opening_shipping_box_%28bottom_side%29.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-be67ed123c.creator: Cepheiden
en-be67ed123c.story: Photograph of a transparent front-opening shipping box (FOSB), a plastic carrier for up to 25 large silicon wafers; through its clear walls the slotted supports and the edges of the stored wafers are visible. Taken by Cepheiden in 2009; the description says eight slots hold 300 mm silicon wafers. It is general chip-factory equipment, not quantum hardware, but it shows the 300 mm wafer handling that foundry-made spin qubits, cryogenic CMOS and superconducting wiring depend on.
en-be67ed123c.title: File:Front opening shipping box (bottom side).jpg

en-bed4132482.attribution: “Atomic Clock041” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Atomic_Clock041.jpg
en-bed4132482.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-bed4132482.story: Black-and-white archival photograph of a hand holding a small sealed glass capsule of caesium beside the metal 'oven' block that vaporizes it into a beam of atoms. Credited to the National Institute of Standards and Technology; the caption calls the caesium the heart of the National Bureau of Standards' atomic clock. This is a clock, not quantum-computing hardware, but it shows the heated atom source also used by atom-based qubit experiments; the clock counts 9,192,631,770 caesium vibrations per second.
en-bed4132482.title: File:Atomic Clock041.jpg

en-c060a2842d.attribution: “IQM Jeffrey Chan” by Ragsxl, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IQM_Jeffrey_Chan.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-c060a2842d.creator: Ragsxl
en-c060a2842d.story: Photograph of an open dilution-refrigerator insert (the 'chandelier', radiation shields removed) beside an engineer touching its bottom cables with a gloved hand. The caption names him as IQM quantum engineer Jeffrey Chan; the photo was taken by Ragsxl in 2020. Notice the stacked gold-plated temperature-stage plates and the dense curtain of coaxial lines running down through them: each superconducting qubit needs its own control and readout lines from room-temperature electronics, and this wiring fills much of the fridge.
en-c060a2842d.title: File:IQM Jeffrey Chan.jpg

en-c45e01dac0.attribution: “Acousto-optical spectrometer sketch” by The original uploader was Onkel~enwiki at English Wikipedia ., https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Acousto-optical_spectrometer_sketch.png, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-c45e01dac0.creator: The original uploader was Onkel~enwiki at English Wikipedia .
en-c45e01dac0.story: Coloured principle drawing of an acousto-optical spectrometer: a laser beam crosses a Bragg cell, a crystal in which the radio-frequency input ('IF signal') sets up sound waves; each frequency, here 1.6 GHz and 2.6 GHz, diffracts the light to its own angle, and a lens focuses it onto its own pixel of a linear CCD, which records the spectrum. Uploaded to English Wikipedia by user Onkel~enwiki on 23 September 2007, later transferred to Wikimedia Commons. It is a classical radio-astronomy instrument, not a quantum one, but it shows the acousto-optic principle: the radio frequency sets the beam angle, which is how multi-tone deflectors steer optical tweezers for atoms.
en-c45e01dac0.title: File:Acousto-optical spectrometer sketch.png

en-c5a37a30d8.attribution: “Quantum Annealing - 5714485682” by Steve Jurvetson, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Quantum_Annealing_-_5714485682.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-c5a37a30d8.creator: Steve Jurvetson
en-c5a37a30d8.story: Close-up photograph of a processed wafer whose dies carry a 'D-Wave' logo and the text 'RAINIER ... C4/128', surrounded by pads and smaller test structures. Taken by Steve Jurvetson in 2011; his caption links it to D-Wave's quantum annealing paper in Nature and notes the processor was made with standard integrated-circuit processes. It shows a quantum annealer built from superconducting flux qubits (rf-SQUID loops) using ordinary chip lithography; the fine-line grid at each die's centre is the processor area.
en-c5a37a30d8.title: File:Quantum Annealing - 5714485682.jpg

en-c63b620771.attribution: “Single-photon-detection-module IDQ” by Geek3, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Single-photon-detection-module_IDQ.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-c63b620771.creator: Geek3
en-c63b620771.story: Photograph of two ID Quantique 'id100' single-photon detection modules, fibre-coupled and cabled on an optical breadboard. Made by Commons user Geek3 in March 2017; the description says they are based on avalanche photodiodes. Such room-temperature silicon avalanche-photodiode counters are workhorse detectors in quantum-optics labs; notice the fibre input on one end and the coax pulse output on the other. They are not the superconducting nanowire or transition-edge detectors used for the highest efficiency.
en-c63b620771.title: File:Single-photon-detection-module IDQ.jpg

en-c7bdb9093f.attribution: “ODIN Ti-Sapphire laser in operation” by FDominec, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ODIN_Ti-Sapphire_laser_in_operation.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-c7bdb9093f.creator: FDominec
en-c7bdb9093f.story: Wide photograph along an optical table bathed in green pump light, showing a Coherent ODIN titanium-sapphire ultrashort-pulse amplifier. Taken by FDominec in April 2009 at the Physical Institute, CAS, Prague; the caption says a 10 W Nd:YAG laser pumps the Ti:sapphire crystal, which sits in a water- and Peltier-cooled holder (the pink-red glow). This is general laser-physics equipment, not quantum hardware; Ti:sapphire is a widely tunable red to near-infrared laser medium also used in atom and ion labs.
en-c7bdb9093f.title: File:ODIN Ti-Sapphire laser in operation.jpg

en-c855c863eb.attribution: “ASTRO-H SXS Detector Assembly (14086785993)” by NASA Blueshift, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ASTRO-H_SXS_Detector_Assembly_%2814086785993%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-c855c863eb.creator: NASA Blueshift
en-c855c863eb.story: Photograph of a gold-plated cryogenic assembly on a large mounting plate, with added labels marking the Detector Assembly, an adiabatic demagnetization refrigerator (ADR) stage with its magnet coil, and two heat switches. Posted by NASA Blueshift in March 2014 for the ASTRO-H SXS instrument; the caption says this is the warmest of the ADR's three stages, running between 1.5 and 4.5 kelvin. It is a space X-ray detector cooler, not a quantum computer, but shows magnetic refrigeration, an alternative route to very low temperatures.
en-c855c863eb.title: File:ASTRO-H SXS Detector Assembly (14086785993).jpg

en-c8a91fd334.attribution: “41586 2021 3289 Fig1 HTML” by C. J. Baker et al., https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:41586_2021_3289_Fig1_HTML.webp, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-c8a91fd334.creator: C. J. Baker et al.
en-c8a91fd334.story: Three-panel figure: (a) cross-section drawing of the ALPHA-2 antihydrogen apparatus, with Penning-trap electrodes that combine antiprotons and positrons inside mirror coils, an octupole magnet and solenoids cooled by liquid helium, a 243.1 nm laser cavity through the trap, a photomultiplier and an annihilation detector. (b) Magnetic field along the axis, flat near 1 T at the centre; (c) energy levels of the 1S, 2S and 2P states versus magnetic field, with the laser transitions used. Figure 1 of a paper by C. J. Baker et al., 31 March 2021. It shows how a Penning trap sits inside its magnets; the optical cavity serves spectroscopy, not an atom–photon quantum interface.
en-c8a91fd334.title: File:41586 2021 3289 Fig1 HTML.webp

en-ca2ec24137.attribution: “Cäsiumatomuhr CS1 Deutsches Museum Bonn” by Tohma, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:C%C3%A4siumatomuhr_CS1_Deutsches_Museum_Bonn.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-ca2ec24137.creator: Tohma
en-ca2ec24137.story: A photograph of a long caesium atomic-beam tube shown in a museum case. Per its record it is the caesium atomic clock CS1, photographed in the Deutsches Museum Bonn; the description lists its parts from left to right: beam oven, sorting magnet, cavity resonator, sorting magnet and detector. It shows how a caesium beam clock, the kind of clock that defines the second, is laid out along one axis. It is not a chip-scale atomic clock, despite its category.
en-ca2ec24137.title: File:Cäsiumatomuhr CS1 Deutsches Museum Bonn.jpg

en-cbd84c0ead.creator: Mbeljaars
en-cbd84c0ead.story: Data plot, not a photograph: the lowest temperature reached by pulse-tube refrigerators, on a logarithmic scale, against year, falling from about 110 K in 1984 to about 1.2 K in 2005, with points labelled Mikulin, Matsubara, Eindhoven, Giessen and Ehv/Gies. Made by Mbeljaars in June 2007 for the topic 'pulse tube refrigerator'. Note the lines for helium-4's boiling point (4.2 K) and lambda point (2.17 K); pulse tubes now give cryogen-free precooling in most dilution refrigerators for superconducting qubits.
en-cbd84c0ead.title: File:Ontwikkelingkoeler.jpg

en-cca6c42aac.attribution: “Cold atoms experiment 02” by Tomasz Kawalec, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cold_atoms_experiment_02.JPG, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-cca6c42aac.creator: Tomasz Kawalec
en-cca6c42aac.story: Photograph along an optical table used to cool and trap rubidium atoms: two diode lasers with Littrow resonators in front, then lenses, mirrors, waveplates, acousto-optic modulators and polarizers, and in the background the vacuum setup where the atoms are trapped. Taken by Tomasz Kawalec in November 2015. It shows how much optics a neutral-atom experiment needs before light reaches the atoms: the frequency, intensity and polarization of every beam must be controlled on the table.
en-cca6c42aac.title: File:Cold atoms experiment 02.JPG

en-cceaff1310.creator: RSchnabel
en-cceaff1310.story: Schematic drawing of a balanced homodyne detector: a strong local-oscillator (LO) beam, passed through a phase shifter, is mixed with a signal carrying squeezed uncertainty on a 50/50 beam splitter, and the two outputs hit photodiodes PD1 and PD2 whose currents are subtracted. Drawn by RSchnabel in 2018. This is the standard readout for continuous-variable photonic quantum computing: the subtraction cancels the laser's own noise, and the phase-shifter angle selects which quadrature of the squeezed light is measured.
en-cceaff1310.title: File:Fig-BHD-E-RS.jpeg

en-cffbd92de9.attribution: “Bose-Einstein condensate, a cloud of super-cooled Rubidium atoms in a Laser trap on an Optical table - In a game of catch & release, the atoms will shoot up a 30 ft. tall Atomic fountain - Stanford” by Steve Jurvetson from Menlo Park, USA, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bose-Einstein_condensate%2C_a_cloud_of_super-cooled_Rubidium_atoms_in_a_Laser_trap_on_an_Optical_table_-_In_a_game_of_catch_%26_release%2C_the_atoms_will_shoot_up_a_30_ft._tall_Atomic_fountain_-_Stanford.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-cffbd92de9.creator: Steve Jurvetson from Menlo Park, USA
en-cffbd92de9.story: A photograph of a busy cold-atom laboratory: a vacuum chamber inside a frame wrapped in red and blue water-cooling hoses for its magnet coils, next to an optical table full of mirrors and fibres. Steve Jurvetson took it in 2010 at Stanford, where rubidium atoms cooled in a laser trap are launched up a 30-foot atomic fountain to test gravity. It is an atom-interferometry experiment, not a quantum computer, but it shows the same laser, vacuum and coil hardware that neutral-atom quantum computers rely on.
en-cffbd92de9.title: File:Bose-Einstein condensate, a cloud of super-cooled Rubidium atoms in a Laser trap on an Optical table - In a game of catch & release, the atoms will shoot up a 30 ft. tall Atomic fountain - Stanford.jpg

en-d148b4a694.creator: PaulT
en-d148b4a694.story: A photograph of a single photomultiplier tube, the K14FS50 made by Zeiss Jena according to its label and Commons description. Behind the mirror-coated photocathode at the top, the clear glass reveals the chain of bent metal dynodes that multiply each photoelectron, ending in a pin base. Photomultipliers like this are classic single-photon counters, the same detector class used to read out trapped-ion qubits by their fluorescence.
en-d148b4a694.title: File:K14FS50.jpg

en-d2b31889aa.attribution: “SNSPD Single-Quantum” by Geek3, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:SNSPD_Single-Quantum.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-d2b31889aa.creator: Geek3
en-d2b31889aa.story: Photograph of a commercial superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (SNSPD) system on an exhibition table: a red box labelled 'Single Quantum Eos 410' with four FC fibre inputs, topped by a stainless-steel cryostat can. Taken by Geek3 in March 2017; the caption says the module holds four fast, highly efficient detectors and that its cooling unit is not shown. It is a detector instrument, not a quantum computer; photonic quantum computing and networking rely on such cryogenic detectors to register single photons.
en-d2b31889aa.title: File:SNSPD Single-Quantum.jpg

en-d2c2f410ee.attribution: “ASEA Quintus Q-20 sphere” by Erik G. Lundblad, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ASEA_Quintus_Q-20_sphere.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-d2c2f410ee.creator: Erik G. Lundblad
en-d2c2f410ee.story: A black-and-white photograph of the QUINTUS Q-20 high-pressure apparatus: a steel sphere of six anvils, one left off to reveal the small cubic pressure chamber at the centre. The file records it as ASEA's press in Stockholm, photographed by Erik G. Lundblad in 1953. This is the high-pressure, high-temperature route to synthetic diamond; related presses still make the nitrogen-rich diamond used for nitrogen-vacancy sensors and as seeds for purer grown diamond.
en-d2c2f410ee.title: File:ASEA Quintus Q-20 sphere.jpg

en-d361e4bdc8.attribution: “Strontium 88 MOT at IOGS” by Xcodexif, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Strontium_88_MOT_at_IOGS.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-d361e4bdc8.creator: Xcodexif
en-d361e4bdc8.story: Photograph through a vacuum-chamber window of a cloud of strontium-88 atoms in a magneto-optical trap, seen as the bright white-blue spot near the centre of the blue-violet glow. Taken by Xcodexif in May 2021; the title places it at IOGS and the caption gives milli-kelvin temperatures. A magneto-optical trap is the first cooling step in neutral-atom quantum computers; strontium is an alkaline-earth atom whose two outer electrons give long-lived states useful for qubits.
en-d361e4bdc8.title: File:Strontium 88 MOT at IOGS.jpg

en-d4f4a2a7aa.attribution: “1-volt standard chip (5940300191)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1-volt_standard_chip_%285940300191%29.jpg
en-d4f4a2a7aa.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-d4f4a2a7aa.story: A photograph of a whole superconducting chip, a few centimetres long, lying on white fibre. According to its NIST record it is the 1985 chip described as the first practical, stable and easy-to-use 1-volt standard (credit Schmidt/NIST). A tapered finline feeds microwaves into long meandering strips holding thousands of Josephson junctions in series, which turn frequency into an exact voltage. It is a Josephson voltage standard, a look-alike of superconducting single-flux-quantum logic, not a qubit control chip.
en-d4f4a2a7aa.title: File:1-volt standard chip (5940300191).jpg

en-d4fa8581f2.attribution: “TiSa crystal” by No machine-readable author provided. Mathieu Perrin assumed (based on copyright claims)., https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:TiSa_crystal.jpg, CC BY 2.5 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5)
en-d4fa8581f2.creator: No machine-readable author provided. Mathieu Perrin assumed (based on copyright claims).
en-d4fa8581f2.story: Low-light photograph of a small titanium-doped sapphire (Ti:sapphire) laser crystal in a square metal holder flanked by two screws, glowing while the laser runs, the holder face lit orange. The crystal is cut at the Brewster angle, the tilt at which light of one polarisation passes its faces without reflection loss; the white streak along the beam path is spontaneous emission near 800 nm, with the green pump light filtered out. Wikimedia Commons credits Mathieu Perrin (assumed from copyright claims), dated 13 January 2007 from camera data. Ti:sapphire lasers provide tunable near-infrared light used in many atomic-physics labs, but this picture shows only the laser crystal.
en-d4fa8581f2.title: File:TiSa crystal.jpg

en-d8288ed27a.attribution: “Quantum Simulator Illustration (6967363146)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Quantum_Simulator_Illustration_%286967363146%29.jpg
en-d8288ed27a.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-d8288ed27a.story: Illustration, not a photograph: about two dozen blue spheres (beryllium ions) form a flat triangular crystal, each with a red arrow for the spin of its outermost electron, which serves as a qubit; the label B0 = 4.5 T marks the magnetic field. Published by NIST in April 2012 to explain its quantum simulator, in which a Penning trap (not drawn) holds the rotating crystal. It shows how trapped ions can mimic interacting spin systems too hard to model on a supercomputer.
en-d8288ed27a.title: File:Quantum Simulator Illustration (6967363146).jpg

en-d8bb2201ed.attribution: “Coulomb crystal 1D TEM” by Tanja Mehlstäubler, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Coulomb_crystal_1D_TEM.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-d8bb2201ed.creator: Tanja Mehlstäubler
en-d8bb2201ed.story: Camera image of a one-dimensional ion Coulomb crystal: about 22 trapped ions glowing as blue fluorescence spots in a single row, held in a linear radio-frequency trap. Recorded by Tanja Mehlstäubler, dated August 2026. Notice the spacing is slightly tighter at the centre than at the ends, as expected for mutually repelling ions in a harmonic trap; such chains form the qubit registers of trapped-ion quantum computers, one atom per spot. One spot near the left looks dimmer.
en-d8bb2201ed.title: File:Coulomb crystal 1D TEM.jpg

en-d9d716dad5.creator: Geek3
en-d9d716dad5.story: Photograph of a LINOS electro-optic modulator: a cream cylindrical housing with a clear aperture, held in a tilt mount on an optical table. Taken by Geek3 in December 2016; the caption describes it as a variable waveplate whose four crystals change their birefringence under a high voltage, shifting the phase or polarization of a passing beam. It is general optics equipment, not quantum-computing hardware itself, but such modulators switch and shape laser beams quickly in ion and atom experiments.
en-d9d716dad5.title: File:Electro-optic-modulator-linos.jpg

en-dc7359cd52.attribution: “Floor Standing Cryostat with DR Insert Removed” by OJB Quantum, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Floor_Standing_Cryostat_with_DR_Insert_Removed.png, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-dc7359cd52.creator: OJB Quantum
en-dc7359cd52.story: Computer render, not a photograph, of a floor-standing cryogen-free cryostat (cooled by a closed-cycle cryocooler instead of a liquid-helium bath) with its dilution-refrigerator insert removed and shown beside it: a long thin probe with small gold rings along its shaft and a gold tip, which carries samples down to millikelvin temperatures. A console with a curved monitor stands at left; an unlabelled grey cabinet sits beside the cryostat. Made by OJB Quantum as own work, published on Wikimedia Commons and dated 3 October 2025. Notice that the dilution refrigerator here is a slim top-loading insert that slides into the cryostat, unlike the open 'chandelier' designs; the model is simplified.
en-dc7359cd52.title: File:Floor Standing Cryostat with DR Insert Removed.png

en-dd17c7dd2c.attribution: “Crossing the quantum frontier (53804559173)” by Oak Ridge National Laboratory, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Crossing_the_quantum_frontier_%2853804559173%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-dd17c7dd2c.creator: Oak Ridge National Laboratory
en-dd17c7dd2c.story: Photograph of a hand holding tweezers above a small iridescent purple chip, a few millimetres across, with an optical fibre in a holder aligned to its edge. Credited to Carlos Jones/ORNL (Oak Ridge National Laboratory), June 2024; the caption says ORNL researchers are investigating whether trapped ions can encode qubits for quantum networking. No ion trap or vacuum hardware is visible, though: what the picture shows is fibre-to-chip edge coupling, the step that brings light onto and off an integrated photonic chip.
en-dd17c7dd2c.title: File:Crossing the quantum frontier (53804559173).jpg

en-de898cc0ba.attribution: “Single-crystal CVD diamond disc” by Matthias Schreck, Stefan Gsell, Rosaria Brescia & Martin Fischer, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Single-crystal_CVD_diamond_disc.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-de898cc0ba.creator: Matthias Schreck, Stefan Gsell, Rosaria Brescia & Martin Fischer
en-de898cc0ba.story: Photograph of a gloved hand holding a thin, unpolished, roughly round single-crystal diamond disc, marked as 92 mm across. Per the caption by Matthias Schreck, Stefan Gsell, Rosaria Brescia and Martin Fischer (2017), it was grown by heteroepitaxy on Ir/YSZ/Si(001), is about 1.6 mm thick and weighs 155 carat. It illustrates synthetic diamond growth, the material basis for colour-centre qubits such as nitrogen-vacancy centres; notice the cloudy patches and dark specks of a raw, unpolished crystal.
en-de898cc0ba.title: File:Single-crystal CVD diamond disc.jpg

en-df20e7a390.creator: Lamboman2008
en-df20e7a390.story: Drawing, with hand-traced curves, of how an optical cavity transmits light: relative intensity versus wavelength shows identical sharp, evenly spaced peaks, one per mode order m=1 … m=n. A red arrow marks the peak width at half height (full width at half maximum) and a blue arrow the spacing between neighbouring peaks (free spectral range). Drawn by Wikimedia Commons user Lamboman2008 as own work, dated 13 December 2011. The ratio of spacing to width, the finesse, measures how many round trips light makes before leaking out; the same mode structure underlies cavities that couple atoms to light, but the drawing is generic and shows no atoms.
en-df20e7a390.title: File:MultipleResonances.png

en-dfcda0251d.creator: Д.Ильин : vectorization
en-dfcda0251d.story: A drawing of a DC SQUID seen at an angle: a superconducting ring (Supraleiter) interrupted by two Josephson junctions, with magnetic flux lines passing through it, a constant current flowing across, and a wave whose period is one flux quantum. It is from Wikimedia Commons (vectorised by Д.Ильин, 2021, CC0), with German labels. It shows the physical layout behind SQUID magnetometers and amplifiers; it is a simplified drawing, not a real device, and not an SFQ control circuit.
en-dfcda0251d.title: File:SQUID de.svg

en-dfdb1ec5e1.attribution: “Google Sycamore Chip 001” by Google (https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCK8sQmJBp8GCxrOtXWBpyEA), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Google_Sycamore_Chip_001.png, CC BY 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/)
en-dfdb1ec5e1.creator: Google (https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCK8sQmJBp8GCxrOtXWBpyEA)
en-dfdb1ec5e1.story: Still frame from a video showing a two-chip stack under blue light: a small dark die mounted face-down on a larger mirror-like die whose fine lines fan out to its edges, resting on a machined aluminium pedestal. The caption says it comes from a Google video (2019-10-23) showing the Sycamore quantum processor. It illustrates flip-chip assembly of a superconducting processor: two dies are bonded face to face so wiring can run on a separate layer; the radial lines are those signal traces.
en-dfdb1ec5e1.title: File:Google Sycamore Chip 001.png

en-e0e5fd96cd.attribution: “Dilution Fridge with Quantum Processors Enclosed 16K Resolution” by OJB Quantum, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Dilution_Fridge_with_Quantum_Processors_Enclosed_16K_Resolution.png, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-e0e5fd96cd.creator: OJB Quantum
en-e0e5fd96cd.story: Computer render, not a photograph, of a dilution refrigerator's interior within see-through shields: six stacked plates (two dark, four gold-plated cold stages) joined by thin rods; about eight bundles of ribbon-like flexible cables with gold connectors running down through every plate; a central column with coils and copper links; and two square processor chips on gold holders at the bottom. Made by OJB Quantum as own work, published on Wikimedia Commons, dated 11 October 2025; the title gives 16K resolution. It illustrates how dense flex cabling carries control and readout lines from room temperature down to the quantum chips; it is an idealised drawing, not a real machine.
en-e0e5fd96cd.title: File:Dilution Fridge with Quantum Processors Enclosed 16K Resolution.png

en-e13011ddd6.attribution: “FZU ebeamlithography 1” by René Volfík, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FZU_ebeamlithography_1.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-e13011ddd6.creator: René Volfík
en-e13011ddd6.story: A photograph of an electron-beam lithography machine made by Raith (type e-Line) in a cleanroom, with its sample-handling bench and a Raith starter kit in front. The metadata places it in the Department of Spintronics and Nanoelectronics of the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences (FZU) in Prague, photographed by René Volfík in 2021. Tools like this write the nanometre patterns, such as Josephson junctions, used in superconducting qubits; this one serves spintronics research, so it shows the method, not a qubit line.
en-e13011ddd6.title: File:FZU ebeamlithography 1.jpg

en-e1ad4953f8.attribution: “IBM Q System One (Fraunhofer) installation” by IBM Research, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IBM_Q_System_One_%28Fraunhofer%29_installation.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-e1ad4953f8.creator: IBM Research
en-e1ad4953f8.story: Photograph of an installation room where workers in masks and gloves fit a large mirror-black cylindrical shell around a cryostat hanging inside an open black enclosure, with a gold-coloured can visible below. Credited to IBM Research (2021-05-28), the caption describes IBM engineers working on the IBM Quantum System One in Ehningen, Germany. It shows the layers around a superconducting processor: dilution refrigerator, nested radiation shields and vacuum cans, and the outer system enclosure; notice the scale of the hardware next to the people.
en-e1ad4953f8.title: File:IBM Q System One (Fraunhofer) installation.jpg

en-e3538c96e6.attribution: “80C196KC wafer” by Mister rf, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:80C196KC_wafer.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-e3538c96e6.creator: Mister rf
en-e3538c96e6.story: Top-down photograph of a whole silicon wafer covered in a grid of identical chips, each showing its circuit blocks and ring of contact pads. Per its Commons description it is an Intel 80C196KC microcontroller wafer. It is a classical chip wafer, smaller and older than today's 300 mm wafers, but it shows clearly what wafer-scale manufacturing means: hundreds of identical dies made at once, the approach silicon spin-qubit and cryogenic control chips are adopting.
en-e3538c96e6.title: File:80C196KC wafer.jpg

en-e4a7816ce1.attribution: “Laboratorium FAMO UMK A 241” by Ciacho5, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Laboratorium_FAMO_UMK_A_241.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-e4a7816ce1.creator: Ciacho5
en-e4a7816ce1.story: A photograph of a laser table that, according to its caption, is part of an optical atomic clock: a blue box labelled 'TA-SHG pro' (a frequency-doubled tapered-amplifier diode laser) beside mirrors glowing with blue light and a small glass tube glowing red. It was taken on 2016-12-13 by Ciacho5 at the National Laboratory of Atomic, Molecular and Optical Physics, Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, Poland. Strontium optical lattice clocks need several stabilised lasers; notice the blue cooling light and the glowing tube, likely a lamp or reference cell.
en-e4a7816ce1.title: File:Laboratorium FAMO UMK A 241.jpg

en-e567a7d52c.attribution: “Photomultiplier Tube (PMT)” by Motokoka, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Photomultiplier_Tube_%28PMT%29.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-e567a7d52c.creator: Motokoka
en-e567a7d52c.story: Photograph of a museum display case holding a very large glass photomultiplier tube, tens of centimetres across, lying on its side: a mirror-like bronze-tinted bulb narrowing to a clear glass neck with the electrode stack inside. Taken by Motokoka on 2020-06-09; the Japanese caption names it a photomultiplier tube at the Gifu-Kakamigahara Air and Space Museum. It is a classical light detector, not quantum-computing hardware: a cascade of electrodes turns single photons into measurable pulses, the job single-photon detectors do in quantum-optics experiments.
en-e567a7d52c.title: File:Photomultiplier Tube (PMT).jpg

en-e5dcf5b6a0.attribution: “Qubits (5940500587)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Qubits_%285940500587%29.jpg
en-e5dcf5b6a0.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-e5dcf5b6a0.story: Computer-generated render, not a photograph: glossy red spheres sit in alternate wells of a blue egg-crate surface. Credited to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (2009-07-06), the caption says it depicts rubidium atoms (red) held apart by an optical lattice for neutral-atom quantum processors, and that NIST scientists isolated and controlled pairs of these atoms with polarized light. The egg-crate stands for the periodic light pattern made by crossing laser beams; each well can hold one atom acting as a qubit.
en-e5dcf5b6a0.title: File:Qubits (5940500587).jpg

en-e61b5060ae.attribution: “Enhancing the brightness of electrically driven single-photon sources using color centers in silicon carbide (Figure 1)” by Igor A. Khramtsov, Andrey A. Vyshnevyy, Dmitry Yu. Fedyanin, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Enhancing_the_brightness_of_electrically_driven_single-photon_sources_using_color_centers_in_silicon_carbide_%28Figure_1%29.png, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-e61b5060ae.creator: Igor A. Khramtsov, Andrey A. Vyshnevyy, Dmitry Yu. Fedyanin
en-e61b5060ae.story: Figure 1 of 'Enhancing the brightness of electrically driven single-photon sources using color centers in silicon carbide' by Igor A. Khramtsov, Andrey A. Vyshnevyy and Dmitry Yu. Fedyanin (2018): a drawing plus simulated data plots, not a photograph. Panel (a) is a cross-section of a silicon carbide p+–n–n+ diode with its doping map and one colour centre in the n-type layer; (b) and (c) plot simulated electron and hole densities. It shows a diode feeding carriers to a colour centre so it emits single photons electrically.

en-e8483a31dc.attribution: “Zorro & Alopeke Instrument Design (full gemini assembly-final-iso-trimmed)” by Dr. Nic Scott/NASA Ames, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Zorro_%26_Alopeke_Instrument_Design_%28full_gemini_assembly-final-iso-trimmed%29.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-e8483a31dc.creator: Dr. Nic Scott/NASA Ames
en-e8483a31dc.story: A computer-aided design drawing, not a photograph, of an instrument about the size of a large box: a pickoff mirror sends telescope light into a housing where a dichroic splits it into red and blue channels, each ending in a blue-bodied camera. The metadata credits Dr. Nic Scott, NASA Ames, and names the Zorro and Alopeke speckle imagers for the Gemini telescopes, whose cameras use electron-multiplying CCDs. It comes from astronomy, but notice the cooled EMCCD camera heads: the same camera class reads out single-atom fluorescence in neutral-atom quantum computers.
en-e8483a31dc.title: File:Zorro & Alopeke Instrument Design (full gemini assembly-final-iso-trimmed).jpg

en-e904126c93.attribution: “Underground Moscow museum - 2026-05 - p03” — Александр Сигачёв, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Underground_Moscow_museum_-_2026-05_-_p03.jpg
en-e904126c93.creator: Александр Сигачёв
en-e904126c93.story: A photograph of a museum demonstration stand: a photomultiplier tube in a metal housing sits above a scintillator, wired to a pulse counter and a pulse oscilloscope. According to the Commons description it was taken in May 2026 at the Underground Moscow Bunker Museum and uses an FEU-49B tube similar to those at the Baksan Neutrino Observatory. It shows the full photon-counting chain - detector, counter, scope - that also underlies fluorescence state detection of trapped ions, though here it counts radioactive decays, not ions.
en-e904126c93.title: File:Underground Moscow museum - 2026-05 - p03.jpg

en-e9a9f72311.attribution: “Diagram of the Cirac-Zoller CNOT gate” — QuarksAndElectrons, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Diagram_of_the_Cirac-Zoller_CNOT_gate.svg
en-e9a9f72311.creator: QuarksAndElectrons
en-e9a9f72311.story: Black-and-white principle diagram: a chain of ions with two marked qubits, A and B, sharing a vibrational (phonon) mode, plus zoomed level schemes of each ion's ground, excited and auxiliary states with numbered laser pulses. Drawn by QuarksAndElectrons (2024-01-21) to illustrate the Cirac–Zoller gate: a π-pulse on ion A, a 2π-pulse on ion B, then another π-pulse on ion A. It shows how trapped-ion qubits interact through shared motion: the chain's vibration acts as a bus carrying ion A's state to ion B.
en-e9a9f72311.title: File:Diagram of the Cirac-Zoller CNOT gate.svg

en-ea4792d528.attribution: “Don't Blink! NIST Studies Why Quantum Dots Suffer from 'Fluorescence Intermittency' (14444840355)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Don%27t_Blink%21_NIST_Studies_Why_Quantum_Dots_Suffer_from_%27Fluorescence_Intermittency%27_%2814444840355%29.jpg
en-ea4792d528.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-ea4792d528.story: Three-panel figure mixing a drawing and real electron micrographs. Panel (a) sketches a laser-excited sample in a cryostat whose light is split between two single-photon avalanche diodes feeding a time correlator; (b) and (c) are tilted micrographs of a ring-shaped 'bullseye' grating and a disk-topped pillar, with 1 µm and 500 nm scale bars. Credited to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (2014), it shows apparatus used to study quantum dot blinking. The two-detector correlation tests whether a source emits one photon at a time.
en-ea4792d528.title: File:Don't Blink! NIST Studies Why Quantum Dots Suffer from 'Fluorescence Intermittency' (14444840355).jpg

en-eaef8eb24a.story: Drawn infographic, not a photograph: a logarithmic length scale from 0.1 nm to 1 mm, with biological objects (molecules, proteins, viruses, cells, a human hair) above and technological ones (crystal lattices, carbon nanotubes, quantum dots, transistor gates, microsystems) below, plus bands for fabrication methods such as UV and electron-beam lithography. Compiled by Guillaume Paumier, Philip Ronan, NIH and other contributors (2008). It gives a sense of scale for qubit fabrication; note its quantum dots are colloidal nanocrystals in vials, not the gate-defined dots used as spin qubits.
