en-ebb537cdaa.attribution: “Laboratorium FAMO UMK A 232” by Ciacho5, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Laboratorium_FAMO_UMK_A_232.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-ebb537cdaa.creator: Ciacho5
en-ebb537cdaa.story: A photograph of a laboratory apparatus for making Bose-Einstein condensates: a small stainless-steel vacuum chamber with windows, wrapped in optics, coils, fibres and cables. According to its Wikimedia Commons record it was taken by Ciacho5 on 13 December 2016 in the National Laboratory of Atomic, Molecular and Optical Physics at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, Poland. It shows how ultracold-atom machines are built around a vacuum chamber reached by many laser beams; no glass cell is visible.
en-ebb537cdaa.title: File:Laboratorium FAMO UMK A 232.jpg

en-ec41f0ceb5.attribution: “TiSa laser” by No machine-readable author provided. Mathieu Perrin assumed (based on copyright claims)., https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:TiSa_laser.jpg, CC BY 2.5 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5)
en-ec41f0ceb5.creator: No machine-readable author provided. Mathieu Perrin assumed (based on copyright claims).
en-ec41f0ceb5.story: A photograph into an open titanium-sapphire laser in operation: a green pump beam lights a small crystal that glows in the middle of a black box of mirrors, with a prism on a micrometer stage in front. It is recorded on Wikimedia Commons (author assumed Mathieu Perrin, 2007) as a KMLabs laser giving pulses under 20 femtoseconds at 80 MHz, pumped by a 5 W Millennia laser. Titanium-sapphire lasers supply near-infrared light for atom tweezers and ion gates; notice the green pump light converted to infrared in the crystal.
en-ec41f0ceb5.title: File:TiSa laser.jpg

en-ed61aa4014.creator: Jpagett
en-ed61aa4014.story: Computer drawing, not an image of real atoms: three glossy blue balls standing for atoms rest in separate wells of a wavy orange egg-crate surface that represents the light potential of a two-dimensional optical lattice. Drawn by Wikimedia Commons user Jpagett as own work, dated 16 December 2020. An optical lattice is a grid of light, formed where crossed laser beams interfere, whose regular dips hold neutral atoms at fixed sites, a starting point for quantum simulation and neutral-atom qubits. Notice that most wells are empty, as in a lattice loaded only in part.
en-ed61aa4014.title: File:AtomsInLattice.png

en-ed6eba67e5.attribution: “Cryogenic Vessels and Cryostats in English” by OJB Quantum, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cryogenic_Vessels_and_Cryostats_in_English.png, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-ed6eba67e5.creator: OJB Quantum
en-ed6eba67e5.story: Three computer renders, not photographs, side by side under the title 'Common Cryostat/Cryogenic Vessel Formfactors': left, a large-frame cryogen-free (cryocooler-cooled) dilution refrigerator, its gold stage plates and copper flex cables seen through translucent cans; centre, a floor-standing cryogen-free cryostat with console, side cabinet and long sample probe; right, a stainless-steel liquid-helium dewar on casters with a dipstick probe, drawn with a small chip board at its top. Made by OJB Quantum, dated 16 October 2025, on Wikimedia Commons. It shows the three usual ways to cool quantum devices and low-temperature samples, from the millikelvin dilution refrigerator that superconducting qubits need to the simple helium-bath dip at about 4 K.
en-ed6eba67e5.title: File:Cryogenic Vessels and Cryostats in English.png

en-eec7049c18.attribution: “Infrared (1064 nm) Laser Beams and Pre-Mode Cleaner” by Tobin from Rochester, NY, USA, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Infrared_%281064_nm%29_Laser_Beams_and_Pre-Mode_Cleaner.jpg, CC BY SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/)
en-eec7049c18.creator: Tobin from Rochester, NY, USA
en-eec7049c18.story: Photograph of part of a laser optical table, where the camera shows scattered 1064 nm infrared light as purple. In the centre sit two small gold-lidded New Focus electro-optic phase modulators, one labelled 33.205 MHz, with a hand-written tag for a two-way radio-frequency splitter in front; behind them glows a quartz block, the pre-mode-cleaner cavity, an optical resonator that passes only a clean single-mode beam. Photographed by Tobin from Rochester, NY, USA, dated 2 April 2007, on Wikimedia Commons. The modulators put sidebands on the laser so it can be locked to a cavity, the same frequency stabilisation used for lasers that control trapped-ion and neutral-atom qubits.
en-eec7049c18.title: File:Infrared (1064 nm) Laser Beams and Pre-Mode Cleaner.jpg

en-f01f513d72.attribution: “Single-Photon-Counting-Module Excelitas” by Geek3, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Single-Photon-Counting-Module_Excelitas.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-f01f513d72.creator: Geek3
en-f01f513d72.story: Photograph of a black single-photon counting module from Excelitas, with finned heat-sink sides, a mounting plate, two BNC output connectors and high-voltage warning labels, lying on a green surface. Taken by Geek3 in March 2017. Such a module contains a single-photon avalanche diode that turns each detected photon into an electrical pulse; it is a classical lab instrument rather than a qubit, used to count photons in photonic experiments and in fluorescence readout of atoms, ions and colour centres.
en-f01f513d72.title: File:Single-Photon-Counting-Module Excelitas.jpg

en-f0f9743eb4.creator: Vegar Ottesen
en-f0f9743eb4.story: Labelled drawing, not a photograph, of the inside of a molecular-beam-epitaxy chamber: heated effusion cells send beams of material onto a rotating, heated substrate, while cryopanels, a RHEED electron gun and screen, a mass spectrometer and gauges monitor the growth. It is a concept drawing by Vegar Ottesen dated 2011-10-11 (origin as recorded: Wikimedia Commons). It explains how the III-V layers behind quantum-dot photon sources and hybrid nanowires are grown one atomic layer at a time.
en-f0f9743eb4.title: File:MBE.svg

en-f16a6f7e19.attribution: “Cold atoms experiment 01” by Tomasz Kawalec, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cold_atoms_experiment_01.JPG, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-f16a6f7e19.creator: Tomasz Kawalec
en-f16a6f7e19.story: A photograph across an optical table in a laser-cooling laboratory: a gold mirror in the foreground reflects a dense setup of small optics, while a rack of diode-laser controllers and a spectrum analyser stand behind. It was taken by Tomasz Kawalec in 2015 and shows part of an experiment for slowing and trapping rubidium atoms, as recorded on Wikimedia Commons. Notice how much control electronics and free-space optics sit around a cold-atom apparatus, the kind of optical and mechanical assembly neutral-atom machines depend on.
en-f16a6f7e19.title: File:Cold atoms experiment 01.JPG

en-f2b01867f1.attribution: “Optical Microresonator” by Phezack, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Optical_Microresonator.png, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-f2b01867f1.creator: Phezack
en-f2b01867f1.story: Labelled cross-section drawing of a micropillar about 2–3 µm wide: two stacks of distributed Bragg reflectors (alternating layers acting as mirrors) trap light around a single quantum dot, the red mark in the middle; a red ellipse shows the trapped light, and a pink cone the output at the top. Drawn by Wikimedia Commons user Phezack as own work, dated 10 December 2017. This is how a quantum-dot single-photon source works, emitting one photon at a time for photonic quantum technology; notice the lower mirror has more layers than the upper, so light exits the top. The dot is an optically active semiconductor dot, not a gate-defined spin qubit.
en-f2b01867f1.title: File:Optical Microresonator.png

en-f5acc66ca3.attribution: “Strontium Atomic Clock Demonstrates Super-Fine 'Ticks' (5941085880)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Strontium_Atomic_Clock_Demonstrates_Super-Fine_%27Ticks%27_%285941085880%29.jpg
en-f5acc66ca3.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-f5acc66ca3.story: Photograph through a round vacuum-chamber window: blue laser light fills the view, with a small bright spot at the centre where the atom cloud glows. Per the NIST caption (2006-11-30), this is JILA's optical atomic clock, where blue light cools and traps strontium atoms in a magneto-optical trap before they are loaded into a lattice made of light; credit includes Martin Boyd. It is a clock, not a quantum computer, but the same cooling and trapping steps start strontium-based neutral-atom qubit machines.
en-f5acc66ca3.title: File:Strontium Atomic Clock Demonstrates Super-Fine 'Ticks' (5941085880).jpg

en-f5c00bb470.attribution: “Table chamber GWMorley” by Gavin Morley, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Table_chamber_GWMorley.jpg, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-f5c00bb470.creator: Gavin Morley
en-f5c00bb470.story: Photograph of a stainless-steel vacuum chamber seen through its large window, with a microscope objective inside and green laser light. Made by Gavin Morley (2016) for the levitated-nanodiamond experiment of Frangeskou et al., New Journal of Physics 2018. It shows how ultra-high-vacuum chambers hold focusing optics inside the vacuum; note this is optical-tweezer levitation of a nanodiamond, a look-alike of, not an example of, alkali-atom tweezer arrays.
en-f5c00bb470.title: File:Table chamber GWMorley.jpg

en-f5c5b5fe67.attribution: “Conditional quantum teleportation of photon polarization” by JozumBjada, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Conditional_quantum_teleportation_of_photon_polarization.png, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-f5c5b5fe67.creator: JozumBjada
en-f5c5b5fe67.story: Shaded 3D-style schematic, not a photograph, of photon teleportation: a violet pump beam enters source S, which emits a polarization-entangled photon pair; one photon meets the input photon at Alice's beam splitter, watched by two detectors and a coincidence unit, while the other travels to Bob. Drawn by JozumBjada (2023-10-06); the caption says the input polarization is transferred only when Alice detects the singlet state |Ψ−⟩. It shows teleportation combining entanglement with a classical signal, the dashed cable to Bob.
en-f5c5b5fe67.title: File:Conditional quantum teleportation of photon polarization.png

en-f6e83a0e54.attribution: “Hot off the press — the latest D-Wave wafer of quantum processors and TIME cover story” by Steve Jurvetson, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hot_off_the_press_%E2%80%94_the_latest_D-Wave_wafer_of_quantum_processors_and_TIME_cover_story.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-f6e83a0e54.creator: Steve Jurvetson
en-f6e83a0e54.story: Top-down photograph of a whole processed silicon wafer in a clear plastic carrier, covered with a grid of square chips of several sizes that throw off rainbow diffraction colours. Taken by Steve Jurvetson on 2014-02-05; title and caption call it the latest D-Wave wafer of quantum processors, photographed at the InQTel CEO Summit, and mention a TIME cover story, which is not in this frame. The chips are superconducting quantum annealers built from flux qubits; notice they are made with wafer-scale lithography like ordinary chips.
en-f6e83a0e54.title: File:Hot off the press — the latest D-Wave wafer of quantum processors and TIME cover story.jpg

en-f79ca6d139.attribution: “FMN Lab team (1)” by FMNLab, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FMN_Lab_team_%281%29.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-f79ca6d139.creator: FMNLab
en-f79ca6d139.story: Photograph in a yellow-lit cleanroom of three people in full cleanroom suits at an electron-microscope workstation, with the instrument column, load-lock and control desk visible; the screens face away, so no device images appear. Posted by FMNLab (2021-03-03); the caption says FMN Laboratory women engineers are studying electron-microscope images of Josephson junctions made in the cleanroom. Josephson junctions are the key nonlinear element of superconducting qubits, and microscopy checks their nanoscale dimensions; the yellow light protects light-sensitive resist.
en-f79ca6d139.title: File:FMN Lab team (1).jpg

en-f7d187472d.attribution: “JEOL Electron Beam Lithography (EBL) (48539692216)” by Simon Fraser University - Communications & Marketing, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:JEOL_Electron_Beam_Lithography_%28EBL%29_%2848539692216%29.jpg, CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)
en-f7d187472d.creator: Simon Fraser University - Communications & Marketing
en-f7d187472d.story: Photograph of a cleanroom electron-beam lithography tool made by JEOL: a stainless electron column on a cabinet base with a load-lock, surrounded by electronics cabinets and a large high-voltage tank, with two people in cleanroom suits at the controls. Photographed by Simon Fraser University Communications & Marketing in 2018. Electron-beam lithography writes nanometre-scale patterns directly with a focused electron beam and is the usual way to define small features such as Josephson junctions and quantum-dot gates; this is general fabrication equipment, not quantum-computing hardware.
en-f7d187472d.title: File:JEOL Electron Beam Lithography (EBL) (48539692216).jpg

en-fa0f87cef3.creator: Д.Ильин : vectorization
en-fa0f87cef3.story: Flat-colour cut-away drawing of a cylindrical Penning trap: three hollow coaxial electrodes, the two end cylinders biased positive by batteries against the grounded middle one, a uniform magnetic field B (green arrow) along the axis, and a blue cloud of charged particles held in the centre. Vectorised by Д.Ильин on 28 January 2025 from the Wikimedia Commons file 'Penning Trap.jpg' by Dhdpla. Penning traps hold ions with static electric plus magnetic fields instead of the radio-frequency fields of Paul traps; notice the E field lines that push particles back toward the centre along the axis while B keeps them from escaping sideways. The positive bias suits positive ions.
en-fa0f87cef3.title: File:Penning Trap1.svg

en-fa7229c37d.attribution: “Si-V diamond PL map” by Yan Liu, Gengxu Chen, Youying Rong, Liam Paul McGuinness, Fedor Jelezko, Syuto Tamura, Takashi Tanii, Tokuyuki Teraji, Shinobu Onoda, Takeshi Ohshima, Junichi Isoya, Takahiro Shinada, E Wu & Heping Zeng, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Si-V_diamond_PL_map.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-fa7229c37d.creator: Yan Liu, Gengxu Chen, Youying Rong, Liam Paul McGuinness, Fedor Jelezko, Syuto Tamura, Takashi Tanii, Tokuyuki Teraji, Shinobu Onoda, Takeshi Ohshima, Junichi Isoya, Takahiro Shinada, E Wu & Heping Zeng
en-fa7229c37d.story: Two false-colour confocal photoluminescence maps of a diamond: a 5 by 5 micrometre surface scan with about twenty bright spots, and a depth scan below it showing emitters roughly 1.5 micrometres under the surface (yellow dashed line). From a 2015 work by Yan Liu, Gengxu Chen, Fedor Jelezko and co-authors; the silicon-vacancy centres were created by implanting silicon ions. Each isolated spot is a single optically active defect, the kind of colour centre used as a spin qubit or photon source; notice how the depth scan locates one circled emitter.
en-fa7229c37d.title: File:Si-V diamond PL map.jpg

en-fa86ff17ad.attribution: “10 receivers inside an ALMA cryostat (ann23013a)” by S. Otarola, ALMA(ESO/NAOJ/NRAO), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:10_receivers_inside_an_ALMA_cryostat_%28ann23013a%29.tiff, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-fa86ff17ad.creator: S. Otarola, ALMA(ESO/NAOJ/NRAO)
en-fa86ff17ad.story: Top-down photograph into an open cryostat holding ten receiver cartridges on a copper cold plate, each tied down by copper-braid thermal links, inside a polished shield and aluminium vessel. By S. Otarola for the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO), uploaded in August 2023; the caption says it is the first ALMA antenna cryostat populated with ten receivers, covering 35 to 950 GHz. This is a radio-astronomy instrument, not quantum-computing hardware, but it shows the same cryogenic practice of stage plates, radiation shields and thermal anchoring.
en-fa86ff17ad.title: File:10 receivers inside an ALMA cryostat (ann23013a).tiff

en-fbc2943ab1.attribution: “Cryostat filled with liquid helium on an optical bench” by Alkamid, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cryostat_filled_with_liquid_helium_on_an_optical_bench.jpg, CC BY SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)
en-fbc2943ab1.creator: Alkamid
en-fbc2943ab1.story: Photograph of a small vertical liquid-helium cryostat hanging over an optical bench, with a frosted neck, labelled electrical connectors on the top head and an optical window at beam height; the pipe on the left is the helium exhaust. Taken by Alkamid in 2011. It is a general laboratory bath cryostat for optical measurements rather than quantum-computing hardware, but it illustrates the older wet-helium way of cooling a sample, with electrical feedthroughs and a window for laser access.
en-fbc2943ab1.title: File:Cryostat filled with liquid helium on an optical bench.jpg

en-fcf26177a1.attribution: “E-beam Marker” by Дагесян Саркис Арменакович, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:E-beam_Marker.JPG, CC BY SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
en-fcf26177a1.creator: Дагесян Саркис Арменакович
en-fcf26177a1.story: Tilted-view scanning electron micrograph of a cross-shaped metal alignment marker about 4 micrometres across, with lines near 100 nanometres wide meeting at the centre (scale bar 1 micrometre). Made by Дагесян Саркис Арменакович in 2015; the caption explains that such markers, written by electron-beam lithography, let later exposures on the same substrate be aligned to earlier ones. Multi-layer devices such as superconducting qubits and spin-qubit gate stacks depend on this layer-to-layer alignment; notice the fine crosshair used for registration.
en-fcf26177a1.title: File:E-beam Marker.JPG

en-fd66718c89.attribution: “Nanotechnology; Quantum Dots (5940486805)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nanotechnology%3B_Quantum_Dots_%285940486805%29.jpg
en-fd66718c89.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-fd66718c89.story: Two blue-tinted scanning electron micrographs of micropillars a few micrometres across (scale bar 1 micrometre): a smooth, layered pillar on top and a damaged pillar with its layers peeled and curled below. From the National Institute of Standards and Technology, dated 2007; the caption says well-made quantum dots, as in the top image, are a source of single photons for quantum communications. The layered walls are mirror stacks around an embedded quantum dot that channel emitted photons upward; the contrast shows how fabrication quality matters.
en-fd66718c89.title: File:Nanotechnology; Quantum Dots (5940486805).jpg

en-fe66f98255.attribution: “Continuous flow cryostat (continuous-flow)” by ESO/H.H.Heyer, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Continuous_flow_cryostat_%28continuous-flow%29.jpg, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
en-fe66f98255.creator: ESO/H.H.Heyer
en-fe66f98255.story: A studio photograph of a compact metal cryostat with electrical connectors, a side inlet tube, valves and a small window. It comes from ESO, photographed by H.H. Heyer in 1992; its description says the continuous-flow technique lets the cryostat be built very compact. In such a cryostat liquid helium flows in through a transfer line instead of sitting in a large bath, a simple way to cool detectors and samples. It does not show a link between refrigerators.
en-fe66f98255.title: File:Continuous flow cryostat (continuous-flow).jpg

en-ff67b67cac.attribution: “Microwave Apparatus (6029992084)” — National Institute of Standards and Technology, public domain (US federal work). Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Microwave_Apparatus_%286029992084%29.jpg
en-ff67b67cac.creator: National Institute of Standards and Technology
en-ff67b67cac.story: Composite photograph of a laboratory apparatus: a small glass vacuum chamber between two large copper-wire coils on an optical breadboard, lit green by an LED for visual effect, with an ultraviolet laser beam colourised blue. From the National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2011; the caption says a pair of ions is trapped by electric fields and manipulated with microwaves inside the chamber. It illustrates trapped-ion qubits controlled by microwaves instead of laser gates; the ions themselves are far too small to see here.

jn-04e83bf0e4.story: A four-part figure of a 30-metre cryogenic link between two refrigerators. Panel (a) is a computer model of the whole set-up: a long horizontal tube joins dilution refrigerators A and B, each holding a superconducting qubit circuit (insets), with a central cooling unit and support stands. Panels (b)–(d) are photographs from end A, the centre and end B, showing the aluminium tube running along a basement corridor on frames. From Nature (2023), 'Loophole-free Bell inequality violation with superconducting circuits', by Simon Storz and co-authors. The waveguide inside is kept below 50 mK over the whole distance, so microwave photons can link qubits in separate cryostats.

jn-0645cd20e5.story: A five-panel theory figure on the dynamics of a chain of 150 Rydberg atoms. Panel (b) is a space-time map of the Rydberg occupation ⟨n_i(t)⟩ for sites 40-100: the regular checkerboard is the periodic revival of a 'scarred' state, and a dashed line follows a mobile defect, a quasi-soliton; panel (c) isolates its density perturbation, moving mostly to the right. Panels (a) and (d) draw the three-site cells that make up the states, and panel (e) plots the decaying fidelity revivals. It is Figure 2 of Kerschbaumer, Desaules, Ljubotina and Serbyn, Nature Communications (2026). It is simulated, not measured, analog Rydberg evolution.

jn-18cb1d8e5f.story: Three matching drawings of a dilution refrigerator wired to read out a superconducting qubit. In (a) the usual microwave chain runs down the stages: attenuated input lines, filters, circulators, a parametric amplifier and a further amplifier; in (b) the output chain is replaced by an electro-optic transducer that sends the signal up an optical fibre; in (c) two fibres and one transducer do the whole job and every cryogenic microwave part is gone. From Nature Physics (2025), 'All-optical superconducting qubit readout', by Georg Arnold, Johannes M. Fink and co-authors. It shows why microwave–optical transducers matter for wiring large cryogenic processors; it is a drawing.

From a 2026 Nature Communications paper by Friederike Butt, Ivan Pogorelov, Thomas Monz, Markus Müller and co-authors. It shows why fast unconditional reset matters: in measurement-free schemes it is the only way entropy leaves the processor.

jn-1a25a181e2.story: Plot of simulated error thresholds, drawn by computer. From Nature Communications (2023), 'Fusion-based quantum computation', by Sara Bartolucci, Terry Rudolph, Chris Sparrow and colleagues. It compares two fusion networks, '6-ring' and '4-star', by the combinations of fusion erasure probability and measurement error probability they can still correct: the shaded areas below each line. The 6-ring network tolerates about 12% erasure when measurements are perfect, far more than the 4-star network's about 7%. Fusion-based quantum computing builds its code from small entangled photon states joined by fusion measurements.

jn-1c41c3c6a1.story: Three-panel schematic of a fast, unconditional reset for superconducting qubits: a level diagram in which modulating the qubit frequency opens a sideband that swaps the qubit's excitation into its readout resonator, where it leaks away at rate κ_r; a circuit of three flux-tunable transmon qubits, each with a readout resonator and Purcell filter on a shared amplified feedline; and the reset pulse, generated by an arbitrary waveform generator and attenuated by 30 dB, modulating the qubit on its flux curve. From a 2021 Nature Communications paper by Yu Zhou, Shengyu Zhang and co-authors. Resetting without measurement in a few hundred nanoseconds shortens every error-correction cycle.

Each marker is one two-dimensional local phase-flip code, coloured by the weight of its checks, plotted as its overhead gain over the simple repetition code (kd/n) against code distance d; the repetition codes sit flat at 1, while the best local codes reach about 5–7 at d = 20–30, under the theoretical bound for local codes and below the best non-local classical codes. jn-bb5a9bde90.story: Wide paper figure: a soft render of photonic-crystal cavities on a chip, a ball-and-stick drawing of an atomic defect, a level scheme and a measured spectrum. From Nature Communications (2024), 'Cavity-enhanced single artificial atoms in silicon', by Valeria Saggio, Carlos Errando-Herranz, Dirk Englund and colleagues. The defect is a G-centre: two carbon atoms replacing silicon with a silicon atom squeezed between them. Excited by green 532 nm light, it emits at 1279 nm in the telecom O band, and the cavity collects that light upward. Notice the single sharp line in the spectrum from one centre. The top panel is a drawing, not a photograph.

Two distributed-feedback lasers are locked, through electro-optic modulators, to modes of one 'super stable' V-shaped optical cavity, shown in a small photograph; their outputs, one optionally shifted by a Mach–Zehnder modulator and a fibre amplifier, are mixed on a photomixer that radiates terahertz waves at their difference frequency. From Nature Communications (2023), 'Frequency stable and low phase noise THz synthesis for precision spectroscopy', by Léo Djevahirdjian, Samir Kassi and co-authors. It illustrates the ultra-stable reference cavities used to narrow lasers; the application is classical spectroscopy, not a quantum processor.

From Light: Science & Applications (2026), 'Two-photon interference between independent atomic and quantum dot single-photon sources for hybrid quantum network', by Kyu-Young Kim, Han Seb Moon and colleagues. Heralded photons from warm caesium atoms (a) and photons from an indium-arsenide quantum dot in a circular Bragg-grating cavity, cooled in a cryostat (b), meet on a beam splitter (c). jn-d4d8312809.story: A drawn concept diagram with a small photograph of the qubit's sample board. In the real-time loop, observations from a superconducting transmon qubit go to a reinforcement-learning agent, a neural network that the caption places on a field-programmable gate array; each cycle it picks an action: terminate, flip or idle. Outside the loop, a PC receives observations and actions, calculates rewards, optimises the strategy and returns updated network parameters. From Nature Communications (2023), 'Realizing a deep reinforcement learning agent for real-time quantum feedback', by Kevin Reuer, Andreas Wallraff, Christopher Eichler and colleagues. Notice the split: decisions are made inside the control loop, training happens on the PC.

mr-62b6a03af7.story: A fluorescence image of 98 trapped atomic ions, seen as cyan spots over a drawn grey outline of the trap electrodes: a large ring labelled memory, an X-shaped junction, and parallel straight legs labelled processor, where gates run. Only the outer enclosure is visible: the cryostats, wiring and Heron processors are hidden inside.
mr-df8af6ffdb.title: IBM Quantum System Two (photo 1)

mr-e073c8fc70.attribution: “Gold Cryostat 8K-4” by Onri Jay Benally, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gold_Cryostat_8K-4.png, CC BY SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/)
mr-e073c8fc70.creator: Onri Jay Benally
mr-e073c8fc70.story: A computer render made in Blender, not a photograph, of the gold-coloured inner 'chandelier' of a dilution refrigerator on black: five stacked round plates of shrinking diameter joined by rods, with lines running between them and coiled and cylindrical parts at two levels. Made by Onri Jay Benally and uploaded to Wikimedia Commons in February 2024. It shows the layered build of the cryostat that cools superconducting qubits: each plate is a colder temperature stage, and wiring is anchored at each on its way down.
mr-e073c8fc70.title: File:Gold Cryostat 8K-4.png

mr-e3050393af.attribution: MON-F5 — Specific cooling power vs temperature — Raveh Neeman (Qodeh), CC BY 4.0 (Superconductor Electronics Monitor 2026 v1.1, © Raveh Neeman 2026). https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22537315
mr-e3050393af.creator: Raveh Neeman (Qodeh)
mr-e3050393af.story: A log–log data plot of the specific power of cryogenic refrigeration (watts from the wall per watt of heat removed) against cold temperature, from 20 mK to 80 K: blue median points with range bars follow a dashed empirical fit, above a grey Carnot-limit curve. Made by Raveh Neeman (Qodeh) as chart MON-F5, dated September 2026. It shows the cooling tax of each cryogenic layer: the colder the stage, the more wall power each watt of cooling costs; note the 250–500 W/W baseline marked for large plants.
mr-e3050393af.title: MON-F5 — Specific cooling power vs temperature

mr-e318c9275b.story: Close-up photograph of part of the vacuum chamber of a Pasqal neutral-atom processor: a polished stainless-steel flange and viewport held by a bolt, with bare copper coil windings across the top and a green optical mount at lower left. It comes from Pasqal's media kit (2025). Such machines hold rubidium atoms inside ultra-high vacuum so background gas does not knock them out; notice the viewport, through which laser and imaging light pass, and the coils that make magnetic fields. The atoms themselves are not visible.
mr-e318c9275b.title: Pasqal's vacuum chamber

From Chuan-Hong Liu et al. (arXiv, 2023), for a transmon qubit driven by single-flux-quantum (SFQ) pulses instead of microwaves. mr-e3e3db3f5f.attribution: MON-F7 — Energy vs delay with 1 mm interconnect — Raveh Neeman (Qodeh), CC BY 4.0 (Superconductor Electronics Monitor 2026 v1.1, © Raveh Neeman 2026). https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22537315
mr-e3e3db3f5f.creator: Raveh Neeman (Qodeh)
mr-e3e3db3f5f.story: Log-log data plot of energy against delay for sending a signal over 1 mm of interconnect. Made by Raveh Neeman (Qodeh), the Map's author, on 6 September 2026, as chart MON-F6 with wire cost added. Grey room-temperature options such as CMOS sit at 10^-15 to 10^-12 J; blue superconducting lines at 4.2 K (reciprocal-quantum-logic transmission lines, adiabatic quantum-flux-parametron logic) sit near 10^-21 to 10^-18 J. Notice the brown points, which multiply each superconducting value by the ×6,965 refrigeration factor to show the real cost of cooling.
mr-e3e3db3f5f.title: MON-F7 — Energy vs delay with 1 mm interconnect

mr-e437ca0f48.cite_as: Fig. 1 — Representative single-shot image of single caesium atoms across an 11,998-site tweezer array — Hannah J. Manetsch, Gyohei Nomura, Elie Bataille, Kon H. Leung, Xudong Lv, Manuel Endres, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09641-4
mr-e437ca0f48.creator: Hannah J. Manetsch, Gyohei Nomura, Elie Bataille, Kon H. Leung, Xudong Lv, Manuel Endres
mr-e437ca0f48.story: Fluorescence image (panel a of Fig. 1) of single caesium atoms, each a bright spot on a square grid of optical-tweezer sites, filling a roughly circular region on black. It is from 'A tweezer array with 6,100 highly coherent atomic qubits' by Hannah J. Manetsch, Manuel Endres and colleagues (Caltech), Nature, September 2025. mr-f5925dd883.story: An optical microscope image of a superconducting chip: a one-volt Josephson voltage standard built from an array of 3020 Josephson junctions in twelve rows, marked 'NBS BOULDER COLORADO'. It was made by the National Bureau of Standards (now NIST), dated 1985, and operates at liquid-helium temperatures. It is a classical metrology device, not a qubit chip, but uses the same superconducting Josephson junctions found in superconducting qubits; notice the tapered finline at left that feeds microwaves into the meandering junction chains.
